C0001.name: extended reality
C0001.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

C0002.name: virtual reality
C0002.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

C0003.name: augmented reality
C0003.definition: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

C0004.name: mixed reality
C0004.definition: Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.

C0005.name: headset
C0005.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

C0008.name: immersive technology
C0008.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

C0009.name: immersive experience
C0009.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

C0010.name: reality-virtuality continuum
C0010.definition: The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real.

C0011.name: augmented virtuality
C0011.definition: Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.

C0056.name: virtual reality system
C0056.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

C0057.name: non-immersive virtual reality system
C0057.definition: From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

C0060.name: computer application
C0060.definition: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

C0061.name: virtual environment
C0061.definition: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

C0062.name: computer system
C0062.definition: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) application is a regular computer system or software that completely takes away the user's attention, so the user is psychologically engaged and may not experience the real world, although the user's eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open and the user is physically attached to the real world.

C0106.name: marker-based augmented reality application
C0106.definition: Augmented reality (AR) applications are categorized by technology rather than by psychological or immersive experience into two broad categories: marker-based augmented reality applications and markerless augmented reality applications.

C0107.name: markerless augmented reality application
C0107.definition: Augmented reality (AR) applications are categorized by technology rather than by psychological or immersive experience into two broad categories: marker-based augmented reality applications and markerless augmented reality applications.

C0108.name: location-based markerless augmented reality application
C0108.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications can have four subcategories: location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based.

C0109.name: superimposition-based markerless augmented reality application
C0109.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications can have four subcategories: location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based.

C0110.name: projection-based markerless augmented reality application

C0111.name: outlining-based markerless augmented reality application
C0111.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications can have four subcategories: location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based.

C0112.name: marker
C0112.definition: Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.

C0113.name: quick response code
C0113.definition: Markers used in marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications include quick response (QR) codes, simple color codes, color bars, and fiducial markers.

C0114.name: simple color code
C0114.definition: Markers used in marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications include quick response (QR) codes, simple color codes, color bars, and fiducial markers.

C0115.name: color bar
C0115.definition: Markers used in marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications include quick response (QR) codes, simple color codes, color bars, and fiducial markers.

C0116.name: fiducial marker
C0116.definition: Markers used in marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications include quick response (QR) codes, simple color codes, color bars, and fiducial markers.

C0117.name: computer vision technique
C0117.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications are more versatile than marker-based augmented reality applications, do not require physical markers, can use computer vision techniques, and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects.

C0118.name: location sensor
C0118.definition: Location-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications rely on a location sensor, such as a global positioning system (GPS) sensor, to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame, and digital content is augmented on the real-world view when the user is at a specific location.

C0119.name: global positioning system
C0119.definition: Sensing approaches that do not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories include acoustic sensing and the global positioning system (GPS).

C0120.name: reference frame
C0120.definition: Location-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications rely on a location sensor, such as a global positioning system (GPS) sensor, to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame, and digital content is augmented on the real-world view when the user is at a specific location.

C0121.name: light projector
C0121.definition: Projection-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications use light projectors to project digital graphics, digital characters, or other digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space, such as in holographic projection.

C0122.name: holographic projection
C0122.definition: Projection-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications use light projectors to project digital graphics, digital characters, or other digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space, such as in holographic projection.

C0123.name: object recognition
C0123.definition: Outlining-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications use object recognition to recreate the user's immediate surroundings and digitally enhance the view, for example by showing cars around a driver that are not clearly visible in low-light conditions.

C0124.name: virtual reality system category
C0124.definition: Virtual reality (VR) system categories are based on the experience or psychological aspect, and comprise non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems.

C0125.name: non-immersive system
C0125.definition: Virtual reality (VR) system categories are based on the experience or psychological aspect, and comprise non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems.

C0126.name: semi-immersive system
C0126.definition: Virtual reality (VR) system categories are based on the experience or psychological aspect, and comprise non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems.

C0127.name: fully immersive system
C0127.definition: Virtual reality (VR) system categories are based on the experience or psychological aspect, and comprise non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems.

C0128.name: augmented reality system category
C0128.definition: Augmented reality (AR) system categories are based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy the systems rather than on the psychological aspect, and broadly comprise marker-based and markerless systems.

C0129.name: marker-based augmented reality system
C0129.definition: Augmented reality (AR) system categories are based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy the systems rather than on the psychological aspect, and broadly comprise marker-based and markerless systems.

C0130.name: markerless augmented reality system
C0130.definition: Augmented reality (AR) system categories are based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy the systems rather than on the psychological aspect, and broadly comprise marker-based and markerless systems.

C0131.name: markerless augmented reality technique
C0131.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) techniques are used to overcome the difficulty of maintaining markers in marker-based systems.

C0132.name: computer vision
C0132.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) techniques rely primarily on computer vision and may rely on other sensors, such as global positioning system (GPS) sensors, in location-based applications.

C0133.name: location-based application
C0133.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) techniques rely primarily on computer vision and may rely on other sensors, such as global positioning system (GPS) sensors, in location-based applications.

C0134.name: computer vision-based augmented reality application
C0134.definition: Computer vision-based augmented reality (AR) applications include superimposition-based and outline-based applications.

C0135.name: superimposition-based application
C0135.definition: Computer vision-based augmented reality (AR) applications include superimposition-based and outline-based applications.

C0136.name: outline-based application
C0136.definition: Computer vision-based augmented reality (AR) applications include superimposition-based and outline-based applications.

C0137.name: projection-based technique
C0137.definition: Projection-based techniques, such as holographic projection, can be used in augmented reality (AR) application development.

C0138.name: virtual reality application
C0138.definition: Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) have broadly similar application domains, but VR applications are characterized as immersive, whereas AR applications emphasize augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than immersive applications.

C0139.name: virtual
C0139.definition: The term virtual means, according to Webster's New Universal Dictionary, being in essence or effect but not in fact, that is, something that is there but cannot be attributed to any factual things.

C0140.name: reality
C0140.definition: The term reality is defined in dictionary terms as the state or quality of being real, as something that exists independently of ideas concerning it, or as something that constitutes a real or actual thing as distinguished from something merely apparent.

C0141.name: artificial environment
C0141.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

C0142.name: sensory experience
C0142.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

C0143.name: computer-generated stimuli
C0143.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

C0144.name: user action

C0145.name: real time
C0145.definition: An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

C0146.name: user interaction
C0146.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

C0147.name: interaction
C0147.definition: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.

C0148.name: computer-aided design system
C0148.definition: A computer-aided design (CAD) system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it supports a virtual environment and interaction, it does not support an immersive experience, since the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the computer screen.

C0149.name: video conferencing system
C0149.definition: A video conferencing system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it is interactive, it is not a virtual environment or an immersive experience, since it presents a real-world environment in real time through a screen and the user remains in the real world, with the screen only aiding interaction.

C0150.name: three-dimensional movie experience
C0150.definition: A three-dimensional (3D) movie experience is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it provides a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, it is not interactive, as the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content.

C0151.name: augmented reality system
C0151.definition: The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

C0152.name: three-dimensional
C0152.definition: The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

C0153.name: sensory organ
C0153.definition: For each of the six senses, receptors are part of the sensory organs, and these receptors receive stimuli depending on the sensory organ.

C0154.name: physical environment
C0154.definition: The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

C0155.name: early era
C0155.definition: The historical evolution of virtual reality is broadly divided into four mostly distinct, sometimes overlapping phases: the early era, which existed before the advent of digital computers, the formative years from roughly 1950 to 1990, the modern phase from 1991 to 2015, and the current growth phase from roughly 2016 onwards.

C0160.definition: The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

C0161.name: Sir Charles Wheatstone
C0161.definition: Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 demonstration of a stereoscopic device established, for the first time in recorded history, that the human brain can process two-dimensional (2D) images as three-dimensional (3D) objects, and this demonstration is roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience.

C0162.name: stereoscopic device

C0165.name: display device
C0165.definition: In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

C0166.name: stereoscopic vision
C0166.definition: In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

C0167.name: three-dimensional space

C0168.name: David Brewster
C0168.definition: David Brewster's 1860 compact-sized stereoscope was an early form of stereoscopic display that created the illusion of depth in viewed images and, as an advancement over Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 stereoscopic device, is roughly considered another step toward practical immersive experiences.

C0169.name: stereoscope

Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

C0175.name: formative years of virtual reality
C0175.definition: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

C0176.name: computer display
C0176.definition: In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.

C0201.name: field of view
C0201.definition: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.

C0202.name: data glove

C0204.name: CAVE system

C0221.definition: In the evolution of virtual reality (VR), the growth phase is the last and continuing phase and began roughly in 2016, when many well-known companies released commercial virtual reality (VR) headsets that made immersive experiences affordable to a large population and spurred growth in the field.

C0222.definition: In virtual reality (VR) headsets, light emitted from the displays reaches the retina and is guided by engineered lenses in the headset and natural lenses in the eye, a combined system that helps the user perceive immersive visual content.

C0223.name: Oculus Rift version 1

C0234.name: immersive display
C0234.definition: The virtual reality (VR) growth phase is a continuing phase because more developments, including better headsets, better immersive displays, and better input devices, will happen, will continue, and may accelerate because there is going to be huge demand.

C0235.name: experimental phase
C0235.definition: The historical evolution of augmented reality (AR) can be broadly divided into four phases that may sometimes overlap, unlike the phases of virtual reality: the experimental phase before the 1980s, the basic research phase from the 1980s to the mid-1990s, the tools or applications phase from the mid-1990s to 2007, and the commercial application phase from 2007 to the present.

C0236.name: basic research phase
C0236.definition: The historical evolution of augmented reality (AR) can be broadly divided into four phases that may sometimes overlap, unlike the phases of virtual reality: the experimental phase before the 1980s, the basic research phase from the 1980s to the mid-1990s, the tools or applications phase from the mid-1990s to 2007, and the commercial application phase from 2007 to the present.

C0237.name: tools or applications phase
C0237.definition: The historical evolution of augmented reality (AR) can be broadly divided into four phases that may sometimes overlap, unlike the phases of virtual reality: the experimental phase before the 1980s, the basic research phase from the 1980s to the mid-1990s, the tools or applications phase from the mid-1990s to 2007, and the commercial application phase from 2007 to the present.

C0238.name: commercial application phase

C0239.name: tracking
C0239.definition: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

C0240.name: interaction technique
C0240.definition: The phases of augmented reality (AR) evolution are characterized as follows: the experimental phase involved early experimentation that defined the concepts and showed the types of technology required for AR; the basic research phase involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices; the tools or applications phase involved developing or exploring early applications and exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques, usability of such applications, and design theory for AR; and the commercial application phase involved widespread AR availability and newer applications appearing in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.

C0241.name: usability
C0241.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

C0242.name: design theory
C0242.definition: The phases of augmented reality (AR) evolution are characterized as follows: the experimental phase involved early experimentation that defined the concepts and showed the types of technology required for AR; the basic research phase involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices; the tools or applications phase involved developing or exploring early applications and exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques, usability of such applications, and design theory for AR; and the commercial application phase involved widespread AR availability and newer applications appearing in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.

C0243.name: Ivan Sutherland
C0243.definition: Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first truly computer-generated augmented reality (AR) prototype in 1968.

C0244.name: Bob Sproull
C0244.definition: Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first truly computer-generated augmented reality (AR) prototype in 1968.

C0245.name: Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality prototype
C0245.definition: Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first truly computer-generated augmented reality (AR) prototype in 1968.

C0246.name: cathode ray tube
C0246.definition: The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker.

C0247.name: optical see-through head-mounted display
C0247.definition: The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker.

C0248.name: mechanical tracking system
C0248.definition: The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker.

C0249.name: PDP-11 computer
C0249.definition: The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker.

C0250.name: graphics hardware
C0250.definition: The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker.

C0251.name: ultrasonic tracker
C0251.definition: The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker.

C0252.name: super cockpit program
C0252.definition: Tom Furness at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base began research on the United States (US) Air Force super cockpit program, which was a major research program that produced technologies relevant to augmented reality (AR).

C0253.name: super cockpit prototype
C0253.definition: In the super cockpit prototype, a pilot wearing a head-mounted display (HMD) in the aircraft cockpit saw computer-generated imagery superimposed over the real-world view in daylight and saw computer-generated imagery replace the real-world view at night or in bad weather.

C0254.name: head-mounted augmented reality display
C0254.definition: The early augmented reality (AR) experiments led to head-mounted augmented reality displays used in modern aircraft, to virtual reality (VR) displays such as the VIVED head-mounted display (HMD), and to input and tracking hardware.

C0255.name: virtual reality display
C0255.definition: The early augmented reality (AR) experiments led to head-mounted augmented reality displays used in modern aircraft, to virtual reality (VR) displays such as the VIVED head-mounted display (HMD), and to input and tracking hardware.

C0256.name: VIVED head-mounted display
C0256.definition: The early augmented reality (AR) experiments led to head-mounted augmented reality displays used in modern aircraft, to virtual reality (VR) displays such as the VIVED head-mounted display (HMD), and to input and tracking hardware.

C0257.name: input hardware
C0257.definition: The early augmented reality (AR) experiments led to head-mounted augmented reality displays used in modern aircraft, to virtual reality (VR) displays such as the VIVED head-mounted display (HMD), and to input and tracking hardware.

C0258.name: tracking hardware
C0258.definition: The early augmented reality (AR) experiments led to head-mounted augmented reality displays used in modern aircraft, to virtual reality (VR) displays such as the VIVED head-mounted display (HMD), and to input and tracking hardware.

C0259.name: experimentation phase
C0259.definition: The basic research phase of augmented reality (AR) came after the experimentation phase and included much influential work in the 1990s that shaped the field of augmented reality.

C0260.name: Tom Caudell
C0260.definition: Tom Caudell is often credited with coining the phrase augmented reality (AR) because he published the first academic article containing the term AR in 1992.

C0261.name: registration tracking
C0261.definition: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research projects at the University of North Carolina included registration tracking techniques in 1993 and 1994, early research in 1995 and 1996 on see-through head-mounted displays typically used in AR, and several applications developed alongside the basic research.

C0262.name: see-through head-mounted display
C0262.definition: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research projects at the University of North Carolina included registration tracking techniques in 1993 and 1994, early research in 1995 and 1996 on see-through head-mounted displays typically used in AR, and several applications developed alongside the basic research.

C0263.name: Columbia University
C0263.definition: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at Columbia University included one of the first academic papers on AR describing the KARMA system in 1993, work in 1993 on AR interaction methods, that is, how to interact with augmented digital content, and some publications on mobile AR systems in 1997.

C0264.name: KARMA system
C0264.definition: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at Columbia University included one of the first academic papers on AR describing the KARMA system in 1993, work in 1993 on AR interaction methods, that is, how to interact with augmented digital content, and some publications on mobile AR systems in 1997.

C0265.name: augmented reality interaction method
C0265.definition: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at Columbia University included one of the first academic papers on AR describing the KARMA system in 1993, work in 1993 on AR interaction methods, that is, how to interact with augmented digital content, and some publications on mobile AR systems in 1997.

C0266.name: mobile augmented reality system
C0266.definition: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at Columbia University included one of the first academic papers on AR describing the KARMA system in 1993, work in 1993 on AR interaction methods, that is, how to interact with augmented digital content, and some publications on mobile AR systems in 1997.

C0267.name: University of Toronto
C0267.definition: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at the University of Toronto included overlaying virtual cues on stereoscopic video from 1991 to 1993 and work on AR applications from 1992 to 1993.

C0268.name: stereoscopic video
C0268.definition: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at the University of Toronto included overlaying virtual cues on stereoscopic video from 1991 to 1993 and work on AR applications from 1992 to 1993.

C0269.name: Chameleon
C0269.definition: Chameleon was an early handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system developed in 1993 that allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display (LCD) over a piece of paper and see virtual content.

C0270.name: liquid-crystal display
C0270.definition: Chameleon was an early handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system developed in 1993 that allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display (LCD) over a piece of paper and see virtual content.

C0271.name: NaviCam
C0271.definition: NaviCam by Rekimoto was a handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system developed in 1995 that superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld and head-mounted displays.

C0272.name: shared augmented reality content
C0272.definition: Work during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase of augmented reality (AR) included systems that allowed people in the same location to see and interact with shared augmented reality content.

C0273.name: medical application
C0273.definition: Medical applications developed during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase of augmented reality (AR) included visualization of laparoscopic surgery, X-ray visualization in a patient's body, and image-guided surgery.

C0274.name: visualization of laparoscopic surgery
C0274.definition: Medical applications developed during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase of augmented reality (AR) included visualization of laparoscopic surgery, X-ray visualization in a patient's body, and image-guided surgery.

C0275.name: x-ray visualization
C0275.definition: Medical applications developed during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase of augmented reality (AR) included visualization of laparoscopic surgery, X-ray visualization in a patient's body, and image-guided surgery.

C0276.name: image-guided surgery
C0276.definition: Medical applications developed during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase of augmented reality (AR) included visualization of laparoscopic surgery, X-ray visualization in a patient's body, and image-guided surgery.

C0277.name: wearable computing
C0277.definition: From the mid-1990s, wearable computing using head-mounted displays (HMDs) emerged as a related research area in augmented reality (AR), although it had existed earlier and people began paying more attention to such head-mounted displays.

C0278.name: real-world marker
C0278.definition: In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

C0279.name: three-dimensional registration
C0279.definition: In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

C0280.name: wearable computer
C0280.definition: In 1997, wearable computers with global positioning system (GPS) tracking produced outdoor augmented reality (AR) interfaces that showed information in place in the real world, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

C0281.name: outdoor augmented reality interface
C0281.definition: In 1997, wearable computers with global positioning system (GPS) tracking produced outdoor augmented reality (AR) interfaces that showed information in place in the real world, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

C0282.name: outdoor wearable augmented reality application
C0282.definition: In 2002 and 2003, outdoor wearable augmented reality (AR) applications included terrestrial navigation, on-site viewing and creation of computer-aided design (CAD) models, and game playing.

C0283.name: terrestrial navigation
C0283.definition: In 2002 and 2003, outdoor wearable augmented reality (AR) applications included terrestrial navigation, on-site viewing and creation of computer-aided design (CAD) models, and game playing.

C0284.name: computer-aided design
C0284.definition: In 2002 and 2003, outdoor wearable augmented reality (AR) applications included terrestrial navigation, on-site viewing and creation of computer-aided design (CAD) models, and game playing.

C0285.name: model
C0285.definition: In 2002 and 2003, outdoor wearable augmented reality (AR) applications included terrestrial navigation, on-site viewing and creation of computer-aided design (CAD) models, and game playing.

C0286.name: game playing
C0286.definition: In 2002 and 2003, outdoor wearable augmented reality (AR) applications included terrestrial navigation, on-site viewing and creation of computer-aided design (CAD) models, and game playing.

C0287.name: wearable augmented reality system
C0287.definition: The wearable augmented reality (AR) systems being developed in 2002 and 2003 were bulky and difficult to use because of the size of their custom computer hardware, batteries, tracking sensors, and display hardware, and their setups were technically wearable computers with a headset, a computer carried in a backpack, and different input devices.

C0288.name: custom computer hardware
C0288.definition: The wearable augmented reality (AR) systems being developed in 2002 and 2003 were bulky and difficult to use because of the size of their custom computer hardware, batteries, tracking sensors, and display hardware, and their setups were technically wearable computers with a headset, a computer carried in a backpack, and different input devices.

C0291.name: display hardware
C0291.definition: The wearable augmented reality (AR) systems being developed in 2002 and 2003 were bulky and difficult to use because of the size of their custom computer hardware, batteries, tracking sensors, and display hardware, and their setups were technically wearable computers with a headset, a computer carried in a backpack, and different input devices.

C0292.name: viewpoint tracking
C0292.definition: Viewpoint tracking was one of the most significant challenges of augmented reality (AR), and it was addressed so that three-dimensional registration of content could happen accurately.

C0293.name: computer-vision tracking system
C0293.definition: In 1996, Rekimoto developed a simple computer-vision tracking system based on a printed matrix that evolved into the cyber code system, as part of software that could enable an augmented reality (AR) system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0294.name: printed matrix
C0294.definition: In 1996, Rekimoto developed a simple computer-vision tracking system based on a printed matrix that evolved into the cyber code system, as part of software that could enable an augmented reality (AR) system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0295.name: cyber code system
C0295.definition: In 1996, Rekimoto developed a simple computer-vision tracking system based on a printed matrix that evolved into the cyber code system, as part of software that could enable an augmented reality (AR) system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0296.name: AR Toolkit
C0296.definition: In 1999, Kato and Billinghurst developed the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit tracking library, which was released in 2000 as open-source software, provided real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker, and could enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0297.name: open-source software
C0297.definition: In 1999, Kato and Billinghurst developed the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit tracking library, which was released in 2000 as open-source software, provided real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker, and could enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0298.name: real-time computer-vision tracking
C0298.definition: In 1999, Kato and Billinghurst developed the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit tracking library, which was released in 2000 as open-source software, provided real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker, and could enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0299.name: square marker
C0299.definition: In 1999, Kato and Billinghurst developed the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit tracking library, which was released in 2000 as open-source software, provided real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker, and could enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

C0300.name: mobile-phone based augmented reality application
C0300.definition: In 2004, the first mobile-phone based augmented reality (AR) application was demonstrated and the AR Toolkit was ported to mobile phones, and although early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones, people still tried to use early mobile phones to develop mobile-based augmented reality applications.

C0301.name: smartphone
C0301.definition: In 2004, the first mobile-phone based augmented reality (AR) application was demonstrated and the AR Toolkit was ported to mobile phones, and although early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones, people still tried to use early mobile phones to develop mobile-based augmented reality applications.

C0302.name: mobile-based augmented reality application
C0302.definition: In 2004, the first mobile-phone based augmented reality (AR) application was demonstrated and the AR Toolkit was ported to mobile phones, and although early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones, people still tried to use early mobile phones to develop mobile-based augmented reality applications.

C0303.name: Sony PlayStation 3
C0303.definition: The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) began in October 2007 with the release of the Sony PlayStation 3-based game The Eye of Judgment, one of the first widely used consumer AR experiences, and with its launch such AR experiences started becoming very popular after AR had previously been neither very popular nor easily available.

C0304.name: The Eye of Judgment
C0304.definition: The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) began in October 2007 with the release of the Sony PlayStation 3-based game The Eye of Judgment, one of the first widely used consumer AR experiences, and with its launch such AR experiences started becoming very popular after AR had previously been neither very popular nor easily available.

C0305.name: Adobe Flash
C0305.definition: Adobe Flash is a popular authoring tool for creating prototypes with multimedia content for web and desktop platforms and can be used, through augmented reality (AR) plugins such as FLAR Toolkit or Flash AR Manager (FLAR Manager), to prototype desktop and mobile augmented reality experiences.

C0306.name: augmented reality authoring tools
C0306.definition: The main factors behind the move of augmented reality (AR) from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology in 2009 were Adobe Flash-based AR authoring tools that made experiencing AR through web browsers possible from 2008, smartphone-based AR because the era of smartphones had begun by then, and the use of AR in global marketing campaigns to increase sales and make products popular.

C0307.name: web browser
C0307.definition: The main factors behind the move of augmented reality (AR) from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology in 2009 were Adobe Flash-based AR authoring tools that made experiencing AR through web browsers possible from 2008, smartphone-based AR because the era of smartphones had begun by then, and the use of AR in global marketing campaigns to increase sales and make products popular.

C0308.name: smartphone-based augmented reality
C0308.definition: The main factors behind the move of augmented reality (AR) from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology in 2009 were Adobe Flash-based AR authoring tools that made experiencing AR through web browsers possible from 2008, smartphone-based AR because the era of smartphones had begun by then, and the use of AR in global marketing campaigns to increase sales and make products popular.

C0309.name: software development kit
C0309.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

C0310.name: ARKit
C0310.definition: Starting in 2017, Apple launched the augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) ARKit for AR system development, and Google released ARCore for Android operating system (OS) or Android platforms; these launches further stimulated AR growth by enabling many developers to create AR applications and increasing the number of AR applications from simple to complex ones.

C0311.name: Google
C0311.definition: Starting in 2017, Apple launched the augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) ARKit for AR system development, and Google released ARCore for Android operating system (OS) or Android platforms; these launches further stimulated AR growth by enabling many developers to create AR applications and increasing the number of AR applications from simple to complex ones.

C0312.name: ARCore
C0312.definition: Starting in 2017, Apple launched the augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) ARKit for AR system development, and Google released ARCore for Android operating system (OS) or Android platforms; these launches further stimulated AR growth by enabling many developers to create AR applications and increasing the number of AR applications from simple to complex ones.

C0313.name: Android operating system
C0313.definition: Starting in 2017, Apple launched the augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) ARKit for AR system development, and Google released ARCore for Android operating system (OS) or Android platforms; these launches further stimulated AR growth by enabling many developers to create AR applications and increasing the number of AR applications from simple to complex ones.

C0314.name: wearable device
C0314.definition: The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) is still ongoing and is expected to continue growing, with more AR applications and tools, hardware improvements in wearable devices, mobile devices, and holographic projection-based devices, and the development of algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and computer vision technologies making three-dimensional (3D) tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices.

C0315.name: mobile device
C0315.definition: The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) is still ongoing and is expected to continue growing, with more AR applications and tools, hardware improvements in wearable devices, mobile devices, and holographic projection-based devices, and the development of algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and computer vision technologies making three-dimensional (3D) tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices.

C0316.name: holographic projection-based device
C0316.definition: The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) is still ongoing and is expected to continue growing, with more AR applications and tools, hardware improvements in wearable devices, mobile devices, and holographic projection-based devices, and the development of algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and computer vision technologies making three-dimensional (3D) tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices.

C0317.name: algorithm
C0317.definition: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

C0318.name: three-dimensional tracking
C0318.definition: The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) is still ongoing and is expected to continue growing, with more AR applications and tools, hardware improvements in wearable devices, mobile devices, and holographic projection-based devices, and the development of algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and computer vision technologies making three-dimensional (3D) tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices.

C0319.name: registration
C0319.definition: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

C0320.name: sensory stimuli
C0320.definition: The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

C0321.name: technological issue
C0321.definition: There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

C0322.name: psychological issue
C0322.definition: There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

C0323.name: human factors
C0323.definition: Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.

C0324.name: presence
C0324.definition: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

C0325.name: extensive
C0325.definition: In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

C0326.name: sensory modality
C0326.definition: Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is.

C0327.name: matching
C0327.definition: In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

C0328.name: surrounding
C0328.definition: In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

C0329.name: vivid
C0329.definition: In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

C0330.name: resolution
C0330.definition: Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

C0331.name: lighting
C0331.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

C0332.name: frame rate
C0332.definition: Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

C0333.name: audio bit rate
C0333.definition: Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

C0334.name: interactivity
C0334.definition: In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

C0335.name: virtual entity
C0335.definition: Interactivity, as a quality of immersion, is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

C0336.name: plot-informing
C0336.definition: In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

C0337.name: perfect presence
C0337.definition: Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.

C0338.name: uncanny valley effect
C0338.definition: The uncanny valley effect is a finding from a scientific study of human perception of artificial objects, originally robots and extendable to digital representations, that digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease or eeriness rather than familiarity because of subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first.

C0339.name: human perception
C0339.definition: Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory.

C0340.name: familiarity
C0340.definition: The uncanny valley effect is a finding from a scientific study of human perception of artificial objects, originally robots and extendable to digital representations, that digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease or eeriness rather than familiarity because of subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first.

C0341.name: human likeness
C0341.definition: In the plot illustrating the uncanny valley effect, with human likeness on the horizontal axis (x-axis) and familiarity on the vertical axis (y-axis), as an artificial object or digital object in virtual reality (VR) becomes more human-like, familiarity first increases for both moving and stationary objects, then decreases, more sharply for moving objects, reaches a minimum in the uncanny valley region, typically between 70 and 85 percent human likeness, and then increases again.

C0342.name: realism
C0342.definition: When creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the uncanny valley effect means that trying to match reality exactly with human-like figures or realistic objects may not produce a good experience if their human-likeness falls in the uncanny valley, so there is a trade-off over how much realism to include.

C0343.name: photorealism
C0343.definition: In virtual reality (VR), presence does not require photorealism or human-like objects; other cues may be equally useful for achieving higher presence.

C0344.name: representational fidelity
C0344.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity, along with immersion and presence.

C0345.name: interaction fidelity
C0345.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity, along with immersion and presence.

C0346.name: experiential fidelity
C0346.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity, along with immersion and presence.

C0347.name: 360-degree video
C0347.definition: The highest representational fidelity is indicated by very good photorealistic immersive film content, such as 360-degree video or images of the real world in a virtual environment, while extremely low representational fidelity is indicated by purely abstract and non-objective worlds that are unfamiliar in real-world experience.

C0348.name: display technology
C0348.definition: Combining real and virtual content in augmented reality (AR) requires suitable display technology to overlay virtual content on the representation of the real world on the device, and the same display issue also exists in virtual reality (VR).

C0349.name: input modality
C0349.definition: Real-time interaction in augmented reality (AR) requires suitable forms of interaction, including different input devices and input modalities, so that the user can interact with digital content overlaid on a representation of the real world.

C0350.name: pose
C0350.definition: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

C0351.name: position
C0351.definition: In a Unity script, the Vector3 data type represents the position of a three-dimensional (3D) point by storing three coordinates as three elements of a vector.

C0352.name: orientation
C0352.definition: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

C0353.name: anchor
C0353.definition: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

C0354.name: pose estimation
C0354.definition: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

C0355.name: registration phase
C0355.definition: Conceptually, pose determination in augmented reality (AR) has two parts, the registration phase and the tracking phase, which can be performed in one phase or as separate phases; the registration phase determines the viewer's pose relative to a real-world anchor when the user starts using the system, and the tracking phase updates that pose relative to a previously known pose because the user is likely to move in an AR application, so that virtual and real-world content appear properly mixed.

C0356.name: tracking phase
C0356.definition: Conceptually, pose determination in augmented reality (AR) has two parts, the registration phase and the tracking phase, which can be performed in one phase or as separate phases; the registration phase determines the viewer's pose relative to a real-world anchor when the user starts using the system, and the tracking phase updates that pose relative to a previously known pose because the user is likely to move in an AR application, so that virtual and real-world content appear properly mixed.

C0357.name: input mechanism
C0357.definition: The major issues in augmented reality (AR) are mostly technological and consist of proper display technology, proper input mechanisms and technology, and pose estimation and updating, which is popularly called tracking, at the beginning and during system use.

C0358.name: cybersickness
C0358.definition: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

C0359.name: symptom
C0359.definition: A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.

C0370.name: acceptability
C0370.definition: Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

C0371.name: user experience
C0371.definition: Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

C0372.name: internal factors
C0372.definition: The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

C0373.name: external factors
C0373.definition: The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

C0374.name: virtual reality content
C0374.definition: The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

C0375.name: age
C0375.definition: Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.

C0376.name: gender
C0376.definition: Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.

C0377.name: motion sickness
