C0379.name: physical condition
C0379.definition: Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.

C0380.name: emotional condition
C0380.definition: Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.

C0381.name: cyber sickness susceptibility
C0381.definition: Age is related to cyber sickness susceptibility: children aged 2 to 12 may show increased sensitivity, that tendency decreases as they grow older, older persons are likely to experience higher levels, cyber sickness is generally uncommon among young children, and it is highly unlikely in users aged 12 to 25.

C0382.name: controllable content
C0382.definition: Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

C0383.name: inter-pupillary distance
C0383.definition: A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

C0384.name: inter-pupillary distance fit
C0384.definition: A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

C0385.name: inter-pupillary distance adjustable range
C0385.definition: A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

C0386.name: cyber sickness risk
C0386.definition: Studies indicate a positive correlation between motion sickness (MS) susceptibility and cyber sickness risk, so individuals with higher MS susceptibility are likely to experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

C0387.name: cyber sickness symptoms
C0387.definition: Studies indicate a positive correlation between motion sickness (MS) susceptibility and cyber sickness risk, so individuals with higher MS susceptibility are likely to experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

C0388.name: prior exposure to virtual reality systems
C0388.definition: Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

C0389.name: repeated exposure to virtual reality
C0389.definition: Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

C0390.name: cybersickness severity
C0390.definition: Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

C0391.name: body awareness
C0391.definition: Body awareness, the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations, is a physical condition related to cyber sickness; poor sleep quality can affect this awareness and may contribute to or increase the severity of cyber sickness.

C0392.name: sleep quality
C0392.definition: Body awareness, the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations, is a physical condition related to cyber sickness; poor sleep quality can affect this awareness and may contribute to or increase the severity of cyber sickness.

C0393.name: retinal eccentricity
C0393.definition: People with greater retinal eccentricity may be more susceptible to cyber sickness.

C0394.name: neurological condition
C0394.definition: Individuals with neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis may experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

C0395.name: multiple sclerosis
C0395.definition: Individuals with neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis may experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

C0396.name: standing posture
C0396.definition: A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

C0397.name: anxiety
C0397.definition: Emotional conditions at the time of use can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness: negative emotions such as anxiety, stress, and frustration are typically associated with it, and personality traits such as neuroticism may also increase the likelihood.

C0398.name: stress
C0398.definition: Emotional conditions at the time of use can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness: negative emotions such as anxiety, stress, and frustration are typically associated with it, and personality traits such as neuroticism may also increase the likelihood.

C0399.name: frustration
C0399.definition: Emotional conditions at the time of use can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness: negative emotions such as anxiety, stress, and frustration are typically associated with it, and personality traits such as neuroticism may also increase the likelihood.

C0400.name: personality trait
C0400.definition: Emotional conditions at the time of use can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness: negative emotions such as anxiety, stress, and frustration are typically associated with it, and personality traits such as neuroticism may also increase the likelihood.

C0401.name: neuroticism
C0401.definition: Emotional conditions at the time of use can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness: negative emotions such as anxiety, stress, and frustration are typically associated with it, and personality traits such as neuroticism may also increase the likelihood.

C0402.name: display resolution
C0402.definition: Display resolution is a hardware factor that reduces cybersickness (CS) up to a certain point; a study evaluating 1K, 2K, 3K, and 4K resolutions found a substantial reduction in CS induction from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or from 3K to 4K.

C0403.name: latency
C0403.definition: Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

C0404.name: latency jitter
C0404.definition: Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

C0405.name: display type
C0405.definition: Display type is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness (CS), with users using head-mounted display (HMD)-based or virtual reality (VR) headset displays experiencing more CS than users using conventional monitors or non-immersive VR systems; in one study comparing stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) videos on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets, VR headset users experienced more CS.

C0406.name: conventional monitor
C0406.definition: Display type is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness (CS), with users using head-mounted display (HMD)-based or virtual reality (VR) headset displays experiencing more CS than users using conventional monitors or non-immersive VR systems; in one study comparing stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) videos on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets, VR headset users experienced more CS.

C0407.name: stereoscopic three-dimensional video
C0407.definition: Display type is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness (CS), with users using head-mounted display (HMD)-based or virtual reality (VR) headset displays experiencing more CS than users using conventional monitors or non-immersive VR systems; in one study comparing stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) videos on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets, VR headset users experienced more CS.

C0408.name: flat screen
C0408.definition: Display type is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness (CS), with users using head-mounted display (HMD)-based or virtual reality (VR) headset displays experiencing more CS than users using conventional monitors or non-immersive VR systems; in one study comparing stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) videos on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets, VR headset users experienced more CS.

C0409.name: panoramic screen
C0409.definition: Display type is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness (CS), with users using head-mounted display (HMD)-based or virtual reality (VR) headset displays experiencing more CS than users using conventional monitors or non-immersive VR systems; in one study comparing stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) videos on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets, VR headset users experienced more CS.

C0410.name: brightness
C0410.definition: Users with higher-end head-mounted displays (HMDs) experience less cybersickness (CS) than users with lower-end HMDs, a difference related to display qualities such as resolution, brightness, clarity, and contrast.

C0411.name: clarity
C0411.definition: Users with higher-end head-mounted displays (HMDs) experience less cybersickness (CS) than users with lower-end HMDs, a difference related to display qualities such as resolution, brightness, clarity, and contrast.

C0412.name: contrast
C0412.definition: Users with higher-end head-mounted displays (HMDs) experience less cybersickness (CS) than users with lower-end HMDs, a difference related to display qualities such as resolution, brightness, clarity, and contrast.

C0413.name: input method
C0413.definition: In virtual reality (VR), the type of input method used, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, can influence the level of cybersickness (CS).

C0414.name: hand controller
C0414.definition: In virtual reality (VR), the type of input method used, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, can influence the level of cybersickness (CS).

C0415.name: treadmill
C0415.definition: Treadmills are output devices that provide the sense of walking or running while staying in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs.

C0416.name: motion sensor
C0416.definition: In virtual reality (VR), the type of input method used, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, can influence the level of cybersickness (CS).

C0417.name: motion controller
C0417.definition: In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

C0418.name: joystick
C0418.definition: In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

C0419.name: gamepad controller
C0419.definition: In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

C0420.name: hardware factor
C0420.definition: The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

C0421.name: input technology
C0421.definition: The causes of cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, such as age and gender, and external factors, which are divided into hardware factors, such as display type, latency, latency jitter, resolution, and input technology, and content factors.

C0422.name: content factor
C0422.definition: The causes of cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, such as age and gender, and external factors, which are divided into hardware factors, such as display type, latency, latency jitter, resolution, and input technology, and content factors.

C0423.name: visual motion
C0423.definition: The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

C0424.name: means of locomotion
C0424.definition: Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness.

C0425.name: type of content
C0425.definition: The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

C0426.name: duration
C0426.definition: The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

C0427.name: visual complexity
C0427.definition: Visual complexity is an external factor that is positively correlated with cybersickness (CS) symptoms, so scenes with more objects of different shapes, sizes, and movements are more likely to induce cybersickness.

C0428.name: vection
C0428.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS).

C0429.name: self-motion
C0429.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS).

C0430.name: peripheral stimulus
C0430.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS).

C0431.name: visual motion stimulus
C0431.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS).

C0432.name: height
C0432.definition: The severity of cyber sickness (CS) also significantly increases with larger height and faster speed in a virtual environment.

C0433.name: speed
C0433.definition: Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

C0434.name: viewpoint
C0434.definition: The viewpoint during motion is also an important factor for cyber sickness (CS).

C0435.name: turbulent visual motion
C0435.definition: Brief exposure to turbulent visual motion alone is not enough to induce cyber sickness (CS), but longer exposure to turbulent visual motion can induce cyber sickness.

C0436.name: angular velocity
C0436.definition: Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis.

C0437.name: rotation
C0437.definition: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

C0438.name: x axis
C0438.definition: Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis.

C0439.name: y axis
C0439.definition: Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis.

C0440.name: z axis
C0440.definition: Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis.

C0441.name: sensory mismatch
C0441.definition: Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness.

C0442.name: control over motion
C0442.definition: Control over motion in a virtual world, meaning whether and how a user controls movement, is an aspect of locomotion that directly affects presence and indirectly affects cybersickness (CS) through presence; greater presence in virtual reality (VR) generally reduces cybersickness, and more control means greater presence and less control means lower presence.

C0443.name: hand-based motion control
C0443.definition: The type and extent of the control mechanism used in virtual reality (VR) determine the likelihood of cybersickness (CS); research studies find that hand-based motion control leads to significantly less cybersickness than whole-body motion control.

C0444.name: whole-body motion control
C0444.definition: The type and extent of the control mechanism used in virtual reality (VR) determine the likelihood of cybersickness (CS); research studies find that hand-based motion control leads to significantly less cybersickness than whole-body motion control.

C0445.name: transition type
C0445.definition: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

C0446.name: teleportation
C0446.definition: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

C0447.name: naturalistic free movement
C0447.definition: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

C0448.name: field of vision
C0448.definition: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.

C0449.name: head movement
C0449.definition: An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.

C0450.name: action content
C0450.definition: The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content.

C0451.name: fast movement
C0451.definition: The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content.

C0452.name: abrupt alteration
C0452.definition: The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content.

C0453.name: neutral content
C0453.definition: The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content.

C0454.name: static content
C0454.definition: The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content.

C0455.name: genre
C0455.definition: The genre of a virtual environment affects cybersickness (CS), and content based on horror scenes is likely to induce more CS than pleasant general content.

C0456.name: geometry
C0456.definition: The geometry and terrain of a virtual environment affect cybersickness (CS); when a user travels over regular bumps and irregular terrain, CS is more likely than when the same travel occurs over flat terrain without bumpy rides.

C0457.name: terrain
C0457.definition: The geometry and terrain of a virtual environment affect cybersickness (CS); when a user travels over regular bumps and irregular terrain, CS is more likely than when the same travel occurs over flat terrain without bumpy rides.

C0458.name: weather conditions
C0458.definition: Weather conditions in a virtual environment affect the induction of cybersickness (CS); stormy conditions are more likely to cause higher CS than clear weather conditions.

C0459.name: exposure duration
C0459.definition: Virtual reality (VR) exposure duration is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and prolonged exposure through head-mounted displays (HMDs) leads to greater cybersickness.

C0460.name: locomotion controller
C0460.definition: Cybersickness (CS) increases with virtual reality (VR) exposure time when users use different locomotion controllers during navigation tasks in a virtual environment, and the effect of the locomotion technique used to move from one point to another on cybersickness is further complicated by longer duration.

C0461.name: navigation task
C0461.definition: Cybersickness (CS) increases with virtual reality (VR) exposure time when users use different locomotion controllers during navigation tasks in a virtual environment, and the effect of the locomotion technique used to move from one point to another on cybersickness is further complicated by longer duration.

C0462.name: locomotion technique
C0462.definition: Locomotion techniques, alternatively travel techniques, are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place.

C0463.name: live-action 180-degree video
C0463.definition: Continuous exposure to live-action 180-degree videos results in higher cybersickness (CS), and the increase in cybersickness grows with exposure time.

C0464.name: measurement technique
C0464.definition: Measurement techniques for cybersickness (CS) rely on three components: the input provided for measurement, the measurement technique itself, and the output generated.

C0465.name: questionnaire-based input
C0465.definition: Inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) can be questionnaire-based, physiological and biometric information, behavioral information, and content-based information.

C0466.definition: Inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) can be questionnaire-based, physiological and biometric information, behavioral information, and content-based information.

C0468.name: content-based information

C0469.name: binary classes
C0469.definition: The output of cybersickness (CS) measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.

C0470.name: multiple classes
C0470.definition: The output of cybersickness (CS) measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.

C0471.name: sickness score
C0471.definition: The output of cybersickness (CS) measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.

C0472.name: simulator sickness questionnaire
C0472.definition: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).

C0473.name: oculomotor subscale
C0473.definition: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) contains 16 items divided into three subscales: the oculomotor subscale, the disorientation subscale, and the nausea subscale.

C0474.name: disorientation subscale
C0474.definition: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) contains 16 items divided into three subscales: the oculomotor subscale, the disorientation subscale, and the nausea subscale.

C0475.name: nausea subscale

C0476.name: Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire
C0476.definition: Questionnaires specifically designed for virtual reality (VR) include the Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire (VRSQ) and the Cyber Sickness Questionnaire (CSQ), which is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays (HMDs).

C0477.name: Cyber Sickness Questionnaire
C0477.definition: The virtual reality sickness questionnaire (VRSQ) and the cyber sickness questionnaire (CSQ) are questionnaires relevant to cyber sickness in extended reality (XR).

C0478.name: Misery Scale
C0478.definition: Shorter and more concise questionnaires used to assess specific conditions include the Misery Scale (MIS) and the Fast Motion Sickness Scale (FMS).

C0479.name: Fast Motion Sickness Scale
C0479.definition: Shorter and more concise questionnaires used to assess specific conditions include the Misery Scale (MIS) and the Fast Motion Sickness Scale (FMS).

C0480.name: Motion History Questionnaire
C0480.definition: Questionnaires used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness (CS) include the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ), the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MS-SQ), and the Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMS or VIMS-SQ).

C0481.name: Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire
C0481.definition: Questionnaires used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness (CS) include the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ), the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MS-SQ), and the Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMS or VIMS-SQ).

C0482.name: Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire
C0482.definition: Questionnaires used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness (CS) include the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ), the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MS-SQ), and the Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMS or VIMS-SQ).

C0483.name: Nausea Scale
C0483.definition: Questionnaires commonly used to assess overall discomfort include the Nausea Scale and the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire (MSAQ).

C0484.name: Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire
C0484.definition: Questionnaires commonly used to assess overall discomfort include the Nausea Scale and the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire (MSAQ).

C0485.name: physiological input
C0485.definition: Physiological or biometric inputs can be used to detect cybersickness (CS) because questionnaire-based inputs can be subjective, are prone to inaccuracies, and may not always be reliable.

C0486.name: electroencephalogram
C0486.definition: Electroencephalogram (EEG) is one of the widely used physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness (CS).

C0487.name: heart rate
C0487.definition: Physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness (CS) include heart rate, galvanic skin response (GSR), electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram (ECG), electrogastrogram (EGG), electrooculography (EOG), respiration signals, photoplethysmography (PPG), and electromyogram (EMG).

C0495.name: behavioral input
C0495.definition: Behavioral inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include blink rate, head and body movement, the manner of those movements, and postural sway.

C0497.definition: Behavioral inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include blink rate, head and body movement, the manner of those movements, and postural sway.

C0498.definition: Behavioral inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include blink rate, head and body movement, the manner of those movements, and postural sway.

C0499.name: axial movement
C0499.definition: Postural sway can be monitored for measuring cybersickness (CS) during virtual reality (VR) exposure using axial movements or changes in the user's center of pressure.

C0500.name: center of pressure
C0500.definition: Postural sway can be monitored for measuring cybersickness (CS) during virtual reality (VR) exposure using axial movements or changes in the user's center of pressure.

C0501.name: postural instability
C0501.definition: Postural instability is positively correlated with the severity of cybersickness (CS), so postural sway can indicate CS severity.

C0502.name: content-based input
C0502.definition: Content-based inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.

C0503.name: optical flow
C0503.definition: Content-based inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.

C0505.name: exceptional motion velocity
C0505.definition: Content-based inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.

C0506.name: physiological and biometric input
C0506.definition: The four categories of inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) are questionnaire-based inputs, which are subjective; physiological and biometric inputs, which are objective; behavioral inputs; and content-based inputs.

C0507.name: manual evaluation
C0507.definition: Cybersickness (CS) measurement techniques based on input are broadly of two types: manual evaluation, which is based on human intervention, and machine learning-based (ML) or automated evaluation, which uses automated algorithms on input to measure cybersickness.

C0508.name: machine learning-based evaluation
C0508.definition: Cybersickness (CS) measurement techniques based on input are broadly of two types: manual evaluation, which is based on human intervention, and machine learning-based (ML) or automated evaluation, which uses automated algorithms on input to measure cybersickness.

C0509.name: questionnaire-based assessment
C0509.definition: Manual evaluation for cybersickness (CS) is entirely based on human intervention and typically uses questionnaire-based assessment, in which a person distributes the questionnaire, collects feedback, and reviews the responses to decide the severity, onset, or possibility of cybersickness.

C0510.name: psychological input
C0510.definition: Machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) can use psychological, physiological, or biometric inputs to train models that automatically determine cybersickness.

C0511.name: biometric input
C0511.definition: Machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) can use psychological, physiological, or biometric inputs to train models that automatically determine cybersickness.

C0512.name: transparent model
C0512.definition: One way to perform machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) is to use transparent models, which provide clear insight into the decision-making process and whose inner workings can easily be understood.

C0513.name: stepwise regression analysis
C0513.definition: Stepwise regression analysis can be considered a transparent model that is utilized to measure cybersickness (CS) using a variety of physiological signals or physiological inputs.

C0514.name: machine learning
C0514.definition: In machine learning (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS), interpretable models are similar to transparent models, offer more flexibility in customization and in how the model is used, and provide more precise details about the relationships between the input and the output.

C0515.name: interpretable model
C0515.definition: In machine learning (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS), interpretable models are similar to transparent models, offer more flexibility in customization and in how the model is used, and provide more precise details about the relationships between the input and the output.

C0516.name: CN2 rule induction
C0516.definition: Interpretable machine learning (ML) algorithms used to measure cybersickness (CS) include CN2 rule induction, bagged decision trees, Naive Bayes classifiers, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and long short-term memory (LSTM) regression analysis.

C0517.name: bagged decision tree
C0517.definition: Interpretable machine learning (ML) algorithms used to measure cybersickness (CS) include CN2 rule induction, bagged decision trees, Naive Bayes classifiers, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and long short-term memory (LSTM) regression analysis.

C0518.name: Naive Bayes classifier
C0518.definition: Interpretable machine learning (ML) algorithms used to measure cybersickness (CS) include CN2 rule induction, bagged decision trees, Naive Bayes classifiers, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and long short-term memory (LSTM) regression analysis.

C0519.name: K-nearest neighbors
C0519.definition: Interpretable machine learning (ML) algorithms used to measure cybersickness (CS) include CN2 rule induction, bagged decision trees, Naive Bayes classifiers, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and long short-term memory (LSTM) regression analysis.

C0520.name: linear discriminant analysis
C0520.definition: Interpretable machine learning (ML) algorithms used to measure cybersickness (CS) include CN2 rule induction, bagged decision trees, Naive Bayes classifiers, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and long short-term memory (LSTM) regression analysis.

C0521.name: long short-term memory
C0521.definition: Interpretable machine learning (ML) algorithms used to measure cybersickness (CS) include CN2 rule induction, bagged decision trees, Naive Bayes classifiers, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and long short-term memory (LSTM) regression analysis.

C0522.name: explainable boosting machine
C0522.definition: Combinations of machine learning (ML) techniques have also been used to identify and provide insight into cybersickness (CS); for example, explainable boosting machine (EBM), decision tree, and logistic regression were combined using biophysiological and subjective measurements as input.

C0523.name: decision tree
C0523.definition: Combinations of machine learning (ML) techniques have also been used to identify and provide insight into cybersickness (CS); for example, explainable boosting machine (EBM), decision tree, and logistic regression were combined using biophysiological and subjective measurements as input.

C0524.name: logistic regression
C0524.definition: Combinations of machine learning (ML) techniques have also been used to identify and provide insight into cybersickness (CS); for example, explainable boosting machine (EBM), decision tree, and logistic regression were combined using biophysiological and subjective measurements as input.

C0525.name: black-box model
C0525.definition: Black-box models in cybersickness (CS) evaluation are models that cannot be easily understood or explained; they take an input and produce an output without revealing how or why that output is generated from the input, unlike transparent or interpretable models.

C0526.name: convolutional neural network
C0526.definition: Black-box models studied for cybersickness (CS) evaluation include long short-term memory (LSTM), convolutional neural network (CNN), and support vector machine (SVM) models.

C0527.name: support vector machine
C0527.definition: Black-box models studied for cybersickness (CS) evaluation include long short-term memory (LSTM), convolutional neural network (CNN), and support vector machine (SVM) models.

C0528.name: prediction accuracy
C0528.definition: Black-box models in cybersickness (CS) evaluation generally provide higher prediction accuracy than transparent and interpretable models, but unlike those other models they require large amounts of data and processing power.

C0529.name: hybrid model
C0529.definition: Hybrid models in machine learning (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) are combinations of different machine learning (ML) models, designed to provide high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process.

C0530.name: deep embedded self-organizing map
C0530.definition: Hybrid models used to predict or classify cybersickness (CS) include a combination of a deep embedded self-organizing map (DESOM) and an autoencoder designed from EEGNET, a specialized convolutional neural network (CNN) for electroencephalography (EEG) prediction, and a voting classifier combining random forest, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), logistic regression, and a multilayer perceptron neural network for binary and three-level classification.

C0537.name: classification based on the event of measurement
C0537.definition: Classification based on the event of measurement is a category of cybersickness (CS) evaluation technique that distinguishes detection, which uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, from prediction, which occurs before the experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur.

C0538.definition: Classification based on the event of measurement is a category of cybersickness (CS) evaluation technique that distinguishes detection, which uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, from prediction, which occurs before the experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur.

C0540.definition: Classification based on the event of measurement is a category of cybersickness (CS) evaluation technique that distinguishes detection, which uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, from prediction, which occurs before the experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur.

C0541.name: mitigation measures
C0541.definition: Most cybersickness (CS) evaluation work focuses on detection rather than prediction, but prediction is important because it can enable mitigation measures before cybersickness occurs.

C0542.name: physiological signals
C0542.definition: Limited research on predicting cybersickness (CS) uses physiological signals and video features, baseline measurements before virtual reality (VR) immersion, and machine learning (ML) studies that predict susceptibility to cybersickness or impending cybersickness episodes.

C0546.definition: The outputs of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness (CS) are generally scores or ratings on rating scales, and these scores or ratings can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

C0547.definition: The outputs of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness (CS) are generally scores or ratings on rating scales, and these scores or ratings can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

C0552.name: regression model
C0552.definition: In machine learning (ML)-based cybersickness (CS) evaluation, a sickness score quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience and is generally produced by a regression model.

C0553.name: cybersickness mitigation
C0553.definition: Because complete prevention of cybersickness (CS) is generally not possible, cybersickness mitigation uses measures to reduce or eliminate cybersickness or at least lessen its impact.

C0554.name: developer perspective
C0554.definition: Cybersickness (CS) mitigation is considered from two important perspectives, the developer's perspective and the user's perspective, because even a good developer solution may fail to prevent cybersickness if the user does not use the system properly or as expected.

C0555.definition: Cybersickness (CS) mitigation is considered from two important perspectives, the developer's perspective and the user's perspective, because even a good developer solution may fail to prevent cybersickness if the user does not use the system properly or as expected.

C0556.name: field of view adjustment
C0556.definition: Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.

C0557.name: dynamic visual blur
C0557.definition: Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.
