C0562.name: peripheral optical flow
C0562.definition: Field of view (FOV) adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness (CS) because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow.

C0563.name: symmetric mask
C0563.definition: A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

C0564.name: translational velocity
C0564.definition: A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

C0565.name: asymmetric mask
C0565.definition: An asymmetric mask is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that is considered an adaptive restrictor because it obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible, so it adapts based on optical flow.

C0566.name: adaptive restrictor
C0566.definition: An asymmetric mask is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that is considered an adaptive restrictor because it obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible, so it adapts based on optical flow.

C0567.name: side restrictor
C0567.definition: A side restrictor, described as an asymmetric mask, is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn, providing a controlled way of restriction.

C0568.name: ground visible restrictor
C0568.definition: A ground visible restrictor is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy in which the ground plane remains visible during movement.

C0569.name: ground plane
C0569.definition: A ground visible restrictor is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy in which the ground plane remains visible during movement.

C0570.name: depth-of-field blur
C0570.definition: Dynamic visual blur is a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness (CS) in which blurring means obscuring or reducing clarity, and it has two types: depth-of-field blur, which uses well-known depth cues in human vision, and peripheral blur, also called dynamic non-salient region blurring.

C0571.name: peripheral blur
C0571.definition: Dynamic visual blur is a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness (CS) in which blurring means obscuring or reducing clarity, and it has two types: depth-of-field blur, which uses well-known depth cues in human vision, and peripheral blur, also called dynamic non-salient region blurring.

C0572.name: head reference frame
C0572.definition: Rest frames are fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements, and rest frames attached to the head reference frame are known as independent visual backgrounds, with examples including clouds, grids, and a virtual nose.

C0573.name: independent visual background
C0573.definition: Rest frames are fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements, and rest frames attached to the head reference frame are known as independent visual backgrounds, with examples including clouds, grids, and a virtual nose.

C0574.name: virtual nose
C0574.definition: Rest frames are fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements, and rest frames attached to the head reference frame are known as independent visual backgrounds, with examples including clouds, grids, and a virtual nose.

C0575.name: perceived optical flow
C0575.definition: Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.

C0576.name: geometrical simplification
C0576.definition: Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.

C0577.name: sparse peripheral display
C0577.definition: Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a sparse peripheral display that expands a head-mounted display (HMD) periphery with a colorful LED matrix, and miniature LED screens placed in the HMD.

C0578.name: light-emitting diode matrix
C0578.definition: Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a sparse peripheral display that expands a head-mounted display (HMD) periphery with a colorful LED matrix, and miniature LED screens placed in the HMD.

C0579.name: light-emitting diode screen
C0579.definition: Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a sparse peripheral display that expands a head-mounted display (HMD) periphery with a colorful LED matrix, and miniature LED screens placed in the HMD.

C0580.name: Noble camera setup twin cam
C0580.definition: Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a Noble camera setup twin cam that reduces motion blur and cybersickness, and a hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig that can be used to reduce cybersickness.

C0581.name: motion blur
C0581.definition: Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a Noble camera setup twin cam that reduces motion blur and cybersickness, and a hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig that can be used to reduce cybersickness.

C0582.name: hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig
C0582.definition: Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a Noble camera setup twin cam that reduces motion blur and cybersickness, and a hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig that can be used to reduce cybersickness.

C0583.name: phantom legs
C0583.definition: Phantom legs is a hardware-level alteration that applies alternating haptic cues synchronized to users' footsteps using additional hardware, and it was found to reduce cybersickness (CS) to a great extent.

C0584.name: haptic cue
C0584.definition: Phantom legs is a hardware-level alteration that applies alternating haptic cues synchronized to users' footsteps using additional hardware, and it was found to reduce cybersickness (CS) to a great extent.

C0585.name: floor vibration
C0585.definition: Floor vibrations are a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness (CS) that uses vibration-driven whole-body tactile feedback to match the vibrations of the virtual environment.

C0586.name: whole-body tactile feedback
C0586.definition: Floor vibrations are a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness (CS) that uses vibration-driven whole-body tactile feedback to match the vibrations of the virtual environment.

C0587.name: simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration
C0587.definition: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness (CS), for example in a walking vibe system that uses two small vibration motors behind the ears for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience.

C0588.name: walking vibe system
C0588.definition: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness (CS), for example in a walking vibe system that uses two small vibration motors behind the ears for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience.

C0589.name: vibration motor
C0589.definition: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness (CS), for example in a walking vibe system that uses two small vibration motors behind the ears for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience.

C0590.name: vibrotactile feedback
C0590.definition: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness (CS), for example in a walking vibe system that uses two small vibration motors behind the ears for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience.

C0591.name: modified motion platform
C0591.definition: Modified motion platforms are a hardware-level alteration in which short bursts of rotational acceleration matching visual forward acceleration were found quite effective in reducing cybersickness (CS), and the platforms can be modified to produce this effect.

C0592.name: rotational acceleration
C0592.definition: Modified motion platforms are a hardware-level alteration in which short bursts of rotational acceleration matching visual forward acceleration were found quite effective in reducing cybersickness (CS), and the platforms can be modified to produce this effect.

C0593.name: visual forward acceleration
C0593.definition: Modified motion platforms are a hardware-level alteration in which short bursts of rotational acceleration matching visual forward acceleration were found quite effective in reducing cybersickness (CS), and the platforms can be modified to produce this effect.

C0594.name: novel walking method
C0594.definition: Locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness (CS) include novel walking methods instead of natural walking, teleportation rather than steering-based locomotion, dynamic steering speed that skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure, viewpoint snapping that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation, and invisible ramps placed on top of stairs.

C0595.name: natural walking
C0595.definition: Locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness (CS) include novel walking methods instead of natural walking, teleportation rather than steering-based locomotion, dynamic steering speed that skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure, viewpoint snapping that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation, and invisible ramps placed on top of stairs.

C0596.name: steering-based locomotion
C0596.definition: Locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness (CS) include novel walking methods instead of natural walking, teleportation rather than steering-based locomotion, dynamic steering speed that skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure, viewpoint snapping that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation, and invisible ramps placed on top of stairs.

C0597.name: dynamic steering speed
C0597.definition: Locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness (CS) include novel walking methods instead of natural walking, teleportation rather than steering-based locomotion, dynamic steering speed that skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure, viewpoint snapping that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation, and invisible ramps placed on top of stairs.

C0598.name: viewpoint snapping
C0598.definition: Locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness (CS) include novel walking methods instead of natural walking, teleportation rather than steering-based locomotion, dynamic steering speed that skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure, viewpoint snapping that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation, and invisible ramps placed on top of stairs.

C0599.name: invisible ramp
C0599.definition: Locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness (CS) include novel walking methods instead of natural walking, teleportation rather than steering-based locomotion, dynamic steering speed that skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure, viewpoint snapping that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation, and invisible ramps placed on top of stairs.

C0600.name: developer-side intervention
C0600.definition: Cybersickness (CS) is subjective and individual susceptibility to cybersickness varies, so a one-size-fits-all approach or developer-side interventions alone may not be sufficient and users need their own countermeasures to reduce the effects of cybersickness.

C0601.name: countermeasure
C0601.definition: Cybersickness (CS) is subjective and individual susceptibility to cybersickness varies, so a one-size-fits-all approach or developer-side interventions alone may not be sufficient and users need their own countermeasures to reduce the effects of cybersickness.

C0602.name: virtual reality session
C0602.definition: To reduce the risk of cybersickness (CS), users may be advised to avoid continuous or long-duration exposure to a virtual environment, and studies suggest that the generally safe maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) session for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness is between 55 and 70 minutes, although the exact duration may vary with device, content, and other factors, and longer exposure is risky.

C0603.name: exposure
C0603.definition: To reduce the risk of cybersickness (CS), users may be advised to avoid continuous or long-duration exposure to a virtual environment, and studies suggest that the generally safe maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) session for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness is between 55 and 70 minutes, although the exact duration may vary with device, content, and other factors, and longer exposure is risky.

C0604.name: maximum duration
C0604.definition: To reduce the risk of cybersickness (CS), users may be advised to avoid continuous or long-duration exposure to a virtual environment, and studies suggest that the generally safe maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) session for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness is between 55 and 70 minutes, although the exact duration may vary with device, content, and other factors, and longer exposure is risky.

C0605.name: habituation
C0605.definition: Habituation is the gradual decrease in the intensity of cybersickness (CS) after repeated experience in a virtual environment.

C0606.name: diaphragmatic breathing
C0606.definition: Users can try slow diaphragmatic breathing, or controlled breathing patterns, to delay the onset, reduce the severity, and, to a large extent, reduce the possibility of cybersickness (CS).

C0607.name: background music
C0607.definition: Playing pleasant background music and ensuring adequate external air flow are user-side strategies that can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness (CS).

C0608.name: air flow
C0608.definition: Playing pleasant background music and ensuring adequate external air flow are user-side strategies that can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness (CS).

C0609.name: user-side strategy
C0609.definition: Playing pleasant background music and ensuring adequate external air flow are user-side strategies that can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness (CS).

C0610.name: complete view
C0610.definition: A complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.

C0611.name: organism
C0611.definition: A complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.

C0612.name: virtual reality hardware
C0612.definition: The overall virtual reality (VR) system has three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.

C0613.name: stimulation
C0613.definition: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

C0614.name: data flow
C0614.definition: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

C0615.name: stimulation data flow
C0615.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the data flow between the hardware and the user (organism) is bidirectional: stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.

C0616.name: stimulus
C0616.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the data flow between the hardware and the user (organism) is bidirectional: stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.

C0617.name: tracking data flow
C0617.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the data flow between the hardware and the user (organism) is bidirectional: stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.

C0618.name: user motion
C0618.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the data flow between the hardware and the user (organism) is bidirectional: stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.

C0619.name: button press
C0619.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

C0620.name: controller movement
C0620.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

C0621.name: eye movement
C0621.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

C0622.name: body part movement
C0622.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

C0623.name: surrounding physical environment
C0623.definition: The overall virtual reality (VR) system has three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.

C0624.name: tracker
C0624.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware may include trackers that track objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than the user directly, and this is required especially when interaction with those objects is part of the experience.

C0625.name: immersive application
C0625.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware may change the surrounding physical environment, for example when an immersive application uses a robotic arm to change the position of objects in the environment, and that change may affect the user's behavior.

C0626.name: robotic arm
C0626.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware may change the surrounding physical environment, for example when an immersive application uses a robotic arm to change the position of objects in the environment, and that change may affect the user's behavior.

C0627.name: controller
C0627.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware is not limited to only the computer, head-mounted display (HMD), or controller used by the user; it may deal with objects in the surrounding physical environment.

C0628.name: visual display
C0628.definition: Output devices for virtual reality (VR) experience include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms and treadmills, and other sensory outputs that stimulate the taste and smell sensory organs, namely the tongue and nose.

C0629.name: tracking device
C0629.definition: In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a sensor or input device is used in a broad sense to mean any tracking device that tracks the user's input and extracts information from the real world, with the discussion restricted to sensors that track the user's movements.

C0630.name: virtual reality input device
C0630.definition: Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate.

C0631.name: hand input device
C0631.definition: Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate.

C0632.name: non-hand input device
C0632.definition: Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate.

C0633.name: world-grounded device
C0633.definition: Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.

C0634.name: non-tracked handheld controller
C0634.definition: Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.

C0635.name: tracked handheld controller
C0635.definition: Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.

C0636.name: hand-worn device
C0636.definition: Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.

C0637.name: bare-hand input
C0637.definition: Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.

C0638.name: portability
C0638.definition: World-grounded hand input devices are devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move; a joystick is an example that is commonly used to interact with desktop or other grounded systems, and portability is an issue because they constrain the user to move within a specified area.

C0639.name: button
C0639.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers.

C0640.name: trigger
C0640.definition: A collider in Unity configured as a trigger using the isTrigger property does not behave as a solid object and simply allows other colliders to pass through.

C0641.name: traditional video game controller
C0641.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers.

C0642.name: break-in presence
C0642.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers can cause break-in presence because the user's untracked hand movements may not produce a corresponding change in the position of the virtual hands in the virtual world, creating discomfort about whether the user is performing the task appropriately and affecting the perception of presence in the virtual world.

C0643.name: six degrees of freedom tracking
C0643.definition: Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR.

C0644.name: VIVE controller
C0644.definition: Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR.

C0645.name: force feedback controller
C0645.definition: Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

C0646.name: tangible interaction
C0646.definition: Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

C0647.name: passive virtual object
C0647.definition: Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

C0648.name: electromyography band
C0648.definition: Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular.

C0649.name: ring
C0649.definition: Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular.

C0650.name: bend-sensing data glove
C0650.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

C0651.name: bend sensor
C0651.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

C0652.name: processing unit
C0652.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

C0653.name: hand posture
C0653.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

C0654.name: gesture
C0654.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

C0655.name: controller-based interaction
C0655.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

C0656.name: pinch glove
C0656.definition: Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

C0657.name: pinch gesture
C0657.definition: Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

C0658.name: discrete input
C0658.definition: Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

C0659.name: object selection
C0659.definition: Object selection and object manipulation are two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, that are related to virtual objects.

C0660.name: mode switching
C0660.definition: Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

C0661.name: line-of-sight issue
C0661.definition: The advantages of hand-worn hand input devices are natural input with potentially rich gesture interaction, comfortable hand positions, no line-of-sight issue unlike some controller-based input, and the ability of the user's hands and fingers to fully interact with real objects, making different sorts of perception possible.

C0662.name: Leap Motion device
C0662.definition: The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.

C0663.name: infrared
C0663.definition: The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.

C0664.name: hand-tracking sensor
C0664.definition: The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.

C0665.name: light-emitting diode
C0665.definition: The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.

C0666.name: wide-angle camera
C0666.definition: The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.

C0667.name: low-cost head-mounted display
C0667.definition: The Leap Motion device can be attached to a head-mounted display (HMD) to provide hand input support even if the HMD does not support hand input, and it is typically useful with low-cost HMDs that do not provide good-quality controllers or controller support, such as cardboard-type devices in which a smartphone provides a stereoscopic view and which do not support interaction.

C0668.name: cardboard-type device
C0668.definition: The Leap Motion device can be attached to a head-mounted display (HMD) to provide hand input support even if the HMD does not support hand input, and it is typically useful with low-cost HMDs that do not provide good-quality controllers or controller support, such as cardboard-type devices in which a smartphone provides a stereoscopic view and which do not support interaction.

C0669.name: stereoscopic view
C0669.definition: The Leap Motion device can be attached to a head-mounted display (HMD) to provide hand input support even if the HMD does not support hand input, and it is typically useful with low-cost HMDs that do not provide good-quality controllers or controller support, such as cardboard-type devices in which a smartphone provides a stereoscopic view and which do not support interaction.

C0670.name: non-hand-based input devices
C0670.definition: Non-hand-based input devices are input devices that capture input from parts of the body other than the hand, including head movement, eye gaze, voice, and body movement.

C0671.name: gaze
C0671.definition: Non-hand-based input devices are input devices that capture input from parts of the body other than the hand, including head movement, eye gaze, voice, and body movement.

C0672.name: head-tracking-based input devices
C0672.definition: Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display (HMD) worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view.

C0673.name: head tracking device
C0673.definition: Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display (HMD) worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view.

C0674.name: yaw
C0674.definition: Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display (HMD) worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view.

C0675.name: roll
C0675.definition: Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display (HMD) worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view.

C0676.name: pitch
C0676.definition: In pitch perception, the frequency of a sound wave is referred to as pitch.

C0677.name: eye tracking devices
C0677.definition: Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system understand the user's eye movement and infer what action to take.

C0678.name: Midas touch problem
C0678.definition: The Midas touch problem in eye tracking-based input is the inability to differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze, so the system may select an object or perform an action even though the user did not intend to.

C0679.name: eye tracking
C0679.definition: Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system understand the user's eye movement and infer what action to take.

C0680.name: multimodal input
C0680.definition: Multimodal input, which uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking, is generally preferable over only eye tracking-based input for interacting with a system because eye tracking alone can cause objects to be selected or actions to be performed from unintentional gazes.

C0681.name: input
C0681.definition: The three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system are input, output, and processor.

C0682.name: output
C0682.definition: The three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system are input, output, and processor.

C0683.name: processor
C0683.definition: The three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system are input, output, and processor.

C0684.name: non-hand input technique
C0684.definition: Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.

C0685.name: full-body tracking
C0685.definition: Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.

C0686.name: sound-based tracking
C0686.definition: Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.

C0687.name: self-embodiment
C0687.definition: Full-body tracking can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in a virtual world because its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves.

C0688.name: social presence
C0688.definition: Full-body tracking can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in a virtual world because its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves.

C0689.name: motion capture suit
C0689.definition: There are two broad approaches to full-body tracking: a motion capture suit (MOCAP) and camera-based tracking.

C0690.name: camera-based tracking
C0690.definition: There are two broad approaches to full-body tracking: a motion capture suit (MOCAP) and camera-based tracking.

C0691.name: raw movement data
C0691.definition: In a motion capture suit (MOCAP) approach to full-body tracking, sensors in the suit capture and transmit raw movement data, which are combined and converted into full-body position and movement; for example, the Perception Neuron suit uses straps with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors on the legs, hands, arms, and head.

C0692.name: Perception Neuron suit
C0692.definition: In a motion capture suit (MOCAP) approach to full-body tracking, sensors in the suit capture and transmit raw movement data, which are combined and converted into full-body position and movement; for example, the Perception Neuron suit uses straps with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors on the legs, hands, arms, and head.

C0693.name: inertial measurement unit
C0693.definition: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).

C0694.name: camera
C0694.definition: In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.

C0695.name: reflective marker
C0695.definition: In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.

C0696.name: OptiTrack
C0696.definition: In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.

C0697.name: Microsoft Kinect
C0697.definition: In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.

C0698.name: voice
C0698.definition: Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

C0699.name: speech
C0699.definition: Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

C0700.name: non-speech sound
C0700.definition: Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

C0701.name: microphone
C0701.definition: Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

C0702.name: microphone array
C0702.definition: Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

C0703.name: processing element
C0703.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the processing part or computer is a device that processes data from input sensors and, based on that processing, activates or actuates output devices.

C0704.name: input sensor
C0704.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the processing part or computer is a device that processes data from input sensors and, based on that processing, activates or actuates output devices.

C0705.name: output device
C0705.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

C0706.name: personal computer
C0706.definition: The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.

C0707.name: workstation
C0707.definition: The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.

C0708.name: graphics processing unit
C0708.definition: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).

C0709.name: distributed computer system
C0709.definition: The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.

C0710.name: communication network
C0710.definition: The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.

C0711.name: central processing unit
C0711.definition: The major components of a computer used as the processing element in a virtual reality (VR) system are the graphics processing unit (GPU), the central processing unit (CPU), and random access memory (RAM).

C0712.name: random access memory
C0712.definition: The major components of a computer used as the processing element in a virtual reality (VR) system are the graphics processing unit (GPU), the central processing unit (CPU), and random access memory (RAM).

C0713.name: rendering
C0713.definition: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.

C0714.name: parallel processing
C0714.definition: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is used to speed up the rendering process because of its inherent parallel processing abilities and the inherent parallelism in the rendering process, and it is therefore very useful for rendering complex graphics and complex scenes that are part of realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.

C0715.name: parallelism
C0715.definition: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is used to speed up the rendering process because of its inherent parallel processing abilities and the inherent parallelism in the rendering process, and it is therefore very useful for rendering complex graphics and complex scenes that are part of realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.

C0716.name: graphics
C0716.definition: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is used to speed up the rendering process because of its inherent parallel processing abilities and the inherent parallelism in the rendering process, and it is therefore very useful for rendering complex graphics and complex scenes that are part of realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.

C0717.name: scene
C0717.definition: The Unity scene view is the developer's interactive view of the scene being created, and it shows the scene while it is being built and lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects, which are the fundamental concepts in Unity, that together comprise the scene.

C0718.name: virtual reality experience
C0718.definition: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is used to speed up the rendering process because of its inherent parallel processing abilities and the inherent parallelism in the rendering process, and it is therefore very useful for rendering complex graphics and complex scenes that are part of realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.

C0719.name: multi-GPU system
C0719.definition: Multi-GPU-enabled systems are typically used for building virtual reality (VR) applications, and a good-quality graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled graphics card or GPU-enabled environment is preferable, especially for rendering.

C0720.name: graphics card
C0720.definition: Multi-GPU-enabled systems are typically used for building virtual reality (VR) applications, and a good-quality graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled graphics card or GPU-enabled environment is preferable, especially for rendering.

C0721.name: multicore processor
C0721.definition: In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default.

C0722.name: computational capacity
C0722.definition: In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default.

C0723.name: unicore processor
C0723.definition: In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default.

C0724.name: extended reality engine
C0724.definition: An extended reality (XR) engine is middleware required to support, develop, and render virtual reality (VR) experiences.

C0725.name: middleware
C0725.definition: Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware.

C0726.name: audio output
C0726.definition: Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality (VR) setup, and it can provide specialized three-dimensional (3D) audio for a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head, and headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

C0727.name: motion platform
C0727.definition: Motion platforms are hardware output devices that move the entire body to produce a sense of physical motion and gravity, conveying a sense of orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks.

C0728.name: sensory output system
C0728.definition: Output devices for virtual reality (VR) experience include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms and treadmills, and other sensory outputs that stimulate the taste and smell sensory organs, namely the tongue and nose.

C0729.name: world-fixed display
C0729.definition: The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.

C0730.name: regular display
C0730.definition: The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.

C0731.name: monoscopic viewing
C0731.definition: A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.

C0732.name: stereoscopic viewing
C0732.definition: A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.

C0733.name: non-see-through head-mounted display
C0733.definition: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

C0734.name: video see-through head-mounted display
C0734.definition: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

C0735.name: cave
C0735.definition: World-fixed displays range from standard monitors to displays that completely surround the user, typically called a cave.

C0736.name: fish tank display
C0736.definition: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

C0737.name: monitor
C0737.definition: World-fixed displays range from standard monitors to displays that completely surround the user, typically called a cave.

C0738.name: optical head tracker
C0738.definition: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

C0739.name: haptic device
C0739.definition: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

C0740.name: stereo perspective view
C0740.definition: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

C0741.name: three-dimensional scene
C0741.definition: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

C0742.name: surround screen
C0742.definition: A more recent world-fixed display example is the surround screen, or cave system, which typically has three to six large screens around the user for visual immersion and is usually driven by a single or group of powerful graphics engines and requires elaborate tracking of the user's movements.

C0743.name: graphics engine
C0743.definition: A more recent world-fixed display example is the surround screen, or cave system, which typically has three to six large screens around the user for visual immersion and is usually driven by a single or group of powerful graphics engines and requires elaborate tracking of the user's movements.

C0744.name: tablet
C0744.definition: Regular displays, which can be mobile or stationary, refer to common tablets or smartphones, are not specialized, are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality (VR), and are mostly used for augmented reality (AR).

C0745.name: non-immersive virtual reality
C0745.definition: Regular displays, which can be mobile or stationary, refer to common tablets or smartphones, are not specialized, are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality (VR), and are mostly used for augmented reality (AR).

C0746.name: three-dimensional audio
C0746.definition: Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality (VR) setup, and it can provide specialized three-dimensional (3D) audio for a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head, and headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

C0747.name: speaker
C0747.definition: Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality (VR) setup, and it can provide specialized three-dimensional (3D) audio for a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head, and headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

C0748.name: headphone
C0748.definition: Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality (VR) setup, and it can provide specialized three-dimensional (3D) audio for a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head, and headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

C0749.name: haptic rendering system
C0749.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0750.name: haptic output
C0750.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0751.name: touch perception
C0751.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0752.name: passive haptic device
C0752.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0753.name: active haptic device
C0753.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0754.name: tactile haptics
C0754.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0755.name: vibrotactile stimulation
C0755.definition: Tactile haptics are haptic devices that provide touch sensations through the skin, and they include vibrotactile stimulation, which uses mechanical vibration of the skin, and electrotactile stimulation, which uses electrodes that pass current through the skin.

C0756.name: electrotactile stimulation
C0756.definition: Tactile haptics are haptic devices that provide touch sensations through the skin, and they include vibrotactile stimulation, which uses mechanical vibration of the skin, and electrotactile stimulation, which uses electrodes that pass current through the skin.

C0757.name: electrode
C0757.definition: Tactile haptics are haptic devices that provide touch sensations through the skin, and they include vibrotactile stimulation, which uses mechanical vibration of the skin, and electrotactile stimulation, which uses electrodes that pass current through the skin.

C0758.name: proprioceptive force-based haptics
C0758.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0759.name: self-grounded haptic device
C0759.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0760.name: world-grounded haptic device
C0760.definition: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

C0761.name: active motion platform
C0761.definition: Motion platforms can be active, meaning they are controlled by computer simulation, or passive, meaning they are controlled by the user with no direct computer control, and passive platforms are likely to result in less motion sickness than active platforms.

C0762.name: passive motion platform
C0762.definition: Motion platforms can be active, meaning they are controlled by computer simulation, or passive, meaning they are controlled by the user with no direct computer control, and passive platforms are likely to result in less motion sickness than active platforms.

C0763.name: omnidirectional treadmill
C0763.definition: Omnidirectional treadmills are common in virtual reality systems and can be active, with computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving, or passive, containing no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and controlled by the user.

C0764.name: active omnidirectional treadmill
C0764.definition: Omnidirectional treadmills are common in virtual reality systems and can be active, with computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving, or passive, containing no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and controlled by the user.

C0765.name: passive omnidirectional treadmill
C0765.definition: Omnidirectional treadmills are common in virtual reality systems and can be active, with computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving, or passive, containing no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and controlled by the user.

C0766.name: augmented reality device
C0766.definition: Augmented reality (AR) devices can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality (spatial AR), head-up displays, and AR contact lenses.

C0767.name: augmented reality headset
C0767.definition: Generally, augmented reality (AR) headsets are larger and more immersive, present more content in the form of real-world content and augmented digital content, and provide a wider field of view.

C0768.name: smart glasses
C0768.definition: Augmented reality (AR) devices can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality (spatial AR), head-up displays, and AR contact lenses.

C0769.name: handheld device
C0769.definition: Augmented reality (AR) devices can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality (spatial AR), head-up displays, and AR contact lenses.

C0770.name: projection-based system
C0770.definition: Augmented reality (AR) devices can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality (spatial AR), head-up displays, and AR contact lenses.

C0771.name: spatial augmented reality
C0771.definition: Augmented reality (AR) devices can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality (spatial AR), head-up displays, and AR contact lenses.

C0772.name: head-up display
C0772.definition: A head-up display (HUD) is an augmented reality (AR) display category that projects images onto a transparent surface, usually a screen or visor; ideally the surface is invisible and only the content is visible, but borders or shades may be visible.

C0773.name: augmented reality contact lens
C0773.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are an emerging display category and a future wearable technology; they are very small, can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens, are not visible to outsiders, and are still in the realm of the future.

C0774.name: Microsoft HoloLens
C0774.definition: The Microsoft HoloLens is one example of an augmented reality (AR) headset, and other such headsets are available.

C0775.name: Google Glass
C0775.definition: Examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices include Microsoft HoloLens as a headset, Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses as smart glasses, and smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices as handheld devices.

C0776.name: Vuzix Blade Glasses
C0776.definition: Examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices include Microsoft HoloLens as a headset, Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses as smart glasses, and smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices as handheld devices.

C0777.name: Nintendo device
C0777.definition: Examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices include Microsoft HoloLens as a headset, Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses as smart glasses, and smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices as handheld devices.

C0778.name: projection keyboard
C0778.definition: Examples of spatial augmented reality (AR) systems discussed as major categories include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping.

C0779.name: interactive projector
C0779.definition: Examples of spatial augmented reality (AR) systems discussed as major categories include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping.

C0780.name: augmented reality sandbox
C0780.definition: Examples of augmented reality (AR) projection-based systems include projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems, while examples of spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) include interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, projection mapping software, laser projectors, and projection keyboards, with interactive projectors and projection keyboards appearing under both categories.

C0781.name: industrial augmented reality system
C0781.definition: Examples of augmented reality (AR) projection-based systems include projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems, while examples of spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) include interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, projection mapping software, laser projectors, and projection keyboards, with interactive projectors and projection keyboards appearing under both categories.

C0782.name: medical system
C0782.definition: Examples of augmented reality (AR) projection-based systems include projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems, while examples of spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) include interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, projection mapping software, laser projectors, and projection keyboards, with interactive projectors and projection keyboards appearing under both categories.

C0783.name: projection mapping software
C0783.definition: Examples of augmented reality (AR) projection-based systems include projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems, while examples of spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) include interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, projection mapping software, laser projectors, and projection keyboards, with interactive projectors and projection keyboards appearing under both categories.

C0784.name: laser projector
C0784.definition: Examples of augmented reality (AR) projection-based systems include projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems, while examples of spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) include interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, projection mapping software, laser projectors, and projection keyboards, with interactive projectors and projection keyboards appearing under both categories.

C0785.name: Innovega
C0785.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research by Google, Innovega, Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens, and Innovega's iOptic system.

C0786.name: Mojo Vision
C0786.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research by Google, Innovega, Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens, and Innovega's iOptic system.

C0787.name: Mojo Lens
C0787.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research by Google, Innovega, Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens, and Innovega's iOptic system.

C0788.name: iOptic system
C0788.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research by Google, Innovega, Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens, and Innovega's iOptic system.

C0789.name: depth sensor
C0789.definition: Augmented reality (AR) headsets typically include built-in sensors, often cameras and depth sensors, and some of these sensors may or may not also be present in virtual reality (VR) headsets.

C0790.name: depth camera
C0790.definition: The Microsoft HoloLens includes two depth cameras, one noise-cancelling microphone, a speaker, a port for attaching headphones, special glasses that project digital content onto the regular real-world view, a tilt mechanism, nose pads, one camera, one projector, sensors, a high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) optical head-mounted display (HMD), and spatial audio capabilities.

C0791.name: port

C0797.name: hologram
C0797.definition: The Microsoft HoloLens integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through its special glasses.

C0798.name: voice command
C0798.definition: Interaction in the Microsoft HoloLens takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions, and the device is equipped with detection of eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.

C0799.name: hand gesture
C0799.definition: Interaction in the Microsoft HoloLens takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions, and the device is equipped with detection of eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.

C0800.name: augmented reality smart glasses
C0800.definition: Compared with augmented reality (AR) headsets, AR smart glasses are lighter, less immersive, wearable devices that resemble standard eyeglasses, usually have a smaller field of view, are less powerful, and are more comfortable to wear for extended periods, whereas AR headsets are more powerful wearables.

C0801.name: natural-language voice command
C0801.definition: Google Glass is an earlier example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that presents data in a format similar to a smartphone, operates hands-free, and supports interaction through natural-language voice commands, with built-in detection of those commands.

C0802.name: gyroscope
C0802.definition: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).

C0803.name: accelerometer
C0803.definition: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).

C0804.name: magnetometer
C0804.definition: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).

C0805.name: ambient light sensor
C0805.definition: Google Glass includes a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, speaker, trackpad, microphone, camera, and projector, but its projector and camera are less powerful than similar components in an augmented reality (AR) headset.

C0806.name: proximity sensor
C0806.definition: Google Glass includes a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, speaker, trackpad, microphone, camera, and projector, but its projector and camera are less powerful than similar components in an augmented reality (AR) headset.

C0807.name: Wi-Fi
C0807.definition: Google Glass includes a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, speaker, trackpad, microphone, camera, and projector, but its projector and camera are less powerful than similar components in an augmented reality (AR) headset.

C0808.name: Bluetooth
C0808.definition: Google Glass includes a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, speaker, trackpad, microphone, camera, and projector, but its projector and camera are less powerful than similar components in an augmented reality (AR) headset.

C0809.name: touchpad
C0809.definition: Google Glass includes a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, speaker, trackpad, microphone, camera, and projector, but its projector and camera are less powerful than similar components in an augmented reality (AR) headset.

C0810.name: Vuzix's Blade
C0810.definition: Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

C0811.name: output actuator
C0811.definition: Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

C0812.name: haptic feedback component
C0812.definition: Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

C0813.name: display engine
C0813.definition: Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

C0814.name: see-through display
C0814.definition: A see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens, which is typically good for mixed reality or augmented reality, enables users to see and interact with the physical world around them, and it adds virtual objects to the real world or visually enhances real objects.

C0815.name: noise-cancelling microphone
C0815.definition: Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

C0816.name: memory storage
C0816.definition: Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

C0817.name: universal serial bus connectivity
