C0817.definition: Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

C0818.name: Epson glasses
C0818.definition: Additional examples of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses include Epson glasses and Magic Leap glasses.

C0819.name: Magic Leap glasses
C0819.definition: Additional examples of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses include Epson glasses and Magic Leap glasses.

C0820.name: handheld augmented reality device
C0820.definition: Handheld augmented reality (AR) devices are familiar devices such as smartphones or tablets and are the most common and accessible devices used in AR.

C0821.name: marker-based augmented reality
C0821.definition: Handheld augmented reality (AR) devices typically rely on two main augmented reality technologies: marker-based AR and markerless AR.

C0822.name: markerless augmented reality
C0822.definition: Handheld augmented reality (AR) devices typically rely on two main augmented reality technologies: marker-based AR and markerless AR.

C0823.name: spatial augmented reality device
C0823.definition: Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices are the third category of augmented reality devices, also known as room-scale augmented reality or tabletop augmented reality, and they typically use projectors to display graphical information on physical objects; unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, they overlay digital content on physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's view of the real world.

C0824.name: spatial augmented reality system
C0824.definition: Major application areas for spatial augmented reality (AR) devices and systems include education, art and design, medical training, industrial applications, museums and exhibits, and entertainment.

C0825.name: projection-based augmented reality system
C0825.definition: Projection-based augmented reality (AR) systems and spatial augmented reality systems generally refer to similar ideas.

C0826.name: air sandbox
C0826.definition: Examples of spatial augmented reality (AR) systems discussed as major categories include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping.

C0827.name: projection mapping
C0827.definition: Examples of spatial augmented reality (AR) systems discussed as major categories include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping.

C0828.name: interactive display
C0828.definition: An interactive projector is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that projects images or interfaces onto any surface, turning the surface into an interactive display; for example, a projector can project an interface onto a tabletop, making the tabletop an interactive display and an augmented reality experience, and Sony Xperia Touch is an example.

C0829.name: Sony Xperia Touch
C0829.definition: An interactive projector is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that projects images or interfaces onto any surface, turning the surface into an interactive display; for example, a projector can project an interface onto a tabletop, making the tabletop an interactive display and an augmented reality experience, and Sony Xperia Touch is an example.

C0830.name: three-dimensional camera
C0830.definition: An air sandbox is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that uses a projector and a sensor, such as a three-dimensional (3D) camera like Microsoft Kinect, to project a topographic map onto a physical box of sand and update the map in real time when users move the sand or gesture, allowing two to three users to interact simultaneously.

C0831.name: infrared sensor
C0831.definition: A projection keyboard is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that projects a virtual keyboard onto a flat surface, converting that surface into an interactive keyboard, and it may use infrared sensors to detect finger positions, which is the more common way to handle key-press interaction.

C0832.name: virtual keyboard
C0832.definition: A projection keyboard is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that projects a virtual keyboard onto a flat surface, converting that surface into an interactive keyboard, and it may use infrared sensors to detect finger positions, which is the more common way to handle key-press interaction.

C0833.name: TouchDesigner
C0833.definition: Projection mapping technology is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality (AR) in which software solutions such as TouchDesigner, MadMapper, or HeavyM are used with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional (3D) space without a surface, for example projecting a map or a model of the Earth in air.

C0834.name: MadMapper
C0834.definition: Projection mapping technology is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality (AR) in which software solutions such as TouchDesigner, MadMapper, or HeavyM are used with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional (3D) space without a surface, for example projecting a map or a model of the Earth in air.

C0835.name: HeavyM
C0835.definition: Projection mapping technology is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality (AR) in which software solutions such as TouchDesigner, MadMapper, or HeavyM are used with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional (3D) space without a surface, for example projecting a map or a model of the Earth in air.

C0836.name: projection mapping display
C0836.definition: Projection mapping displays can be interacted with by rotating, pinching, zooming in, or zooming out.

C0837.name: wearable technology
C0837.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are an emerging display category and a future wearable technology; they are very small, can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens, are not visible to outsiders, and are still in the realm of the future.

C0838.name: imager
C0838.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can contain miniaturized components placed on the lens, including imagers made on complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, a display, wireless components, motion sensors, and other sophisticated components.

C0839.name: complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology
C0839.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can contain miniaturized components placed on the lens, including imagers made on complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, a display, wireless components, motion sensors, and other sophisticated components.

C0840.name: wireless component
C0840.definition: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can contain miniaturized components placed on the lens, including imagers made on complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, a display, wireless components, motion sensors, and other sophisticated components.

C0841.name: smart contact lens project
C0841.definition: Examples of current activities developing augmented reality (AR) contact lenses include Google's smart contact lens project, InnoVega's eye optic system, and Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens.

C0842.name: eye optic system
C0842.definition: Examples of current activities developing augmented reality (AR) contact lenses include Google's smart contact lens project, InnoVega's eye optic system, and Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens.

C0843.name: sense-organ tracking
C0843.definition: Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user.

C0844.name: body-part tracking
C0844.definition: Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user.

C0845.name: environment tracking
C0845.definition: Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user.

C0846.name: sense organ
C0846.definition: The perceptual process proceeds from sensing, which is the lowest level, to perception, which is at a very abstract level, and perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.

C0847.name: eye
C0847.definition: Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.

C0848.name: ear
C0848.definition: Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.

C0849.name: body-controlled degree of freedom
C0849.definition: Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.

C0850.name: avatar
C0850.definition: Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone.

C0851.name: virtual hand
C0851.definition: Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone.

C0852.name: facial expression
C0852.definition: Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone.

C0853.name: matched zone
C0853.definition: A matched zone is a place where the real world and the virtual world perfectly align; it corresponds to the safe real-world region where a user's physical movement is restricted, although the virtual world is not similarly confined, and movement within that region is translated to movement in other parts of the virtual world.

C0854.name: movement
C0854.definition: For tracking of the user's other body parts, perfect matching is not required; approximate movement or an approximate representation of the body-part movement in the virtual world can provide a good experience.

C0855.name: input signal
C0855.definition: A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking.

C0856.name: body configuration
C0856.definition: A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking.

C0857.name: physical object
C0857.definition: Tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user may involve tracking physical objects in the real world around the user; it is more important in augmented reality (AR), but also important in virtual reality (VR).

C0858.name: real-world view
C0858.definition: In augmented reality (AR), a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in three-dimensional (3D) space.

C0859.name: digital content
C0859.definition: In augmented reality (AR), a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in three-dimensional (3D) space.

C0860.name: user tracking
C0860.definition: In virtual reality (VR), tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, to reduce harm; for this, tracking the user is not useful, and the environment itself must be tracked.

C0861.name: touch feedback
C0861.definition: In virtual reality (VR), tracked physical objects may be matched in the virtual world so that the user receives touch feedback while interacting with them, giving a better, more natural experience.

C0862.name: telepresence
C0862.definition: In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

C0863.name: live capture
C0863.definition: In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

C0864.name: tracking method
C0864.definition: The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

C0865.name: tracker position
C0865.definition: The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

C0866.name: tracking process
C0866.definition: The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

C0867.name: tracker types
C0867.definition: The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

C0868.name: outside-in tracking
C0868.definition: Based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking, tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking.

C0869.name: inside-out tracking
C0869.definition: Based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking, tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking.

C0870.name: external sensor
C0870.definition: In outside-in tracking, the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors or trackers; instead, external trackers or sensors in the real world, such as cameras or markers, provide data that helps the system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation.

C0871.name: motion
C0871.definition: In outside-in tracking, the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors or trackers; instead, external trackers or sensors in the real world, such as cameras or markers, provide data that helps the system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation.

C0872.name: sensor range
C0872.definition: Outside-in tracking is restricted to the specific area where its external sensors are placed and works only when the user is in that environment within the sensor range, whereas inside-out tracking has no such restriction because the user wears the sensors or the sensors are attached to the user.

C0873.name: Intel Project Alloy
C0873.definition: Examples of inside-out tracking are Microsoft HoloLens, Intel Project Alloy, and Qualcomm VR820.

C0874.name: Qualcomm VR820
C0874.definition: Examples of inside-out tracking are Microsoft HoloLens, Intel Project Alloy, and Qualcomm VR820.

C0875.name: inside-out
C0875.definition: There are two broad ways to obtain input for tracking: inside-out and outside-in.

C0876.name: outside-in
C0876.definition: There are two broad ways to obtain input for tracking: inside-out and outside-in.

C0877.name: calibration
C0877.definition: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

C0878.name: integration
C0878.definition: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

C0879.name: drift correction
C0879.definition: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

C0880.name: sensor error
C0880.definition: In the tracking process, calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.

C0881.name: sensory measurement
C0881.definition: In the tracking process, integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.

C0882.name: estimation error
C0882.definition: In the tracking process, drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.

C0883.name: linear acceleration
C0883.definition: In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes.

C0884.name: magnetic field strength
C0884.definition: In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes.

C0885.name: drift error
C0885.definition: Inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation but can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

C0886.name: measured angular velocity
C0886.definition: In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a.

C0887.name: actual angular velocity
C0887.definition: In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a.

C0888.name: measurement error
C0888.definition: In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a.

C0889.name: calibration model
C0889.definition: One simple calibration model assumes a linear relationship between measured angular velocity (omega_g) and actual angular velocity (omega_a), for example omega_g = a + b omega_a, where the ideal condition omega_g = omega_a corresponds to a = 0 and b = 1, but this ideal condition never happens in practice and the linear relationship is not the only possible relationship.

C0890.name: linear relationship
C0890.definition: One simple calibration model assumes a linear relationship between measured angular velocity (omega_g) and actual angular velocity (omega_a), for example omega_g = a + b omega_a, where the ideal condition omega_g = omega_a corresponds to a = 0 and b = 1, but this ideal condition never happens in practice and the linear relationship is not the only possible relationship.

C0891.name: paired samples
C0891.definition: The presented calibration uses many, sometimes thousands, paired samples from two sensors: a cheap, inaccurate inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor that produces the measured values (omega_g), and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values (omega_a), although the benchmark is very close rather than exact or ideal.

C0892.name: benchmark sensor
C0892.definition: The presented calibration uses many, sometimes thousands, paired samples from two sensors: a cheap, inaccurate inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor that produces the measured values (omega_g), and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values (omega_a), although the benchmark is very close rather than exact or ideal.

C0893.name: linear least squares regression
C0893.definition: A simple calibration method compares the paired samples by computing, for n pairs, the sum of the squared differences between the expression C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual values omega_a, and it finds the constants C1 and C2 that minimize this sum; this classical optimization is linear least squares regression, one of many techniques that is used here for simplicity.

C0894.name: calibrated value
C0894.definition: After the constants C1 and C2 are determined, calibration mathematically transforms the cheap sensor reading into a calibrated value omega_cal, defined as omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g, mapping the inexpensive measured angular velocity omega_g to the closest possible match with the actual value rather than by using an actually expensive or highly accurate sensor.

C0895.name: initial orientation
C0895.definition: Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0.

C0896.name: initial alignment
C0896.definition: Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0.

C0897.name: tracking system
C0897.definition: A simplifying assumption for understanding registration is that the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on is taken as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction.

C0898.name: reflector
C0898.definition: Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags; it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and the process is simpler when such aids are present.

C0899.name: tag
C0899.definition: Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags; it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and the process is simpler when such aids are present.

C0900.name: current sensor orientation
C0900.definition: Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

C0901.name: calibrated angular velocity sample
C0901.definition: Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

C0902.name: sampling interval
C0902.definition: Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

C0903.name: sensor data stream
C0903.definition: Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

C0904.name: angular velocity sample
C0904.definition: A calibrated angular velocity sample W_cal_i is the angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at instant i, and it indicates a change in orientation equal to W_cal_i multiplied by the sampling interval delta_t.

C0905.name: gyroscopic sensor
C0905.definition: A calibrated angular velocity sample W_cal_i is the angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at instant i, and it indicates a change in orientation equal to W_cal_i multiplied by the sampling interval delta_t.

C0906.name: drift
C0906.definition: Drift correction is usually done with the help of extra sensors and, in general, requires at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift.

C0907.name: drift-corrected orientation
C0907.definition: A classic approach to drift correction combines the two individually computed orientations at the same time instant using the expression theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where theta_gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values at the kth instant, theta_ck is the orientation obtained with a camera at the kth instant, theta_dk is the drift-corrected orientation, and alpha is the gain parameter, a normalized value between 0 and 1.

C0908.name: gain parameter
C0908.definition: A classic approach to drift correction combines the two individually computed orientations at the same time instant using the expression theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where theta_gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values at the kth instant, theta_ck is the orientation obtained with a camera at the kth instant, theta_dk is the drift-corrected orientation, and alpha is the gain parameter, a normalized value between 0 and 1.

C0909.name: tracking technology
C0909.definition: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

C0910.name: electromechanical tracking
C0910.definition: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

C0911.name: electromagnetic tracking
C0911.definition: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

C0912.name: acoustic tracking
C0912.definition: Acoustic tracking, also called ultrasonic tracking, uses ultrasonic signals from stationary transmitters, which can be called speakers, to determine the real-time position of receivers, which can be called microphones, that are attached to a head-mounted display (HMD), so the head's position or orientation can be tracked.

C0913.name: vision-based tracking
C0913.definition: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

C0914.name: inertial tracking
C0914.definition: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

C0915.name: location-based tracking
C0915.definition: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

C0916.name: hybrid tracking
C0916.definition: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

C0917.name: electromechanical tracker
C0917.definition: Electromechanical trackers consist of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

C0918.name: kinematic structure
C0918.definition: Electromechanical trackers consist of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

C0919.name: link
C0919.definition: Electromechanical trackers consist of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

C0920.name: joint
C0920.definition: The Unity physics engine includes rigid bodies, colliders, joints, physics articulation, and character controllers as components essential to give a realistic feeling.

C0921.name: world-fixed tracker
C0921.definition: Electromechanical trackers are of two types: world-fixed trackers and wearable trackers.

C0922.name: wearable tracker
C0922.definition: Electromechanical trackers are of two types: world-fixed trackers and wearable trackers.

C0923.name: counterbalance
C0923.definition: A world-fixed electromechanical tracker is a setup that is quite cumbersome, with a display attached to an electromechanically tracked setup that has mechanical pivoting, tracking sensors, and a counterbalance to make it stable.

C0924.name: IGS 190
C0924.definition: Wearable electromechanical trackers include products such as IGS 190, Gypsy 6, Gypsy Gyro, and exoskeleton tracker.

C0925.name: Gypsy 6
C0925.definition: Wearable electromechanical trackers include products such as IGS 190, Gypsy 6, Gypsy Gyro, and exoskeleton tracker.

C0926.name: Gypsy Gyro
C0926.definition: Wearable electromechanical trackers include products such as IGS 190, Gypsy 6, Gypsy Gyro, and exoskeleton tracker.

C0927.name: exoskeleton tracker
C0927.definition: Wearable electromechanical trackers include products such as IGS 190, Gypsy 6, Gypsy Gyro, and exoskeleton tracker.

C0928.name: electromagnetic tracker
C0928.definition: Electromagnetic trackers are non-contact position measurement devices in which a stationary transmitter in the environment produces a magnetic field, and a receiver attached to the headset moves with the head, and the receiver's real-time position is obtained from the magnetic field direction.

C0929.name: transmitter
C0929.definition: Electromagnetic trackers are non-contact position measurement devices in which a stationary transmitter in the environment produces a magnetic field, and a receiver attached to the headset moves with the head, and the receiver's real-time position is obtained from the magnetic field direction.

C0930.name: magnetic field
C0930.definition: Electromagnetic trackers are non-contact position measurement devices in which a stationary transmitter in the environment produces a magnetic field, and a receiver attached to the headset moves with the head, and the receiver's real-time position is obtained from the magnetic field direction.

C0931.name: receiver
C0931.definition: Electromagnetic trackers are non-contact position measurement devices in which a stationary transmitter in the environment produces a magnetic field, and a receiver attached to the headset moves with the head, and the receiver's real-time position is obtained from the magnetic field direction.

C0932.name: antenna
C0932.definition: In an electromagnetic tracker, the transmitter generally has three antennas that produce three orthogonal magnetic fields, and these fields generate alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC) in the receiver; the resulting currents help track the head's position relative to a fixed position in the environment.

C0933.name: alternating current
C0933.definition: In an electromagnetic tracker, the transmitter generally has three antennas that produce three orthogonal magnetic fields, and these fields generate alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC) in the receiver; the resulting currents help track the head's position relative to a fixed position in the environment.

C0934.name: direct current
C0934.definition: In an electromagnetic tracker, the transmitter generally has three antennas that produce three orthogonal magnetic fields, and these fields generate alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC) in the receiver; the resulting currents help track the head's position relative to a fixed position in the environment.

C0935.name: ultrasonic signal
C0935.definition: Acoustic tracking, also called ultrasonic tracking, uses ultrasonic signals from stationary transmitters, which can be called speakers, to determine the real-time position of receivers, which can be called microphones, that are attached to a head-mounted display (HMD), so the head's position or orientation can be tracked.

C0936.name: line of sight
C0936.definition: Acoustic or ultrasonic tracking requires line of sight between the transmitter and receiver, with no obstacle in between, whereas electromagnetic tracking does not require this line of sight.

C0937.name: vision-based tracker
C0937.definition: Vision-based trackers are more prevalent trackers that determine poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras.

C0938.name: optical sensor
C0938.definition: Vision-based trackers are more prevalent trackers that determine poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras.

C0939.name: visible light sensor
C0939.definition: The three main categories of optical sensors that can be deployed to detect or track a pose are infrared sensors, visible light sensors, and three-dimensional (3D) structure sensors.

C0940.name: three-dimensional structure sensor
C0940.definition: The three main categories of optical sensors that can be deployed to detect or track a pose are infrared sensors, visible light sensors, and three-dimensional (3D) structure sensors.

C0941.name: infrared tracking
C0941.definition: Infrared tracking is considered to be among the earliest vision-based tracking techniques developed and used in virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

C0942.name: target
C0942.definition: Infrared tracking uses targets that emit or reflect light, which makes detection easy due to high brightness compared with the surroundings.

C0943.name: infrared sensing
C0943.definition: Infrared tracking is robust to adverse illumination effects such as poor ambient lighting or harsh shadows because it relies on infrared sensing rather than visible light sensing.

C0944.name: visible light sensing
C0944.definition: Infrared tracking is robust to adverse illumination effects such as poor ambient lighting or harsh shadows because it relies on infrared sensing rather than visible light sensing.

C0945.name: outside looking in
C0945.definition: Infrared tracking can be done in two ways: outside looking in and inside looking out.

C0946.name: inside looking out
C0946.definition: Infrared tracking can be done in two ways: outside looking in and inside looking out.

C0947.name: visible light tracking
C0947.definition: Visible light tracking uses visible light sensors or optical cameras; optical cameras are the most common optical sensor type and are available in almost all consumer-grade electronic devices, including laptops, smartphones, and tablet personal computers (PCs), and in wearable devices, giving an abundant supply of such sensors.

C0948.name: optical camera
C0948.definition: Visible light tracking uses visible light sensors or optical cameras; optical cameras are the most common optical sensor type and are available in almost all consumer-grade electronic devices, including laptops, smartphones, and tablet personal computers (PCs), and in wearable devices, giving an abundant supply of such sensors.

C0949.name: fiducial tracking
C0949.definition: Visible light tracking is classified into three tracking techniques: fiducial tracking, natural feature tracking, and model-based tracking.

C0950.name: natural feature tracking
C0950.definition: Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features already present in the natural environment, and it requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques.

C0951.name: model-based tracking
C0951.definition: Visible light tracking is classified into three tracking techniques: fiducial tracking, natural feature tracking, and model-based tracking.

C0952.name: fiducial
C0952.definition: Fiducial tracking adds fiducials, which are artificial landmarks in the environment, to aid registration and tracking of the object being tracked.

C0953.name: multi-ring fiducial
C0953.definition: The complexity of fiducial tracking depends on the kind of fiducial used, such as small colored light-emitting diodes (LEDs) or pieces of paper, multi-ring fiducials for detection at greater distances, proportional width ring fiducials whose appearance changes with distance, or constant width ring fiducials whose ring width remains constant.

C0954.name: proportional width ring fiducial
C0954.definition: The complexity of fiducial tracking depends on the kind of fiducial used, such as small colored light-emitting diodes (LEDs) or pieces of paper, multi-ring fiducials for detection at greater distances, proportional width ring fiducials whose appearance changes with distance, or constant width ring fiducials whose ring width remains constant.

C0955.name: constant width ring fiducial
C0955.definition: The complexity of fiducial tracking depends on the kind of fiducial used, such as small colored light-emitting diodes (LEDs) or pieces of paper, multi-ring fiducials for detection at greater distances, proportional width ring fiducials whose appearance changes with distance, or constant width ring fiducials whose ring width remains constant.

C0956.name: visual light-based sensing
C0956.definition: Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features already present in the natural environment, and it requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques.

C0957.name: camera pose
C0957.definition: Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features already present in the natural environment, and it requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques.

C0958.name: image processing
C0958.definition: Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features already present in the natural environment, and it requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques.

C0959.name: feature
C0959.definition: Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features already present in the natural environment, and it requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques.

C0960.name: point
C0960.definition: In natural feature tracking, the advanced image processing algorithms or computer vision techniques detect features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked, such as points, corners, and line intersections.

C0961.name: corner
C0961.definition: In natural feature tracking, the advanced image processing algorithms or computer vision techniques detect features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked, such as points, corners, and line intersections.

C0962.name: line intersection
C0962.definition: In natural feature tracking, the advanced image processing algorithms or computer vision techniques detect features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked, such as points, corners, and line intersections.

C0963.name: feature descriptor
C0963.definition: In natural feature tracking, unique descriptors are calculated for each detected feature, and their role is to identify and differentiate one feature from other features.

C0964.name: scale invariant feature transform
C0964.definition: Popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking include scale invariant feature transform (SIFT), speeded up robust features (SURF), binary robust independent elementary features (BRIEF), and binary robust invariant scalable key points (BRISK).

C0965.name: speeded up robust features
C0965.definition: Popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking include scale invariant feature transform (SIFT), speeded up robust features (SURF), binary robust independent elementary features (BRIEF), and binary robust invariant scalable key points (BRISK).

C0966.name: binary robust independent elementary features
C0966.definition: Popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking include scale invariant feature transform (SIFT), speeded up robust features (SURF), binary robust independent elementary features (BRIEF), and binary robust invariant scalable key points (BRISK).

C0967.name: binary robust invariant scalable key points
C0967.definition: Popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking include scale invariant feature transform (SIFT), speeded up robust features (SURF), binary robust independent elementary features (BRIEF), and binary robust invariant scalable key points (BRISK).

C0968.name: visible light-based sensing
C0968.definition: Model-based tracking is the third category of visible light-based sensing.

C0969.name: simultaneous localization and mapping
C0969.definition: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it, and as time passes the map is updated with the object's changing position, enabling real-time tracking.

C0970.name: map
C0970.definition: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it, and as time passes the map is updated with the object's changing position, enabling real-time tracking.

C0971.name: localization
C0971.definition: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it, and as time passes the map is updated with the object's changing position, enabling real-time tracking.

C0972.name: robot navigation
C0972.definition: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) was originally developed for robot navigation and subsequently adapted for augmented reality.

C0973.name: parallel tracking and mapping
C0973.definition: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) is a further optimization of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) that allows tracking of the camera and mapping of the environment as separate activities.

C0974.name: mapping
C0974.definition: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) is a further optimization of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) that allows tracking of the camera and mapping of the environment as separate activities.

C0975.name: tracking accuracy
C0975.definition: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) improved both the accuracy of tracking and the overall performance.

C0976.name: performance
C0976.definition: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) improved both the accuracy of tracking and the overall performance.

C0977.name: computational requirement
C0977.definition: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) is more suitable for smaller environments because the computational requirements for larger environments are quite high.

C0978.name: three-dimensional structure tracking
C0978.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

C0979.name: commercial sensor
C0979.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

C0980.name: three-dimensional position
C0980.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

C0981.name: three-dimensional model
C0981.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

C0982.name: structure
C0982.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

C0983.name: environment
C0983.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

C0984.name: augmentation
C0984.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

C0985.name: three-dimensional structure information
C0985.definition: Commercial sensors capable of detecting 3D structure information from the environment became affordable in recent years, a trend that started with the introduction of the Microsoft Kinect device, and similar devices are available.

C0986.name: Kinect Fusion
C0986.definition: Kinect Fusion, an augmented reality (AR) system by Microsoft and an example of 3D structure tracking, uses data from the Kinect's structured light depth sensor to create high-quality 3D models of real objects and environments, and the models are also used for tracking the pose of the Kinect.

C0987.name: structured light depth sensor
C0987.definition: Kinect Fusion, an augmented reality (AR) system by Microsoft and an example of 3D structure tracking, uses data from the Kinect's structured light depth sensor to create high-quality 3D models of real objects and environments, and the models are also used for tracking the pose of the Kinect.

C0988.name: inertial tracker
C0988.definition: Inertial trackers are self-contained sensors that measure rate of change in object orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration, and they measure only changes rather than absolute values.

C0989.name: microelectromechanical system
C0989.definition: Inertial trackers are typically based on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and are part of the device that the user is using, for example most smartphones and head-mounted displays (HMDs) nowadays, so they have no range limitation and can be readily used for tracking.

C0990.name: hybrid software-level sensor
C0990.definition: Hybrid software-level sensors can be designed using the primary inertial sensors (a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer) and can be part of the device.

C0991.name: electromechanical tracking sensor
C0991.definition: Basic types of tracking sensors typically used include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional (3D) structure sensing, and light-based sensing.

C0992.name: electromagnetic tracking sensor
C0992.definition: Basic types of tracking sensors typically used include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional (3D) structure sensing, and light-based sensing.

C0993.name: three-dimensional structure sensing
C0993.definition: Basic types of tracking sensors typically used include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional (3D) structure sensing, and light-based sensing.

C0994.name: light-based sensing
C0994.definition: Basic types of tracking sensors typically used include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional (3D) structure sensing, and light-based sensing.

C0995.name: acoustic sensing
C0995.definition: Sensing approaches that do not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories include acoustic sensing and the global positioning system (GPS).

C0996.name: positional tracking
C0996.definition: The global positioning system (GPS) is a positional tracking device that is particularly useful in outdoor environments.

C0997.name: real time kinematic
C0997.definition: Real time kinematic (RTK) technology can be used with a basic global positioning system (GPS) sensor to improve detection accuracy by using global positioning system signal carrier waves for measurement, providing further accuracy than the basic global positioning system.

C0998.name: hybrid tracking system
C0998.definition: The global positioning system (GPS) is typically utilized when accurate position registration is not important, when an approximation is good enough, or as part of a hybrid tracking system with other tracking systems.

C0999.name: motion capture
C0999.definition: Motion capture is a technique for digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans, and it can be based on any tracking method, so it is not a fundamentally new tracking method.

C1000.name: wearable suit
C1000.definition: Motion capture is packaged as wearable suits that include tracking sensors, typically using one or two facial trackers and four or five full body tracking devices that can be cameras, and it records the movements of users who wear the suits and make movements.

C1001.name: facial tracker
C1001.definition: Motion capture is packaged as wearable suits that include tracking sensors, typically using one or two facial trackers and four or five full body tracking devices that can be cameras, and it records the movements of users who wear the suits and make movements.

C1002.name: full body tracking device
C1002.definition: Motion capture is packaged as wearable suits that include tracking sensors, typically using one or two facial trackers and four or five full body tracking devices that can be cameras, and it records the movements of users who wear the suits and make movements.

C1003.name: real-time tracking
C1003.definition: Motion capture need not be real-time tracking; it can be non-real-time tracking as well.

C1004.name: non-real-time tracking
C1004.definition: Motion capture need not be real-time tracking; it can be non-real-time tracking as well.

C1005.name: external display
C1005.definition: Eye-tracking systems can be part of other trackers and can be head-mounted or remotely attached to a display or an external display.

C1006.name: optical tracking
C1006.definition: Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

C1007.name: camera-based tracking device
C1007.definition: Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

C1008.name: infrared lighting-based eye tracking
C1008.definition: Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

C1009.name: video-oculography
C1009.definition: Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

C1010.name: gaze point
C1010.definition: Eye-tracking systems typically track the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

C1011.name: gaze area
C1011.definition: Eye-tracking systems typically track the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

C1012.name: hybrid tracker
C1012.definition: A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that uses two or more basic tracking systems or approaches, formed by combining basic tracking methods, and emotion capture is an example of a hybrid tracker.

C1013.name: emotion capture
C1013.definition: A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that uses two or more basic tracking systems or approaches, formed by combining basic tracking methods, and emotion capture is an example of a hybrid tracker.

C1014.name: single-technology-based tracking
C1014.definition: Typically, hybrid trackers have been found to perform better than single-technology-based tracking.

C1015.name: virtual reality software
C1015.definition: The role of virtual reality (VR) software is to drive virtual reality hardware or augmented reality (AR) hardware, not merely to drive the hardware, so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.

C1016.name: augmented reality hardware
C1016.definition: The role of virtual reality (VR) software is to drive virtual reality hardware or augmented reality (AR) hardware, not merely to drive the hardware, so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.

C1017.name: human sense organs
C1017.definition: The role of virtual reality (VR) software is to drive virtual reality hardware or augmented reality (AR) hardware, not merely to drive the hardware, so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.

C1018.name: human senses
C1018.definition: The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

C1019.name: interaction design
C1019.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

C1020.name: perceptual design
C1020.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

C1021.name: modeling
C1021.definition: The data flow between a user and virtual reality (VR) hardware requires proper interaction design and modeling for the user's interaction with input devices, perceptual design and modeling so that stimuli generated by output devices suitably stimulate the user's sense organs, and software to process input data and generate output data.

C1022.name: virtual reality engine
C1022.definition: A layered virtual reality (VR) software architecture consists, from top to bottom, of the VR application layer, the software development kit (SDK) layer, the VR engine or game engine layer, the native rendering library layer with libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan and Direct3D, the operating system layer, and the hardware layer including the graphics processing unit (GPU); the application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK layer calls the VR engine layer, the VR engine calls the application programming interfaces (APIs) of the native rendering libraries to perform rendering, the native rendering libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, and the operating system layer sits on top of the hardware layer.

C1023.name: software-and-database component
C1023.definition: The software part of the virtual reality (VR) data-flow diagram is represented by two components: the virtual reality engine and a software-and-database component.

C1024.name: environment modeling
C1024.definition: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.

C1025.name: stereoscopic output view
C1025.definition: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.

C1026.name: high-level description
C1026.definition: Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware.

C1027.name: low-level detail
C1027.definition: Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware.

C1028.name: software library
C1028.definition: Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware.

C1029.name: platform
C1029.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

C1030.name: operating system
C1030.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

C1031.name: device driver
C1031.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

C1032.name: display output
C1032.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

C1033.name: game engine
C1033.definition: A game engine can be used as middleware for virtual reality (VR) application development; game engines are generally developed for games, which need not be immersive VR games, and can be adopted for VR development or specific VR engines can be developed.

C1034.name: virtual world generator
C1034.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality (VR) software system, treated as a black box whose internal operation is not considered.

C1035.name: black box
C1035.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality (VR) software system, treated as a black box whose internal operation is not considered.

C1036.name: head tracker
C1036.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

C1037.name: head position
C1037.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

C1038.name: head orientation
C1038.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

C1039.name: game controller
C1039.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

C1040.name: input event
C1040.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

C1041.name: queue
C1041.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

C1042.name: renderer
C1042.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) must maintain an internal reality that appears real to the user, convert incoming input into output so that renderers can extract information and calculate outputs for their displays, and keep output devices synchronized with the input data to maintain an input-output match.

C1043.name: synchronization
C1043.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) must maintain an internal reality that appears real to the user, convert incoming input into output so that renderers can extract information and calculate outputs for their displays, and keep output devices synchronized with the input data to maintain an input-output match.

C1044.name: input-output match
C1044.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) must maintain an internal reality that appears real to the user, convert incoming input into output so that renderers can extract information and calculate outputs for their displays, and keep output devices synchronized with the input data to maintain an input-output match.

C1045.name: visual renderer
C1045.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) can use several output renderers, including a visual renderer that generates a visual display, an aural renderer that generates an aural display sensed by the ears, and a haptic renderer that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin, along with other possible renderers.

C1046.name: aural renderer
C1046.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) can use several output renderers, including a visual renderer that generates a visual display, an aural renderer that generates an aural display sensed by the ears, and a haptic renderer that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin, along with other possible renderers.

C1047.name: aural display
C1047.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) can use several output renderers, including a visual renderer that generates a visual display, an aural renderer that generates an aural display sensed by the ears, and a haptic renderer that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin, along with other possible renderers.

C1048.name: haptic renderer
C1048.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) can use several output renderers, including a visual renderer that generates a visual display, an aural renderer that generates an aural display sensed by the ears, and a haptic renderer that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin, along with other possible renderers.

C1049.name: haptic display
C1049.definition: The virtual world generator (VWG) can use several output renderers, including a visual renderer that generates a visual display, an aural renderer that generates an aural display sensed by the ears, and a haptic renderer that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin, along with other possible renderers.

C1050.name: triangular mesh
C1050.definition: Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input.

C1051.name: material surface property
C1051.definition: A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces.

C1052.name: physical surface property
C1052.definition: A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces.

C1053.name: light
C1053.definition: A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces.

C1054.name: sound
C1054.definition: Sound is vibration in a medium, usually air but also water, other gases, liquids, or solids, and it requires a medium to propagate, so there is no sound in a vacuum unlike light, which can propagate without a medium or through a vacuum.

C1055.name: force
C1055.definition: A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces.

C1056.name: computer graphics
C1056.definition: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.

C1057.name: computer-generated image
C1057.definition: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.

C1058.name: synthetic model
C1058.definition: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.

C1059.name: texture mapping
C1059.definition: One possibility for creating a virtual world is texture mapping, in which camera images of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object; this is a common computer-graphics operation that virtual reality (VR) software should ideally support.

C1060.name: synthetic object
C1060.definition: One possibility for creating a virtual world is texture mapping, in which camera images of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object; this is a common computer-graphics operation that virtual reality (VR) software should ideally support.

C1061.name: matched motion
C1061.definition: Matched motion in virtual reality (VR) is the maintenance of correspondence between a user's motions in the real world and the virtual world.

C1062.name: obstacle mismatch
C1062.definition: In an immersive virtual reality (VR) application that is not carefully implemented, an obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle.

C1063.name: virtual obstacle
C1063.definition: In an immersive virtual reality (VR) application that is not carefully implemented, an obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle.

C1064.name: physical obstacle
C1064.definition: In an immersive virtual reality (VR) application that is not carefully implemented, an obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle.

C1065.name: user locomotion
C1065.definition: User locomotion in virtual reality (VR), which is closely related to matched motion, is moving oneself in the virtual world while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched; it is motivated because users often want to move well outside the matched zone.

C1066.name: locomotion operation
C1066.definition: Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.

C1067.name: vehicle metaphor
C1067.definition: A popular option for user locomotion in virtual reality (VR) is operating a game controller, mouse, or keyboard so the user's avatar can walk, run, jump, swim, climb, board a vehicle, and operate its controls while the user remains seated; the vehicle option is a vehicle metaphor.

C1068.name: physics support
C1068.definition: Physics support is a required key support in a virtual world generator, in addition to computer graphics and computer vision support for rendering, locomotion support, and matched motion support.

C1069.name: locomotion support
C1069.definition: Physics support is a required key support in a virtual world generator, in addition to computer graphics and computer vision support for rendering, locomotion support, and matched motion support.

C1070.name: matched motion support
C1070.definition: Physics support is a required key support in a virtual world generator, in addition to computer graphics and computer vision support for rendering, locomotion support, and matched motion support.

C1071.name: object motion
C1071.definition: In most cases, object motion in a virtual world generator should be governed by basic laws of mechanics; support for basic laws should be good enough, while support for advanced laws can make motion more realistic, which sometimes may be desirable.

C1072.name: basic laws of mechanics
C1072.definition: In most cases, object motion in a virtual world generator should be governed by basic laws of mechanics; support for basic laws should be good enough, while support for advanced laws can make motion more realistic, which sometimes may be desirable.

C1073.name: gravity
C1073.definition: Physics support in a virtual world generator should make a dropped ball accelerate toward the ground due to gravity rather than move it at constant speed.

C1074.name: collision support
C1074.definition: Collision support in a virtual world generator should ideally include collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.

C1075.name: collision detection
C1075.definition: Collision support in a virtual world generator should ideally include collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.

C1076.name: collision response
C1076.definition: Collision support in a virtual world generator should ideally include collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.

C1077.name: collision
C1077.definition: Collision support in a virtual world generator should ideally include collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.

C1078.name: body
C1078.definition: Collision support in a virtual world generator should ideally include collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.

C1079.name: surface
C1079.definition: Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

C1080.name: light source
C1080.definition: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.

C1081.name: illumination
C1081.definition: Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

C1082.name: smell
C1082.definition: The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

C1083.name: networked collaborative virtual reality experience
C1083.definition: A networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is a collaborative virtual reality experience created over a network, in which a shared virtual world is maintained by a system or a server, although such a network experience may not be required everywhere.

C1084.name: collaborative virtual reality experience
C1084.definition: A networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is a collaborative virtual reality experience created over a network, in which a shared virtual world is maintained by a system or a server, although such a network experience may not be required everywhere.

C1085.name: shared virtual world
