C1085.definition: A networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is a collaborative virtual reality experience created over a network, in which a shared virtual world is maintained by a system or a server, although such a network experience may not be required everywhere.

C1086.name: physical collision
C1086.definition: In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, each user has a distinct matched zone; matched zones may overlap in the real world, but most often they are disjoint and distributed around the Earth, so unwanted physical collision must be avoided when users are close, while users spread around the globe have no possibility of physical collision.

C1087.name: body language
C1087.definition: In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, the virtual world generator (VWG) should support eye movements, facial expressions, and body language when social interaction is important, and the burden of matched motion may increase as users meet each other.

C1088.name: social interaction
C1088.definition: In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, the virtual world generator (VWG) should support eye movements, facial expressions, and body language when social interaction is important, and the burden of matched motion may increase as users meet each other.

C1089.name: driver
C1089.definition: A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

C1090.name: application programming interface
C1090.definition: A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements.

C1091.name: tracking data
C1091.definition: A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

C1092.name: graphical rendering library
C1092.definition: A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

C1093.name: locomotion
C1093.definition: The travel part of navigation, also called locomotion, is the motor component of navigation and refers to the actual movement between two locations.

C1094.name: physics
C1094.definition: A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

C1095.name: collaborative virtual reality
C1095.definition: A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

C1096.name: lighting model
C1096.definition: In the computer graphics pipeline, the third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene; if a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced, whereas properly assigning colors can give a more realistic perception.

C1097.name: audio support
C1097.definition: When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required.

C1098.name: OpenSimulator
C1098.definition: OpenSimulator and Unity3D can provide ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) support; OpenSimulator is an open-source alternative to Second Life designed to support developers in building a virtual society of avatars, and Unity3D is a popular game engine adapted to work for virtual reality (VR).

C1099.name: Second Life
C1099.definition: OpenSimulator and Unity3D can provide ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) support; OpenSimulator is an open-source alternative to Second Life designed to support developers in building a virtual society of avatars, and Unity3D is a popular game engine adapted to work for virtual reality (VR).

C1100.name: Unity3D
C1100.definition: OpenSimulator and Unity3D can provide ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) support; OpenSimulator is an open-source alternative to Second Life designed to support developers in building a virtual society of avatars, and Unity3D is a popular game engine adapted to work for virtual reality (VR).

C1101.name: application software
C1101.definition: A virtual reality (VR) engine, also called a game engine, is middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers of extended reality (XR) applications, and provides support for hardware abstractions.

C1102.name: hardware abstraction
C1102.definition: A virtual reality (VR) engine, also called a game engine, is middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers of extended reality (XR) applications, and provides support for hardware abstractions.

C1103.name: software development environment
C1103.definition: A game engine is a software development environment for building extended reality (XR) experiences, and a developer can build their own application on top of it.

C1104.name: physics engine
C1104.definition: A physics engine is one of the crucial components of a game engine and is responsible for emulating the laws of physics realistically within the application by providing a set of functions for simulating physical forces and collisions acting on various objects within the scene at runtime.

C1105.name: rendering engine
C1105.definition: A rendering engine in a game engine helps generate animated three-dimensional (3D) graphics by rendering methods such as rasterization or ray tracing, a particular rendering engine may support a particular rendering method, and the rendering method adopted may depend on the sophistication level of the engine or platform.

C1106.name: audio engine
C1106.definition: An audio engine is a part of basic game engine support that consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system.

C1107.name: user interface
C1107.definition: A game engine can be thought of schematically as comprising multiple components, for example a physics engine, a rendering engine, an audio engine, and a user interface.

C1108.name: authoring tool
C1108.definition: An authoring tool for a game engine lets a developer access the different functionalities supported by the game engine in order to develop their own software that runs on top of the game engine.

C1109.name: scripting
C1109.definition: An authoring tool for a game engine may provide loading options, feature-setting options, and logic-setting options, and its logic setting can sometimes be done through scripting, which can be part of a game engine development environment.

C1110.name: game engine development environment
C1110.definition: An authoring tool for a game engine may provide loading options, feature-setting options, and logic-setting options, and its logic setting can sometimes be done through scripting, which can be part of a game engine development environment.

C1111.name: unity three-dimensional development environment
C1111.definition: A development environment that comprises a game engine plus other components can include the entire authoring tool, and Unity three-dimensional (3D) Development Environment or Unity Hub is an example of such a development environment.

C1112.name: rendering support
C1112.definition: Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

C1113.name: networking support
C1113.definition: Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

C1114.name: low-level support
C1114.definition: Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

C1115.name: platform-specific task
C1115.definition: Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

C1116.name: memory management
C1116.definition: Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

C1117.name: threading
C1117.definition: Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

C1118.name: localization support
C1118.definition: Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

C1119.name: three-dimensional graphics
C1119.definition: A rendering engine in a game engine helps generate animated three-dimensional (3D) graphics by rendering methods such as rasterization or ray tracing, a particular rendering engine may support a particular rendering method, and the rendering method adopted may depend on the sophistication level of the engine or platform.

C1120.name: rendering method
C1120.definition: A rendering engine in a game engine helps generate animated three-dimensional (3D) graphics by rendering methods such as rasterization or ray tracing, a particular rendering engine may support a particular rendering method, and the rendering method adopted may depend on the sophistication level of the engine or platform.

C1121.name: rasterization
C1121.definition: In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.

C1122.name: ray tracing
C1122.definition: A rendering engine in a game engine helps generate animated three-dimensional (3D) graphics by rendering methods such as rasterization or ray tracing, a particular rendering engine may support a particular rendering method, and the rendering method adopted may depend on the sophistication level of the engine or platform.

C1123.name: Direct3D
C1123.definition: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).

C1124.name: open graphics library
C1124.definition: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).

C1125.name: vulkan
C1125.definition: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).

C1126.name: memory
C1126.definition: In a typical virtual reality (VR) system that uses a game engine as middleware, the layers from lowest to highest are hardware, rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), game engine, and application software, and the hardware layer includes a graphics processing unit (GPU), a central processing unit (CPU), and memory.

C1127.name: speaker system
C1127.definition: An audio engine is a part of basic game engine support that consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system.

C1128.name: application-specific integrated circuit
C1128.definition: An audio engine can perform its calculations on a central processing unit (CPU) or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), so it does not require a graphics processing unit (GPU), and audio engines are not typically associated with a GPU because a GPU is generally associated with graphics or rendering.

C1129.name: open audio library
C1129.definition: An audio engine can be built on top of abstraction application programming interfaces (APIs) such as Open Audio Library (OpenAL), Simple DirectMedia Layer (SDL) audio, X audio 2, and Wave audio.

C1130.name: simple directmedia layer audio
C1130.definition: An audio engine can be built on top of abstraction application programming interfaces (APIs) such as Open Audio Library (OpenAL), Simple DirectMedia Layer (SDL) audio, X audio 2, and Wave audio.

C1131.name: x audio 2
C1131.definition: An audio engine can be built on top of abstraction application programming interfaces (APIs) such as Open Audio Library (OpenAL), Simple DirectMedia Layer (SDL) audio, X audio 2, and Wave audio.

C1132.name: wave audio
C1132.definition: An audio engine can be built on top of abstraction application programming interfaces (APIs) such as Open Audio Library (OpenAL), Simple DirectMedia Layer (SDL) audio, X audio 2, and Wave audio.

C1133.name: physical force
C1133.definition: A physics engine is one of the crucial components of a game engine and is responsible for emulating the laws of physics realistically within the application by providing a set of functions for simulating physical forces and collisions acting on various objects within the scene at runtime.

C1134.name: runtime
C1134.definition: A physics engine is one of the crucial components of a game engine and is responsible for emulating the laws of physics realistically within the application by providing a set of functions for simulating physical forces and collisions acting on various objects within the scene at runtime.

C1135.name: unreal engine
C1135.definition: Unity 3D, Unreal Engine 4, CryEngine, Godot, Lumberyard, and Amazon Sumerian are examples of game engines.

C1136.name: cryengine
C1136.definition: Unity 3D, Unreal Engine 4, CryEngine, Godot, Lumberyard, and Amazon Sumerian are examples of game engines.

C1137.name: godot
C1137.definition: Unity 3D, Unreal Engine 4, CryEngine, Godot, Lumberyard, and Amazon Sumerian are examples of game engines.

C1138.definition: Unity 3D, Unreal Engine 4, CryEngine, Godot, Lumberyard, and Amazon Sumerian are examples of game engines.

C1139.name: amazon sumerian
C1139.definition: Unity 3D, Unreal Engine 4, CryEngine, Godot, Lumberyard, and Amazon Sumerian are examples of game engines.

C1140.name: deployment
C1140.definition: Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

C1141.name: native application deployment
C1141.definition: Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

C1142.name: web application deployment

C1254.name: library

C1255.name: prototype
C1255.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

C1256.name: augmented reality plugin

C1257.name: flar toolkit

C1260.name: augmented reality marker
C1260.definition: FLAR Toolkit lets a user, with a few lines of code, activate a camera, track augmented reality (AR) markers in the camera view, and load and overlay virtual content onto the tracked image for three-dimensional (3D) registering.

C1261.name: three-dimensional registering

C1262.name: overlay
C1262.definition: FLAR Toolkit makes it possible for anyone with a Flash-enabled web browser and a camera connected to a computer to have or develop an augmented reality (AR) experience with minimal effort because the required tracking and overlay activities can be done with a few lines of code.

C1263.name: flar tracker
C1263.definition: In Flash augmented reality Manager (FLAR Manager), an augmented reality tracking library such as FLAR Toolkit or FLAR Tracker can be combined with a three-dimensional (3D) graphics library such as Alternative 3D, Away 3D, Away 3D Lite, Paper Vision 3D, or Sandy 3D, and such combinations are used primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.

C1271.name: non-flash-based authoring tool
C1271.definition: Non-Flash-based authoring tools for augmented reality prototyping exist, but they may be less popular than Flash-based tools because Flash-based tools have greater market penetration.

C1289.name: plugin to existing tools
C1289.definition: Plugins to existing tools are a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) content authoring tool that may not itself support AR content or system development, and the plugin adds AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration of digital content over the real-world view, while relying on the main authoring tool for content authoring.

C1290.name: augmented reality software

C1294.name: interactive three-dimensional graphics authoring tool
C1294.definition: Many interactive three-dimensional (3D) graphics authoring tools, including Unity, Vizard, and Lumion, are used to create interactive 3D applications, and most of these tools have plugins for augmented reality (AR) visualization; Unity has the widest range of available solutions for AR visualization.

C1295.name: Unity
C1295.definition: Unity is a popular and well-known programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems.

C1296.name: Vizard

C1299.name: AR Toolkit for Unity
C1299.definition: The augmented reality (AR) Toolkit for Unity from the AR Tool Works is an example of an AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.

C1300.name: image-based tracking
C1300.definition: The augmented reality (AR) Toolkit for Unity from the AR Tool Works is an example of an AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.

C1301.name: software configuration
C1301.definition: Limitations of using plugins to add augmented reality (AR) support to existing content authoring tools are that user interface and interaction design can be limited to what the underlying authoring tool provides, software and hardware configuration depends on that tool, and content produced with the authoring tool usually becomes dependent on proprietary player software in most cases.

C1304.name: low-level software development tool
C1304.definition: A way to resolve the limitations of higher-level augmented reality (AR) tools or plugins is to use low-level software development tools, such as software libraries, and build the system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool, an approach that applies to any higher-level tool.

C1307.name: standalone authoring tool
C1307.definition: Standalone authoring tools are applications that allow users to create augmented reality (AR) experiences without programming experience.

C1308.name: scene construction
C1308.definition: Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior, with capabilities ranging from scene construction only to the full capability of building complex interactive behavior.

C1309.name: animation
C1309.definition: Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior, with capabilities ranging from scene construction only to the full capability of building complex interactive behavior.

C1310.name: interactive behavior

C1311.name: graphical user interface
C1311.definition: Most standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces (GUIs) that allow developers to create applications or experiences without coding, so users with basic personal computer (PC) skills and non-programmers can learn and use them.

C1312.name: scripting language
C1312.definition: Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools can provide scripting-language support for developers who know scripting languages, and applications built with absolute zero coding have limited utility compared with advanced systems that use scripting support for more flexibility.

C1313.name: Wikitude Studio
C1313.definition: Wikitude Studio is an example of a standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tool; it is a web-based package that allowed users to create rich mobile augmented reality content and deploy it either to the Wikitude augmented reality browser app or as a custom mobile app, and it supported various media, including three-dimensional (3D) models and animations registered to the real world.

C1314.name: Wikitude augmented reality browser app

C1315.name: low-level library
C1315.definition: Augmented reality (AR) software tools and packages are available in four categories based on the programming skill required: low-level libraries and frameworks, which require the highest programming skill; standalone authoring tools, which require the least programming skill; and, between these extremes, rapid prototyping tools and plugins to existing systems.

C1317.name: extended reality system

C1318.name: interactive system
C1318.definition: Extended reality systems belong to the broad class of systems called interactive systems.

C1319.name: disappearing technology
C1319.definition: Mark Weiser's 1991 paper 'The Computer for the 21st Century', published in Scientific American, stated that the most profound technologies are those that disappear.

C1320.name: earliest computer
C1320.definition: The earliest computers occupied huge rooms with many wires, programming referred to the idea of reconnecting the wires, and they were accessible only to a very few select people.

C1321.name: programming
C1321.definition: The earliest computers occupied huge rooms with many wires, programming referred to the idea of reconnecting the wires, and they were accessible only to a very few select people.

C1322.name: flexible device
C1322.definition: In the development of computer systems, people have tried to make technology disappear from the user's point of view, and the current stage defined by popular technological products such as wearable devices, mobile devices, flexible devices, and connected devices is referred to as Internet of Things (IoT) or ubiquitous computing, in which users are surrounded by multiple connected computers that can communicate with each other without the user separately operating them, moving toward making technology disappear.

C1326.name: interactive computing system
C1326.definition: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.

C1327.name: lay person
C1327.definition: In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.

C1328.name: error message

C1333.name: user-centric approach

C1335.name: interface element
C1335.definition: The key characteristics of a user-centric approach are designing interface elements that are acceptable to users, designing layouts that organize elements on the screen or interface to meet user expectations, helping users perceive the system state from their point of view rather than from technical details, and designing interactions that fulfill users' needs by taking them to desired system states, allowing users to get work done by easily transitioning from one state to a goal state.

C1340.name: human-computer interaction
C1340.definition: Human-computer interaction (HCI) is a discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with the study of major phenomena surrounding interactive computing systems.

C1341.name: ACM SIGCHI
C1341.definition: ACM SIGCHI is the official body that deals with human-computer interaction (HCI) and provides the definition of HCI.

C1342.name: system design
C1342.definition: Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.

C1343.name: field study
C1343.definition: Converting the Satra site into a graph representation is an iterative process that requires detailed field study and revision of an initial graph.

C1344.name: novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization
C1344.definition: Empirical or field studies of user behavior are typically needed to understand who the users of an interactive system are and how they behave, but they are time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning, so interactive-system designers can rely on the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization instead of always starting with field studies.

C1345.name: novice user
C1345.definition: A three-class classification of interactive-system users consists of novice users, who use the system for the first time, intermittent users, who use it occasionally, and expert users, who use it regularly over a long period of time.

C1346.name: intermittent user
C1346.definition: A three-class classification of interactive-system users consists of novice users, who use the system for the first time, intermittent users, who use it occasionally, and expert users, who use it regularly over a long period of time.

C1347.name: expert user
C1347.definition: A three-class classification of interactive-system users consists of novice users, who use the system for the first time, intermittent users, who use it occasionally, and expert users, who use it regularly over a long period of time.

C1348.name: interactive-system design
C1348.definition: The novice, intermittent, and expert user classes provide a starting point for understanding users and making interactive-system design decisions when designers assume their potential users belong to one of these classes, because users in different classes are likely to behave differently and designers can broadly understand the behavior of each class.

C1349.name: word processing application
C1349.definition: A word processing or similar processing application can provide multiple options, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, for the same task to cater to different user groups.

C1350.name: hotkey combination
C1350.definition: A word processing or similar processing application can provide multiple options, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, for the same task to cater to different user groups.

C1351.name: menu option
C1351.definition: A word processing or similar processing application can provide multiple options, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, for the same task to cater to different user groups.

C1352.name: task
C1352.definition: A word processing or similar processing application can provide multiple options, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, for the same task to cater to different user groups.

C1353.name: file
C1353.definition: For saving a file, the menu option takes longer than the hotkey combination but is suitable for novice first-time users because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them, while the hotkey combination may be a better alternative for intermittent users and is always preferable for expert users.

C1354.name: user-centric design
C1354.definition: The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, particularly by designer role: for a user interface or user experience designer it primarily concerns the design of interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect informed by user characteristics; for an industrial product designer it concerns the form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look; and for an electronic engineer it concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery.

C1355.name: chip
C1355.definition: The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, particularly by designer role: for a user interface or user experience designer it primarily concerns the design of interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect informed by user characteristics; for an industrial product designer it concerns the form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look; and for an electronic engineer it concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery.

C1356.name: development lifecycle
C1356.definition: An application software developer building software such as a virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) system incorporates user characteristics by following a development or design lifecycle that accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations so that the system is easier for the user to use and better matches the users' needs and expectations.

C1357.name: International Standards Organization 9241-210-2009 standard
C1357.definition: The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

C1358.name: effectiveness
C1358.definition: The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

C1360.name: satisfaction

C1361.name: context of use
C1361.definition: The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

C1362.name: user-centered design
C1362.definition: User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.

C1363.name: design lifecycle
C1363.definition: User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.

C1364.name: cooperative design
C1364.definition: Cooperative design (coined by Greenbaum and Kyng in 1992), participatory design (Schuler and Namioka, 1993), contextual design (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1997), and human-centered design (the standard term preferred by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) rather than user-centered design) are related terms that are more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process.

C1365.name: participatory design
C1365.definition: Cooperative design (coined by Greenbaum and Kyng in 1992), participatory design (Schuler and Namioka, 1993), contextual design (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1997), and human-centered design (the standard term preferred by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) rather than user-centered design) are related terms that are more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process.

C1366.name: contextual design
C1366.definition: Cooperative design (coined by Greenbaum and Kyng in 1992), participatory design (Schuler and Namioka, 1993), contextual design (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1997), and human-centered design (the standard term preferred by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) rather than user-centered design) are related terms that are more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process.

C1369.name: user-centric software design
C1369.definition: In user-centric software design and software development, the core design concern is the design of usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of lay persons or layman users.

C1370.name: software development
C1370.definition: In user-centric software design and software development, the core design concern is the design of usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of lay persons or layman users.

C1371.name: software development lifecycle
C1371.definition: Obtaining usable application software requires following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle rather than working in a haphazard or ad hoc manner.

C1372.name: extended reality software
C1372.definition: The core concern of Extended Reality (XR) software is to create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment, and both software and hardware play important roles in building that relationship.

C1373.name: xr engine
C1373.definition: An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer.

C1374.name: application layer
C1374.definition: An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer.

C1375.name: input data
C1375.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

C1376.name: output data
C1376.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

C1377.name: user input modeling
C1377.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

C1378.name: output modeling
C1378.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

C1379.name: output stimulus
C1379.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

C1380.name: perception
C1380.definition: The perceptual process proceeds from sensing, which is the lowest level, to perception, which is at a very abstract level, and perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.

C1381.name: perceptual stimuli
C1381.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

C1382.name: illusion of reality
C1382.definition: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

C1383.name: perceptual system
C1383.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.

C1384.name: artificial stimulation
C1384.definition: Human bodies and sensory organs are designed to perceive the real world, not a virtual world, and applying artificial stimulation in virtual reality affects biological mechanisms that evolved over a long period in a natural environment.

C1385.name: biological mechanism
C1385.definition: Human bodies and sensory organs are designed to perceive the real world, not a virtual world, and applying artificial stimulation in virtual reality affects biological mechanisms that evolved over a long period in a natural environment.

C1386.name: physiology
C1386.definition: Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory.

C1387.name: long-term memory
C1387.definition: Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory.

C1388.name: sensory signal
C1388.definition: Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

C1389.name: adaptation
C1389.definition: One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

C1390.name: non-adaptation
C1390.definition: Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

C1391.name: perceptual psychology
C1391.definition: Perceptual psychology is the science of understanding how the brain converts sensory stimulation, received by sensors from the real world, into perceived phenomena.

C1392.name: video resolution
C1392.definition: Perceptual psychology provides guidelines for building better hardware and for understanding the effects of an extended reality (XR) system on the user by answering questions such as how far away an object appears in a given virtual world, how much video resolution is needed to avoid seeing pixels in a virtual world or virtual object, how many frames per second are enough to perceive motion as continuous, whether the user's head appears at the proper height in the virtual world for the point of view that should correspond to the user's height, where virtual sound appears to come from, why a user feels nauseated, why one system experience is more tiring than another, and what presence is.

C1393.name: pixel
C1393.definition: A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

C1397.name: neural pathway
C1397.definition: Perceptual psychology requires knowledge of the basic physiology of the human body, including sense organs, neural pathways, and how they are connected to the brain; the key theories and insights of experimental perceptual psychology; and the interference of an engineered extended reality (XR) system with common perceptual processes, with its implications or side effects.

C1450.definition: The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.
