C1451.definition: The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.

C1452.name: neural network
C1452.definition: The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.

C1453.name: deep learning
C1453.definition: The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.

C1454.name: input edge
C1454.definition: The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.

C1455.name: output edge
C1455.definition: The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.

C1456.name: synapse
C1456.definition: For an interconnection between neurons, an axon of one neuron is paired with a dendrite of the next neuron, but the axon and dendrite are not physically connected; communication occurs across a gap called the synapse, through which electrical or chemical signals are passed.

C1457.name: chemical signal
C1457.definition: For an interconnection between neurons, an axon of one neuron is paired with a dendrite of the next neuron, but the axon and dendrite are not physically connected; communication occurs across a gap called the synapse, through which electrical or chemical signals are passed.

C1458.name: synaptic connection
C1458.definition: In the human brain, each neuron has on average about 7,000 synaptic connections to other neurons, which results in about 10^15 edges in the brain's neuron-interconnection graph.

C1459.name: edge
C1459.definition: The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.

C1460.name: hierarchical processing
C1460.definition: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex.

C1461.name: neural processing
C1461.definition: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex.

C1462.name: signal
C1462.definition: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex.

C1463.name: staged aggregation
C1463.definition: Hierarchical processing works by staged aggregation, in which signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels by neurons until the cerebral cortex is reached, and aggregated information at each level is higher-level information rather than the same lower-level information.

C1464.name: sensory input
C1464.definition: In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification.

C1465.name: interpretation of a stimulus
C1465.definition: In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification.

C1466.name: perceptual phenomena
C1466.definition: In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification.

C1467.name: face recognition
C1467.definition: In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification.

C1468.name: song identification
C1468.definition: In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification.

C1469.name: long-term experience
C1469.definition: In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification.

C1470.name: perceptual processing
C1470.definition: Overall perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience.

C1471.name: proprioception
C1471.definition: Proprioception is another aspect of perception, slightly different from direct perception through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste; it is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and because it has no direct sensory organ or receptor it can be called a sixth sense.

C1472.name: muscular effort
C1472.definition: Proprioception is another aspect of perception, slightly different from direct perception through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste; it is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and because it has no direct sensory organ or receptor it can be called a sixth sense.

C1473.name: motor cortex
C1473.definition: The motor cortex, which controls body motion, sends signals called efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate what motions have been executed, and this information is processed to understand the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort required to move them.

C1474.name: body motion
C1474.definition: The motor cortex, which controls body motion, sends signals called efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate what motions have been executed, and this information is processed to understand the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort required to move them.

C1475.name: efference copy
C1475.definition: The motor cortex, which controls body motion, sends signals called efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate what motions have been executed, and this information is processed to understand the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort required to move them.

C1476.name: sensory processing
C1476.definition: In an immersive virtual reality (VR) system, interfering with the brain's long-term learned sensory processing can create a mismatch because the brain cannot be retuned to process the new inputs in a short span of time.

C1477.name: visual input
C1477.definition: Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a person moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict.

C1478.name: retina
C1478.definition: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

C1479.name: lens
C1479.definition: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

C1480.name: human eye
C1480.definition: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

C1481.name: light propagation
C1481.definition: Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is important for understanding how virtual reality (VR) headsets work and how they lead to visual perception.

C1482.name: visual perception
C1482.definition: Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is important for understanding how virtual reality (VR) headsets work and how they lead to visual perception.

C1483.name: camera setup
C1483.definition: Knowledge of how light propagates, how lenses and the eye work, and how cameras work is used to understand camera setups, choose camera positions in virtual worlds for the best experience, and present virtual worlds through panoramic videos.

C1484.name: camera position
C1484.definition: The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

C1485.name: panoramic video
C1485.definition: Knowledge of how light propagates, how lenses and the eye work, and how cameras work is used to understand camera setups, choose camera positions in virtual worlds for the best experience, and present virtual worlds through panoramic videos.

C1486.name: tracking software
C1486.definition: Understanding how a camera works helps build tracking hardware and software.

C1487.name: photon view
C1487.definition: Light can be described by three views—the photon (particle) view, the wave view, and the ray view—and these views can be used to explain different phenomena related to light.

C1488.name: wave view
C1488.definition: Light can be described by three views—the photon (particle) view, the wave view, and the ray view—and these views can be used to explain different phenomena related to light.

C1489.name: ray view
C1489.definition: Light can be described by three views—the photon (particle) view, the wave view, and the ray view—and these views can be used to explain different phenomena related to light.

C1490.name: photon
C1490.definition: The photon (particle) view of light describes light as a large number of photons, tiny energy particles that move through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and it is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.

C1491.name: speed of light
C1491.definition: The photon (particle) view of light describes light as a large number of photons, tiny energy particles that move through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and it is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.

C1492.name: wave
C1492.definition: The wave view of light describes light as waves, ripples through space, and it is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color rather than explaining color in terms of light as particles.

C1493.name: color spectrum
C1493.definition: The wave view of light describes light as waves, ripples through space, and it is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color rather than explaining color in terms of light as particles.

C1494.name: color
C1494.definition: Color is perceived when the red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display is mixed in the eye, so the observed color is a combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue.

C1495.name: ray
C1495.definition: The ray view of light describes light as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon, and it is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

C1496.name: visibility
C1496.definition: The ray view of light describes light as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon, and it is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

C1497.name: light ray
C1497.definition: When light rays strike a material surface, the possible interactions are transmission, absorption, and reflection, and either one of these interactions or all three can occur.

C1498.name: material surface
C1498.definition: When light rays strike a material surface, the possible interactions are transmission, absorption, and reflection, and either one of these interactions or all three can occur.

C1499.name: transmission
C1499.definition: When light rays strike a material surface, the possible interactions are transmission, absorption, and reflection, and either one of these interactions or all three can occur.

C1500.name: absorption
C1500.definition: When light rays strike a material surface, the possible interactions are transmission, absorption, and reflection, and either one of these interactions or all three can occur.

C1501.name: reflection
C1501.definition: When light rays strike a material surface, the possible interactions are transmission, absorption, and reflection, and either one of these interactions or all three can occur.

C1502.name: color perception
C1502.definition: In color perception, the perceived color of a surface point is determined by the intensity of the light reaching the viewer's eye.

C1503.name: perceived color
C1503.definition: In color perception, the perceived color of a surface point is determined by the intensity of the light reaching the viewer's eye.

C1504.name: intensity
C1504.definition: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.

C1505.name: ambient light
C1505.definition: Ambient light is light in the environment, reflected from surrounding objects, that reaches the viewer's eye together with light reflected from the object's surface.

C1506.name: cornea
C1506.definition: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

C1507.name: pupil
C1507.definition: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

C1508.name: aqueous humor
C1508.definition: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

C1509.name: vitreous humor
C1509.definition: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

C1510.name: iris
C1510.definition: The iris controls the amount of light entering the human eye by dilating or constricting the pupil, typically dilating it in dark surroundings to admit more light and constricting it in bright light to admit less.

C1511.name: optic nerve fiber
C1511.definition: The retina at the back of the eye consists of photoreceptors, which are the bodily sensors required for visual perception, and optic nerve fibers, which are neurons that carry the signal to the brain.

C1512.name: rod
C1512.definition: The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.

C1513.name: cone
C1513.definition: The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.

C1514.name: fovea
C1514.definition: The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.

C1515.name: image acuity
C1515.definition: Multiple rods can share a single optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light, whereas approximately one optic nerve fiber serves each cone, which aids image acuity.

C1516.name: photopic vision
C1516.definition: Vision accomplished only with cones is photopic vision, which is more related to direct or central vision, and vision accomplished only with rods is scotopic vision, which is more related to peripheral vision.

C1517.name: central vision
C1517.definition: Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly.

C1518.name: scotopic vision
C1518.definition: Vision accomplished only with cones is photopic vision, which is more related to direct or central vision, and vision accomplished only with rods is scotopic vision, which is more related to peripheral vision.

C1519.name: peripheral vision
C1519.definition: Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly.

C1520.name: spectrum
C1520.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

C1521.name: frequency
C1521.definition: Sound waves are primarily characterized by three properties relevant for dealing with sound waves: frequency, amplitude, and phase, because sound can be represented as a wave.

C1522.name: electromagnetic light wave
C1522.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

C1523.name: red light
C1523.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

C1524.name: hertz
C1524.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

C1525.name: wavelength
C1525.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

C1526.name: nanometer
C1526.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

C1527.name: violet light
C1527.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

C1528.name: photoreceptor density
C1528.definition: Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly.

C1529.name: angular range
C1529.definition: The innermost part of the fovea has a diameter of only 0.5 millimeters or an angular range of 0.85 plus or minus 0.85 degrees and contains almost entirely cones.

C1530.name: rod density
C1530.definition: Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where rays entering the cornea from the sides land, rod density is lower and cone density is very low, and photoreceptor density is lower, with a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones.

C1531.name: cone density
C1531.definition: Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where rays entering the cornea from the sides land, rod density is lower and cone density is very low, and photoreceptor density is lower, with a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones.

C1532.name: blind spot
C1532.definition: The blind spot is a region of the retina with no photoreceptors, caused by the retina's inside-out anatomy, which leaves no other way to route neural signals to the brain, and by the optic nerve spreading out around the retina, so light or visual stimuli falling there produce no perception.

C1533.name: optic nerve
C1533.definition: The blind spot is a region of the retina with no photoreceptors, caused by the retina's inside-out anatomy, which leaves no other way to route neural signals to the brain, and by the optic nerve spreading out around the retina, so light or visual stimuli falling there produce no perception.

C1534.name: neural signal
C1534.definition: The blind spot is a region of the retina with no photoreceptors, caused by the retina's inside-out anatomy, which leaves no other way to route neural signals to the brain, and by the optic nerve spreading out around the retina, so light or visual stimuli falling there produce no perception.

C1535.name: visual stimulus
C1535.definition: The blind spot is a region of the retina with no photoreceptors, caused by the retina's inside-out anatomy, which leaves no other way to route neural signals to the brain, and by the optic nerve spreading out around the retina, so light or visual stimuli falling there produce no perception.

C1536.name: natural lens
C1536.definition: The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

C1537.name: neural pulse
C1537.definition: The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

C1538.name: focal depth
C1538.definition: The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

C1539.name: lens setup
C1539.definition: Compared with an artificially created lens setup, the human eye has no focal plane as such; its non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces the focal plane.

C1540.name: focal plane
C1540.definition: Compared with an artificially created lens setup, the human eye has no focal plane as such; its non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces the focal plane.

C1541.name: medium
C1541.definition: In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.

C1542.name: refractive index
C1542.definition: In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.

C1543.name: aqueous fluid
C1543.definition: In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.

C1544.name: vitreous fluid
C1544.definition: In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.

C1545.name: diopter
C1545.definition: Because the outer diameter of the human eyeball is approximately 24 millimeters, a single lens of at least 40 diopters would be required to converge parallel rays onto the center of the retina.

C1546.name: convex lens
C1546.definition: The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

C1547.name: optical power
C1547.definition: The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

C1548.name: engineered lens
C1548.definition: For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

C1549.name: focal length
C1549.definition: For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

C1550.name: virtual image
C1550.definition: For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

C1551.name: real image
C1551.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

C1552.name: view frustum
C1552.definition: Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

C1553.name: horizontal field of view
C1553.definition: The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

C1554.name: vertical field of view
C1554.definition: The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

C1555.name: binocular vision
C1555.definition: In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye.

C1556.name: left eye
C1556.definition: In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye.

C1557.name: right eye
C1557.definition: In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye.

C1558.name: depth perception
C1558.definition: Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand the relationship between objects in three-dimensional (3D) space.

C1559.name: stereoscopy
C1559.definition: Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processes the left image, the right eye processes the right image, and there is a common part seen by both eyes while some parts are seen by only one eye.

C1560.name: three-dimensional view
C1560.definition: When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

C1561.name: translational movement
C1561.definition: A virtual world may allow up to two types of movement in three-dimensional (3D) space: translational movement, used for navigating in that space, and rotational movement, primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

C1562.name: rotational movement
C1562.definition: A virtual world may allow up to two types of movement in three-dimensional (3D) space: translational movement, used for navigating in that space, and rotational movement, primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

C1563.name: degree of freedom
C1563.definition: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

C1564.name: six degrees of freedom
C1564.definition: In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

C1565.name: rotational degree of freedom
C1565.definition: In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

C1566.name: translational degree of freedom
C1566.definition: In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

C1567.name: visual display hardware
C1567.definition: Basic physiological properties such as photoreceptor density can directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) display should ideally be designed to match the performance of the human visual sense, being good enough to fool the visual sense without needing quality beyond the limits of human receptors.

C1568.name: human visual sense
C1568.definition: Basic physiological properties such as photoreceptor density can directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) display should ideally be designed to match the performance of the human visual sense, being good enough to fool the visual sense without needing quality beyond the limits of human receptors.

C1569.name: spatial resolution
C1569.definition: To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

C1570.name: intensity resolution
C1570.definition: To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

C1571.name: intensity range
C1571.definition: To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

C1572.name: temporal resolution
C1572.definition: To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

C1573.name: jitter
C1573.definition: To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

C1574.name: aliasing
C1574.definition: Aliasing in a display is the perception of a sharp diagonal line as jagged or staircase-shaped when individual display lights are visible, such as when the display is highly magnified or zoomed out.

C1575.name: screen door effect
C1575.definition: The screen door effect is an effect, commonly noticed in images produced by liquid crystal display (LCD) projectors, in which an image appears to have a screen on top of it.

C1576.name: retina display
C1576.definition: A retina display is a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), a threshold claimed by Steve Jobs of Apple in 2010 as sufficient for a retina display.

C1577.name: pixels per linear inch
C1577.definition: A retina display is a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), a threshold claimed by Steve Jobs of Apple in 2010 as sufficient for a retina display.

C1578.name: retina display criterion
C1578.definition: A retina display is a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), a threshold claimed by Steve Jobs of Apple in 2010 as sufficient for a retina display.

C1579.name: wearable display
C1579.definition: For augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays and virtual reality (VR) headsets or other wearable displays close to the eye, the traditional 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) retina display criterion is not very suitable; a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, so the required pixels per linear inch (ppi) is probably 7 to 8 times higher than a retina display.

C1580.name: magnifying lens
C1580.definition: For augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays and virtual reality (VR) headsets or other wearable displays close to the eye, the traditional 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) retina display criterion is not very suitable; a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, so the required pixels per linear inch (ppi) is probably 7 to 8 times higher than a retina display.

C1581.name: corrective mechanism
C1581.definition: To avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect in virtual reality (VR) headsets, corrective mechanisms can be used, including adjusting the field of view of the headsets, foveated rendering techniques, and other ways of rendering content, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.

C1582.name: foveated rendering
C1582.definition: To avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect in virtual reality (VR) headsets, corrective mechanisms can be used, including adjusting the field of view of the headsets, foveated rendering techniques, and other ways of rendering content, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.

C1583.name: motion perception
C1583.definition: For motion perception in an immersive environment, temporal resolution in a virtual reality (VR) headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards such as 24 frames per second (fps) or 60 fps, with higher frame rates preferred.

C1584.name: immersive environment
C1584.definition: Immersive environments block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, so improved interaction techniques are needed to provide a better immersive experience.

C1585.name: audio component
C1585.definition: The audio component of virtual reality (VR) is powerful for providing an immersive experience, and technologies exist to bring high-fidelity audio into VR, so using those technologies will clearly improve the immersive experience.

C1586.name: high-fidelity audio
C1586.definition: The audio component of virtual reality (VR) is powerful for providing an immersive experience, and technologies exist to bring high-fidelity audio into VR, so using those technologies will clearly improve the immersive experience.

C1587.name: visual sense
C1587.definition: The objective in dealing with an immersive experience is to include as many senses as possible, because the visual sense alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, which will affect the immersive experience, and augmenting vision with audio enhances the immersive experience.

C1588.name: audio recording
C1588.definition: Audio recording, that is recording of sound, speech or non-speech sound, and audio reproduction, that is output generation, can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing, and it can provide a better surround sound effect in cave-like VR versions, a surround environment surrounded by display devices, and a better immersive experience in headset VR versions, the wearable display version.

C1589.name: audio reproduction
C1589.definition: Audio recording, that is recording of sound, speech or non-speech sound, and audio reproduction, that is output generation, can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing, and it can provide a better surround sound effect in cave-like VR versions, a surround environment surrounded by display devices, and a better immersive experience in headset VR versions, the wearable display version.

C1590.name: surround sound effect
C1590.definition: Audio recording, that is recording of sound, speech or non-speech sound, and audio reproduction, that is output generation, can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing, and it can provide a better surround sound effect in cave-like VR versions, a surround environment surrounded by display devices, and a better immersive experience in headset VR versions, the wearable display version.

C1591.name: cave-like virtual reality version
C1591.definition: Audio recording, that is recording of sound, speech or non-speech sound, and audio reproduction, that is output generation, can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing, and it can provide a better surround sound effect in cave-like VR versions, a surround environment surrounded by display devices, and a better immersive experience in headset VR versions, the wearable display version.

C1592.name: headset virtual reality version
C1592.definition: Audio recording, that is recording of sound, speech or non-speech sound, and audio reproduction, that is output generation, can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing, and it can provide a better surround sound effect in cave-like VR versions, a surround environment surrounded by display devices, and a better immersive experience in headset VR versions, the wearable display version.

C1593.name: size
C1593.definition: Combining sound with vision or visual effects affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and although looking alone partly gives an idea of those properties, perception of them is reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects.

C1594.name: volume
C1594.definition: Combining sound with vision or visual effects affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and although looking alone partly gives an idea of those properties, perception of them is reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects.

C1595.name: material
C1595.definition: A Unity model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data, and, if the object represents an animated character, it can also contain animation-related data.

C1596.name: distance
C1596.definition: Combining sound with vision or visual effects affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and although looking alone partly gives an idea of those properties, perception of them is reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects.

C1597.name: virtual experience
C1597.definition: Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, that is, as closer to reality and everyday experience, and vision coupled with audio helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment, which vision alone may not be able to achieve.

C1598.name: believable
C1598.definition: Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, that is, as closer to reality and everyday experience, and vision coupled with audio helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment, which vision alone may not be able to achieve.

C1599.name: emotional connection
C1599.definition: Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, that is, as closer to reality and everyday experience, and vision coupled with audio helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment, which vision alone may not be able to achieve.

C1600.name: attachment
C1600.definition: Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

C1601.name: propagation
C1601.definition: Sound is vibration in a medium, usually air but also water, other gases, liquids, or solids, and it requires a medium to propagate, so there is no sound in a vacuum unlike light, which can propagate without a medium or through a vacuum.

C1602.name: vacuum
C1602.definition: Sound is vibration in a medium, usually air but also water, other gases, liquids, or solids, and it requires a medium to propagate, so there is no sound in a vacuum unlike light, which can propagate without a medium or through a vacuum.

C1603.name: pressure variation
C1603.definition: Sound propagation through a medium is caused by pressure variations created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, and these pressure variations range from a compression extreme, where pressure is extremely high, to a decompression extreme, also called a rarefaction extreme, where pressure is very low.

C1604.name: compression extreme
C1604.definition: Sound propagation through a medium is caused by pressure variations created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, and these pressure variations range from a compression extreme, where pressure is extremely high, to a decompression extreme, also called a rarefaction extreme, where pressure is very low.

C1605.name: decompression extreme
C1605.definition: Sound propagation through a medium is caused by pressure variations created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, and these pressure variations range from a compression extreme, where pressure is extremely high, to a decompression extreme, also called a rarefaction extreme, where pressure is very low.

C1606.name: eardrum
C1606.definition: Pressure variation at the human eardrum is converted into a perceptual auditory experience, because pressure at the human eardrum varies as a function of time.

C1607.name: sound wave
C1607.definition: Sound can be represented as a sound wave, which is a plot of pressure variation against time with time on the x-axis and air pressure on the y-axis, and the pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave as time progresses.

C1608.name: human audible frequency range
C1608.definition: The human audible frequency range, which is a limitation of human physiology, is from 20 hertz (Hz) to 20,000 hertz, and frequencies inside this range are audible to a human ear while frequencies outside this range are not, although other animals can perceive a higher range outside the human range.

C1609.name: human ear
C1609.definition: The human audible frequency range, which is a limitation of human physiology, is from 20 hertz (Hz) to 20,000 hertz, and frequencies inside this range are audible to a human ear while frequencies outside this range are not, although other animals can perceive a higher range outside the human range.

C1610.name: amplitude
C1610.definition: Sound waves are primarily characterized by three properties relevant for dealing with sound waves: frequency, amplitude, and phase, because sound can be represented as a wave.

C1611.name: decibel
C1611.definition: Amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave, measured in decibel (dB) relative to the minimum sound detectable by humans at 1000 hertz (Hz).

C1612.name: phase
C1612.definition: Sound waves are primarily characterized by three properties relevant for dealing with sound waves: frequency, amplitude, and phase, because sound can be represented as a wave.

C1613.name: human hearing system
C1613.definition: The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

C1614.name: outer ear
C1614.definition: The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

C1615.name: middle ear
C1615.definition: The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

C1616.name: inner ear
C1616.definition: The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

C1617.name: receiver part
C1617.definition: In the outer ear, the receiver part receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the crucial outer-ear canal, which works as an amplifier by boosting the sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

C1618.name: outer-ear canal
C1618.definition: In the outer ear, the receiver part receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the crucial outer-ear canal, which works as an amplifier by boosting the sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

C1619.name: amplifier
C1619.definition: In the outer ear, the receiver part receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the crucial outer-ear canal, which works as an amplifier by boosting the sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

C1620.name: sound pressure
C1620.definition: In the outer ear, the receiver part receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the crucial outer-ear canal, which works as an amplifier by boosting the sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

C1621.name: tympanic membrane
C1621.definition: In the middle ear, a sound wave passing through the outer-ear canal strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate, and the vibration is transferred to three ossicles in an air-filled chamber: the malleus, the incus, and the stapes.

C1622.name: ossicle
C1622.definition: In the middle ear, a sound wave passing through the outer-ear canal strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate, and the vibration is transferred to three ossicles in an air-filled chamber: the malleus, the incus, and the stapes.

C1623.name: malleus
C1623.definition: In the middle ear, a sound wave passing through the outer-ear canal strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate, and the vibration is transferred to three ossicles in an air-filled chamber: the malleus, the incus, and the stapes.

C1624.name: incus
C1624.definition: In the middle ear, a sound wave passing through the outer-ear canal strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate, and the vibration is transferred to three ossicles in an air-filled chamber: the malleus, the incus, and the stapes.

C1625.name: stapes
C1625.definition: In the middle ear, a sound wave passing through the outer-ear canal strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate, and the vibration is transferred to three ossicles in an air-filled chamber: the malleus, the incus, and the stapes.

C1626.name: cochlea
C1626.definition: The inner ear houses the cochlea, which is the sense organ for hearing, in a structure the size of a marble.

C1627.name: nerve
C1627.definition: The cochlea is connected to nerves or neurons and converts sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain through the neural network.

C1628.name: sound energy
C1628.definition: The cochlea is connected to nerves or neurons and converts sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain through the neural network.

C1629.name: sound perception
C1629.definition: Sound perception occurs at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.

C1630.name: social-level sound perception
C1630.definition: Sound perception occurs at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.

C1631.name: warning-level sound perception
C1631.definition: Sound perception occurs at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.

C1632.name: primitive-level sound perception
C1632.definition: Sound perception occurs at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.

C1633.name: auditory effects
C1633.definition: Identifying the desired sound perception level helps a developer generate suitable auditory effects when generating sound effects for a virtual reality (VR) system; for example, if social-level perception is required, the developer should generate stimuli that support social-level perception rather than stimuli that typically produce primitive-level perception.

C1634.name: sound effects
C1634.definition: Identifying the desired sound perception level helps a developer generate suitable auditory effects when generating sound effects for a virtual reality (VR) system; for example, if social-level perception is required, the developer should generate stimuli that support social-level perception rather than stimuli that typically produce primitive-level perception.

C1635.name: psychophysics
C1635.definition: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by physical stimuli.

C1636.name: physical stimulus
C1636.definition: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by physical stimuli.

C1637.name: psychoacoustics
C1637.definition: Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics and is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by acoustic stimuli or sound.

C1638.name: acoustic stimulus
C1638.definition: Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics and is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by acoustic stimuli or sound.

C1639.name: Stevens' power law
C1639.definition: Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units.

C1640.name: perceived magnitude
C1640.definition: Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units.

C1641.name: exponent
C1641.definition: Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units.

C1642.name: just noticeable difference
C1642.definition: The just noticeable difference (JND) is a result from psychophysics that specifies the amount of change in a stimulus that is required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.

C1643.name: Weber's law
C1643.definition: Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND), the change in magnitude that is noticeable, by representing it as delta M divided by M equals C, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the stimulus, delta M is the just noticeable difference, and C is a constant; equivalently, delta M equals M times C.

C1644.name: auditory perception
C1644.definition: Weber's law and Stevens' power law are laws from psychophysics that also apply to psychoacoustics, or auditory perception, when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli.

C1645.name: perceived loudness
C1645.definition: For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.

C1646.name: pure tone
C1646.definition: For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.

C1647.name: pressure level
C1647.definition: For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.

C1648.name: pitch perception
C1648.definition: In pitch perception, the frequency of a sound wave is referred to as pitch.

C1649.name: sound localization
C1649.definition: Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.

C1650.name: sound source
C1650.definition: Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.

C1651.name: minimum audible angle
C1651.definition: The minimum audible angle (MAA) is the minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener, obtained by applying the just noticeable difference (JND) concept to sound localization and represented in a spherical coordinate system with the listener's head as the origin.

C1652.name: spherical coordinate system
C1652.definition: The minimum audible angle (MAA) is the minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener, obtained by applying the just noticeable difference (JND) concept to sound localization and represented in a spherical coordinate system with the listener's head as the origin.

C1653.name: azimuth
C1653.definition: The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

C1654.name: elevation
C1654.definition: The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

C1655.name: radius
C1655.definition: The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

C1656.name: direction
C1656.definition: The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

C1657.name: sound localization cue
C1657.definition: Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears.

C1658.name: monaural sound localization cue
C1658.definition: Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears.

C1659.name: binaural sound localization cue
C1659.definition: Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears.

C1660.name: interaural level difference
C1660.definition: Interaural level difference (ILD) is a binaural sound localization cue that is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the ear without obstruction receiving a stronger sound, and the difference can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming.

C1661.name: acoustic shadow
C1661.definition: An acoustic shadow occurs when a sound wave does not reach one ear, caused by an object in front of the sound source or by the position of the head.

C1662.name: interaural time difference
C1662.definition: Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears; in an average human head, the ears are 21.5 centimeters apart, sound travels that distance in about 0.6 milliseconds, and this small time difference can be used to locate the source.

C1663.name: auditory component
C1663.definition: The auditory component of an extended reality (XR) system should ideally be non-stationary, moving with the user, and interactive, dependent on the listener's actions.

C1664.name: head-related transfer function
C1664.definition: Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) model how a listener receives sound from a location in space, and this model is relevant for dealing with sound in any system, including extended reality (XR) systems.

C1665.name: binaural sound
C1665.definition: A pair of head-related transfer functions (HRTF) for both ears can be used to synthesize binaural sound, and by generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to the HRTF, a localization effect can be implemented in an extended reality (XR) system.

C1666.name: human somatosensory system
C1666.definition: The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

C1667.name: sensory system
C1667.definition: The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

C1668.name: visual perceptual system
C1668.definition: The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

C1669.name: auditory perceptual system
C1669.definition: The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

C1670.name: kinesthesis
C1670.definition: The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

C1671.name: body part
C1671.definition: Proprioception, called the sixth sense, is the conscious awareness of the pose and movement of each movable human body part, such as legs, arms, fingers, tongue, mouth, and lips, relative to other body parts.

C1672.name: velocity
C1672.definition: Kinesthesis is the awareness of the parameters associated with moving body parts, and it provides information on velocities, accelerations, and forces during movement.

C1673.name: touch receptor
C1673.definition: The human somatosensory system has at least nine major kinds of receptors, of which six are fully devoted to the sense of touch and the remaining three are devoted to proprioception and kinesthesis.

C1674.name: epidermis
C1674.definition: Touch receptors are embedded in the epidermis and dermis, which are the first and second layers of the skin, and the skin also has a hypodermis layer.

C1675.name: dermis
C1675.definition: Touch receptors are embedded in the epidermis and dermis, which are the first and second layers of the skin, and the skin also has a hypodermis layer.

C1676.name: hypodermis
C1676.definition: Touch receptors are embedded in the epidermis and dermis, which are the first and second layers of the skin, and the skin also has a hypodermis layer.

C1677.name: Merkel's disc
C1677.definition: The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles.

C1678.name: hair follicle receptor
C1678.definition: The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles.

C1679.name: free nerve ending
C1679.definition: The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles.

C1680.name: Ruffini's ending
C1680.definition: The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles.

C1681.name: Meissner's corpuscle
C1681.definition: The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles.

C1682.name: Pacinian corpuscle
C1682.definition: The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles.

C1683.name: muscle spindle
C1683.definition: The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

C1684.name: muscle length
C1684.definition: The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

C1685.name: Golgi tendon organ
C1685.definition: The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

C1686.name: tendon
C1686.definition: The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

C1687.name: bone
C1687.definition: The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

C1688.name: muscle tension
C1688.definition: The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

C1689.name: joint receptor
C1689.definition: The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

C1690.name: muscle movement

C1692.name: hand
C1692.definition: When a hand touches an object, activated somatosensory receptors transform the input into neural impulses that are transmitted through a neural network from neuron to neuron to the brain, and the brain processes these impulses into touch perception and can send messages back through the same pathway to cause corrective motor actions, such as removing the hand from a hot object, and the same process is equally applicable to the proprioceptive sense.

C1695.name: haptic perception
C1695.definition: Haptic perception is a major part of somatosensory perception, and it is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects as part of touch perception.

C1696.name: somatosensory perception

C1698.name: haptic exploration
C1698.definition: Haptic exploration is the handling or manipulation of geometric objects that is used to infer the overall geometric shape of the object.

C1699.name: lateral motion
C1699.definition: The six types of haptic exploration, each needed for a different object property perception, are lateral motion for texture perception, pressure for hardness perception, enclosure for global shape or volume perception, static contact for temperature perception, unsupported holding for weight perception, and contour following for local shape perception.

C1711.name: spatial information
C1711.definition: Each haptic exploration used to perceive different properties of objects involves different kinds of receptors and a combination of spatial and temporal information.

C1712.name: temporal information
C1712.definition: Each haptic exploration used to perceive different properties of objects involves different kinds of receptors and a combination of spatial and temporal information.

C1713.name: somatosensory signals
C1713.definition: The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness.

C1714.name: geometric mental model
C1714.definition: The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness.

C1715.name: shape
C1715.definition: The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness.

C1717.name: hardness

C1718.name: mental model
C1718.definition: Haptic perception is important for creating a mental model of the surrounding world, and because mental model creation is an essential part of an immersive experience, haptic perception can improve an immersive experience.

C1719.name: touch sensation
C1719.definition: Touch sensation in extended reality (XR) can be provided by engineered devices, and the most popular form is force feedback, typically in the form of vibrations, provided by force feedback devices such as a force feedback mouse, smart gloves, and body suits, which are common in many XR systems, particularly virtual reality (VR) systems.

C1720.name: force feedback
C1720.definition: Touch sensation in extended reality (XR) can be provided by engineered devices, and the most popular form is force feedback, typically in the form of vibrations, provided by force feedback devices such as a force feedback mouse, smart gloves, and body suits, which are common in many XR systems, particularly virtual reality (VR) systems.

C1721.name: force feedback mouse
C1721.definition: Touch sensation in extended reality (XR) can be provided by engineered devices, and the most popular form is force feedback, typically in the form of vibrations, provided by force feedback devices such as a force feedback mouse, smart gloves, and body suits, which are common in many XR systems, particularly virtual reality (VR) systems.

C1722.name: smart glove
