C1723.name: KGS dot view model DV-2
C1723.definition: The KGS dot view model DV-2 is a haptic pin array with a matrix of pins that a computer controls, and the pins are forced upward, according to signals generated for objects in the virtual world, to simulate the texture of an object surface when the user's fingertip scans across it.

C1724.name: haptic pin array
C1724.definition: The KGS dot view model DV-2 is a haptic pin array with a matrix of pins that a computer controls, and the pins are forced upward, according to signals generated for objects in the virtual world, to simulate the texture of an object surface when the user's fingertip scans across it.

C1725.name: virtual avatar
C1725.definition: Real-world objects whose virtual avatars appear in a virtual world and that are used in place of computer-controlled haptic devices to provide feedback to the user's somatosensory system are sometimes called tangible user interfaces.

C1726.name: somatosensory system
C1726.definition: The human somatosensory system has several receptors, of which six are dedicated to touch and three are dedicated to proprioception and kinesthesis.

C1727.name: tangible user interface
C1727.definition: Real-world objects whose virtual avatars appear in a virtual world and that are used in place of computer-controlled haptic devices to provide feedback to the user's somatosensory system are sometimes called tangible user interfaces.

C1728.name: wearable device sensor
C1728.definition: In a see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens, the computer uses wearable device sensors to detect which real object the user is dealing with and can change the view of that object or add virtual objects to the real world.

C1729.name: chemical sense
C1729.definition: Taste and smell are generally grouped as chemical senses because their chemoreceptors work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.

C1730.name: chemical stimuli
C1730.definition: Taste and smell are generally grouped as chemical senses because their chemoreceptors work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.

C1731.name: touch sense
C1731.definition: There is much less research on integrating smell and taste into extended reality (XR) systems than on visual, auditory, and touch senses, and fewer electronic devices have been made or are being made to provide stimuli to the nose and tongue, the body organs responsible for smell and taste.

C1732.name: odor
C1732.definition: Adding scent or smell to films is an old idea that can be traced back to the early 20th century, and historical systems that included smells include Smell-O-Vision, developed in 1960, which injected 30 different odors into movie theater seats at different points during a film according to the scenery, and Sensorama.

C1733.name: Smell-O-Vision
C1733.definition: Adding scent or smell to films is an old idea that can be traced back to the early 20th century, and historical systems that included smells include Smell-O-Vision, developed in 1960, which injected 30 different odors into movie theater seats at different points during a film according to the scenery, and Sensorama.

C1734.name: smell interface
C1734.definition: A smell interface, also called an olfactory display, provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose, with other components that help create the odor.

C1735.name: air pump
C1735.definition: A smell interface, also called an olfactory display, provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose, with other components that help create the odor.

C1736.name: micropump
C1736.definition: A smell interface, also called an olfactory display, provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose, with other components that help create the odor.

C1737.name: chemical compound
C1737.definition: A smell interface, also called an olfactory display, provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose, with other components that help create the odor.

C1738.name: room-scale delivery
C1738.definition: For smell interfaces, delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than delivering it on a room scale for social or larger experiences, because room-scale delivery generally makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization, which is not easy with current research.

C1739.name: odor intensity
C1739.definition: For smell interfaces, delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than delivering it on a room scale for social or larger experiences, because room-scale delivery generally makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization, which is not easy with current research.

C1740.name: uniformity
C1740.definition: For smell interfaces, delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than delivering it on a room scale for social or larger experiences, because room-scale delivery generally makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization, which is not easy with current research.

C1741.name: odor concentration

C1742.name: visually induced motion sickness
C1742.definition: When olfactory displays can generate odor effects, they are shown to induce strong cognitive and emotional responses that make an immersive experience more attractive and more immersive, and pleasant odors can help reduce visually induced motion sickness, also called cybersickness, to some extent.

C1743.name: taste interface
C1743.definition: A taste interface can place electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation that simulates the main taste types.

C1744.name: main taste types
C1744.definition: A taste interface can place electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation that simulates the main taste types.

C1745.name: user-centered software
C1745.definition: The core design concern for user-centered software is designing usable systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons.

C1746.name: interactive software
C1746.definition: The extended reality (XR) application software being developed is interactive software intended for laypersons, who may not know or need to know how the hardware or software works.

C1747.name: software engineering
C1747.definition: Software engineering can be used as a single term that represents the idea of a software development lifecycle, and engineering software means building the software in stages.

C1748.name: design space
C1748.definition: A design space is the set of all possible designs, and when n distinct objects are placed on a screen without repetition, the typical size of the design space is n factorial, with the number of arrangements increasing if repetition is allowed.

C1749.name: calendar application
C1749.definition: A calendar application has a fixed and large number of elements to be displayed, such as month names, dates, and possibly the year, so it has a very large design space.

C1750.name: stage
C1750.definition: A software development lifecycle is a set of stages that should ideally be followed in a particular sequence.

C1751.name: participant
C1751.definition: In interactive system design, users must be taken into account in every stage and involved as active or passive participants.

C1752.name: user-centric design approach
C1752.definition: A highly iterative software development lifecycle is required for a user-centric design approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software, because including users' needs and expectations changes the stage sequence and creates loops where a developer may return to a previous stage instead of proceeding to the next stage.

C1753.name: iteration
C1753.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs for interactive systems using user feedback through many iterations, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated to identify problems, and refined until not many significantly different problems are identified, after which the design is stabilized and the next stage can begin.

C1754.name: user feedback
C1754.definition: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

C1755.name: feasibility study
C1755.definition: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

C1756.name: requirement gathering
C1756.definition: The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements, and it is aimed at ensuring usability.

C1757.name: analysis
C1757.definition: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

C1758.name: specification
C1758.definition: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

C1759.name: design-prototype-evaluate cycle
C1759.definition: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

C1760.name: design
C1760.definition: In the design of immersive experiences, the term design refers to interface and interaction design rather than code design.

C1761.name: early evaluation
C1761.definition: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

C1762.name: code design
C1762.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.

C1763.name: implementation
C1763.definition: Implementation in interactive system development involves coding followed by code testing; primary-level testing may be review-based, secondary-level testing may be more systematic or structured, such as black box or white box testing, and testing can be performed at unit levels, then integration, and then system-level testing.

C1764.name: code testing
C1764.definition: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

C1765.name: empirical study
C1765.definition: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

C1766.name: usability study
C1766.definition: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

C1767.name: maintenance
C1767.definition: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

C1768.name: end user
C1768.definition: In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client.

C1769.name: requirement-gathering stage
C1769.definition: In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client.

C1770.name: requirement analysis
C1770.definition: In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client.

C1771.name: requirement
C1771.definition: A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application for correcting mistakes is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable, and it does not specify how to implement it.

C1772.name: contextual inquiry
C1772.definition: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

C1773.name: ethnographic study
C1773.definition: Methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.

C1774.name: cultural probe
C1774.definition: Methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.

C1775.name: design-prototype-evaluate loop
C1775.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs for interactive systems using user feedback through many iterations, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated to identify problems, and refined until not many significantly different problems are identified, after which the design is stabilized and the next stage can begin.

C1776.name: turnaround time
C1776.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop and each of its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise the overall turnaround time will increase significantly.

C1777.name: interface design
C1777.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

C1778.name: coding
C1778.definition: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

C1779.name: interactive system development
C1779.definition: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

C1780.name: iterative software development life cycle
C1780.definition: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

C1781.name: executability
C1781.definition: Code testing tests the executability of code by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view.

C1782.name: usability testing
C1782.definition: The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.

C1783.name: iterative design
C1783.definition: In the iterative design of usable extended reality systems, the design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly, and other loops, such as the loop between requirement gathering and the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the loop between code design, coding, and code testing, and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, should not be frequent.

C1784.name: development cost
C1784.definition: Frequent loops other than the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, particularly the loop between code design, coding, and code testing and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, significantly affect a project's overall outcome and turnaround time, escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment.

C1785.name: development stage
C1785.definition: When building usable extended reality systems, the development stages should be completed carefully so that the need to return to previous stages does not arise.

C1786.name: interactive system development lifecycle
C1786.definition: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

C1787.name: design-prototype-evaluate
C1787.definition: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

C1788.name: system development lifecycle
C1788.definition: Extended reality systems are examples of interactive systems, so the same system development lifecycle used for interactive systems can essentially be followed to build extended reality systems.

C1789.name: Majuli case study
C1789.definition: The Majuli case study is about the digital preservation of the physical heritage of the physical space of the Majuli River Island, focusing on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system that digitally preserves the ecological and cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.

C1790.name: digital preservation
C1790.definition: Digital preservation is defined by UNESCO as the use of digital media to preserve educational, scientific, and other resources.

C1791.name: evaluation
C1791.definition: The Majuli case study is about the digital preservation of the physical heritage of the physical space of the Majuli River Island, focusing on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system that digitally preserves the ecological and cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.

C1792.name: Majuli River Island
C1792.definition: Majuli River Island is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the eastern part of Assam, Northeast India, and it is considered the world's largest inhabited river island and a potential United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site contender.

C1793.name: river island
C1793.definition: Majuli River Island is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the eastern part of Assam, Northeast India, and it is considered the world's largest inhabited river island and a potential United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site contender.

C1794.name: Brahmaputra River
C1794.definition: Majuli River Island is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the eastern part of Assam, Northeast India, and it is considered the world's largest inhabited river island and a potential United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site contender.

C1795.name: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization World Heritage Site
C1795.definition: Majuli River Island is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the eastern part of Assam, Northeast India, and it is considered the world's largest inhabited river island and a potential United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site contender.

C1796.name: monsoon season
C1796.definition: Majuli's monsoon season is typically May to September, its non-monsoon season is October to April, and it has an average annual precipitation of 1704 millimeters, an average maximum temperature of 33 degrees Celsius, and a minimum temperature of 7 degrees Celsius.

C1797.name: non-monsoon season
C1797.definition: Majuli's monsoon season is typically May to September, its non-monsoon season is October to April, and it has an average annual precipitation of 1704 millimeters, an average maximum temperature of 33 degrees Celsius, and a minimum temperature of 7 degrees Celsius.

C1801.name: area
C1801.definition: Majuli's area was about 1250 square kilometers around 1900, had reduced to about 570 square kilometers in 1975, and had further reduced to about 427 square kilometers by 2021, with 2021 data giving about 427.09 square kilometers, an overall reduction of almost two-thirds and about a 25 percent reduction from 1975 to 2021.

C1802.name: flood
C1802.definition: Majuli has been constantly hit by severe annual floods and erosion, and river erosion is consuming the island and reducing its habitable area, so formerly habitable areas are no longer habitable and have become sandbars, river banks, underwater areas, or barren areas.

C1808.name: cultural resource
