C1932.name: active mode
C1932.definition: Contextual inquiry can be performed in two broad modes: active mode, where the observer is physically present in the environment where the users are doing their tasks, and passive mode, where no observer is present, user activities are recorded or videotaped and later observed by the observer, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.

C1933.name: passive mode
C1933.definition: Contextual inquiry can be performed in two broad modes: active mode, where the observer is physically present in the environment where the users are doing their tasks, and passive mode, where no observer is present, user activities are recorded or videotaped and later observed by the observer, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.

C1934.name: master-apprentice model
C1934.definition: In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, the master-apprentice model, learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave; such advice is prohibited.

C1935.name: plan stage
C1935.definition: The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

C1936.name: initiate stage
C1936.definition: The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

C1937.name: execute stage
C1937.definition: The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

C1938.name: close stage
C1938.definition: The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

C1939.name: reflect stage
C1939.definition: The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

C1940.name: design goal
C1940.definition: The reflect stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals.

C1941.name: affinity diagram method
C1941.definition: The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals.

C1942.name: design specification
C1942.definition: The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals.

C1943.name: group header
C1943.definition: In the affinity diagram method, a group header is a name or identifier assigned to a group after the ideas have been sorted, and it refers to the pattern that binds the ideas within that group; the header is not present in the initial ideas.

C1944.name: class note-taking application
C1944.definition: In the class note-taking application example, the 19 affinity-diagram ideas are organized into six groups with the headers navigation in notebook, media content, navigation in notes, note organization, text formatting, and storage and privacy, containing 3, 5, 2, 2, 4, and 3 ideas respectively.

C1945.name: design recommendation
C1945.definition: After the finished affinity diagram is drawn, reflection means deciding what to do with the data and formulating a set of design recommendations based on the data.

C1946.name: informed design choice
C1946.definition: Design recommendations or guidelines derived from contextual inquiry are informed design choices because they are produced by analyzing the collected inquiry data, whereas guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices that do not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.

C1947.name: uninformed design choice
C1947.definition: Design recommendations or guidelines derived from contextual inquiry are informed design choices because they are produced by analyzing the collected inquiry data, whereas guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices that do not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.

C1948.name: affinity diagram
C1948.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the observations that all users set reminders and that three out of five users used a mobile app to check the day and date and set a reminder for assignment submission are grouped under the header reminder setting.

C1949.name: header
C1949.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the observations that all users set reminders and that three out of five users used a mobile app to check the day and date and set a reminder for assignment submission are grouped under the header reminder setting.

C1950.name: reminder setting
C1950.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the observations that all users set reminders and that three out of five users used a mobile app to check the day and date and set a reminder for assignment submission are grouped under the header reminder setting.

C1951.name: work scheduling
C1951.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the five contextual inquiry (CI) observations that do not relate to reminder setting, namely checking upcoming deadlines, checking the date and then the timetable, checking meeting dates, checking meeting schedules on a particular day, and checking lecture schedules on a particular day, were first grouped under the header work scheduling and then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling, giving a finished diagram with three groups: reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling.

C1952.name: overall scheduling
C1952.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the five contextual inquiry (CI) observations that do not relate to reminder setting, namely checking upcoming deadlines, checking the date and then the timetable, checking meeting dates, checking meeting schedules on a particular day, and checking lecture schedules on a particular day, were first grouped under the header work scheduling and then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling, giving a finished diagram with three groups: reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling.

C1953.name: day-wise scheduling
C1953.definition: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the five contextual inquiry (CI) observations that do not relate to reminder setting, namely checking upcoming deadlines, checking the date and then the timetable, checking meeting dates, checking meeting schedules on a particular day, and checking lecture schedules on a particular day, were first grouped under the header work scheduling and then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling, giving a finished diagram with three groups: reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling.

C1954.name: design guideline
C1954.definition: Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is good, bad, usable, or unusable, so the design needs to be implemented and tested to determine whether it will work.

C1955.name: design principle
C1955.definition: The outcome of contextual inquiry, a usability requirement gathering method, can be utilized as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, and also as functional requirements.

C1956.name: function
C1956.definition: Functional requirements are requirements specified in terms of functions that have a well-defined input and a well-defined output, and this functional specification makes them easy to convert to code so that the transition to code design becomes easier.

C1957.name: functional specification
C1957.definition: Functional requirements are requirements specified in terms of functions that have a well-defined input and a well-defined output, and this functional specification makes them easy to convert to code so that the transition to code design becomes easier.

C1958.name: code
C1958.definition: Functional requirements are requirements specified in terms of functions that have a well-defined input and a well-defined output, and this functional specification makes them easy to convert to code so that the transition to code design becomes easier.

C1959.name: note-taking application
C1959.definition: In the note-taking application example, guidelines framed from observations are generic and specify what the application should or should not do, not how to do it.

C1960.name: guideline
C1960.definition: In the note-taking application example, guidelines framed from observations are generic and specify what the application should or should not do, not how to do it.

C1961.name: feedback
C1961.definition: In the note-taking application example, guidelines based on behaviors observed in the context of use are used to include those behaviors in the overall system, thereby ensuring that the user is involved in the design based on observations and feedback.

C1962.name: software requirements specification
C1962.definition: A software requirements specification (SRS) is the textual document that specifies all requirements of a system, both functional and non-functional, and it includes the formal specification of the functional requirements.

C1963.name: requirement hierarchy
C1963.definition: In a software requirements specification (SRS), requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement, and each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.

C1964.name: requirement identifier
C1964.definition: In a software requirements specification (SRS), requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement, and each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.

C1965.name: top-level requirement
C1965.definition: In a software requirements specification (SRS), requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement, and each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.

C1966.name: sub-requirement
C1966.definition: In a software requirements specification (SRS), requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement, and each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.

C1967.name: Majuli virtual reality tour
C1967.definition: Usability requirements for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour were gathered by making field trips to Majuli, interviewing people, observing people in their natural work settings, and collecting data in the form of notes.

C1968.name: virtual reality tour
C1968.definition: Virtual locomotion techniques (VLTs), used to navigate or perform a virtual reality (VR) tour by moving from one point to another, are broadly categorized into walking-based techniques (full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques, involving physical walking), steering-based techniques, selection-based techniques, and manipulation-based techniques.

C1969.name: field trips
C1969.definition: Usability requirements for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour were gathered by making field trips to Majuli, interviewing people, observing people in their natural work settings, and collecting data in the form of notes.

C1970.name: students or learners
C1970.definition: Three potential user groups in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study were identified through field trips, interviews, observations, and local people's experience of typical visitors and their activities: students or learners interested in knowing about the island, tourists interested in exploring tourist spots or other interesting places on the island, and pilgrims interested in religious places and practices.

C1971.name: tourists
C1971.definition: Three potential user groups in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study were identified through field trips, interviews, observations, and local people's experience of typical visitors and their activities: students or learners interested in knowing about the island, tourists interested in exploring tourist spots or other interesting places on the island, and pilgrims interested in religious places and practices.

C1972.name: pilgrims
C1972.definition: Three potential user groups in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study were identified through field trips, interviews, observations, and local people's experience of typical visitors and their activities: students or learners interested in knowing about the island, tourists interested in exploring tourist spots or other interesting places on the island, and pilgrims interested in religious places and practices.

C1973.name: system features
C1973.definition: Contextual inquiry (CI) in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was conducted after the user groups were identified, on samples from those user groups, to learn their needs and expectations, identify the system features to be supported for each group, and identify specific issues for those groups related to broad design challenges.

C1974.name: design challenge
C1974.definition: A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide a comprehensive view of a large geographical area with large multimodal data while avoiding cyber sickness, because exploring the entire island with all collected data is time consuming and may cause cyber sickness.

C1975.name: large geographical area
C1975.definition: A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide a comprehensive view of a large geographical area with large multimodal data while avoiding cyber sickness, because exploring the entire island with all collected data is time consuming and may cause cyber sickness.

C1976.name: multimodal data
C1976.definition: A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide a comprehensive view of a large geographical area with large multimodal data while avoiding cyber sickness, because exploring the entire island with all collected data is time consuming and may cause cyber sickness.

C1977.name: data subset restriction
C1977.definition: The large geographical area and cyber sickness challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was addressed by allowing each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, with each subset identified through contextual inquiry (CI) based on what that group typically does.

C1978.name: data set
C1978.definition: The data-subset restriction in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study reduced the expanse of information and the need to explore everything in detail, reduced the possibility of cyber sickness, and increased interest for each group, whereas making the entire data set accessible to all users could confuse users, reduce their interest, and lead to cyber sickness.

C1979.name: location information
C1979.definition: Accurate location information in any virtual reality (VR) tour is crucial, especially for large geographies, because it prevents disorientation and gives users more confidence and purpose by telling them where they are in the geographical space.

C1980.name: geographical space
C1980.definition: Accurate location information in any virtual reality (VR) tour is crucial, especially for large geographies, because it prevents disorientation and gives users more confidence and purpose by telling them where they are in the geographical space.

C1981.name: location awareness
C1981.definition: Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.

C1982.name: tangible heritage experiences
C1982.definition: A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide both tangible and intangible heritage experiences and to combine them for a seamless user experience.

C1983.name: intangible heritage experiences
C1983.definition: A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide both tangible and intangible heritage experiences and to combine them for a seamless user experience.

C1984.name: interaction aid
C1984.definition: Another key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was interaction aid for enhanced user experience, which includes navigation support to cover a large geography, user-friendly interfaces, and increased presence through natural interactions.

C1985.name: navigation support
C1985.definition: Another key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was interaction aid for enhanced user experience, which includes navigation support to cover a large geography, user-friendly interfaces, and increased presence through natural interactions.

C1986.name: user-friendly interfaces
C1986.definition: Another key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was interaction aid for enhanced user experience, which includes navigation support to cover a large geography, user-friendly interfaces, and increased presence through natural interactions.

C1987.name: non-interactive software development
C1987.definition: In the interactive system development lifecycle, code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

C1988.name: design-prototype-evaluation cycle
C1988.definition: Designing an immersive experience involves the design-prototype-evaluation cycle in order to incorporate user requirements.

C1989.name: interface and interaction design
C1989.definition: Interface and interaction design involves two issues: where or how to start the design process and how to express a design so that it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language.

C1990.name: design process
C1990.definition: Interface and interaction design involves two issues: where or how to start the design process and how to express a design so that it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language.

C1991.name: design language
C1991.definition: Interface and interaction design involves two issues: where or how to start the design process and how to express a design so that it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language.

C1992.name: Shneiderman's eight golden rules
C1992.definition: Some design guidelines are generic, small in number, and cover broad high-level aspects of interactive systems; examples are Shneiderman's eight golden rules and Donald Norman's seven principles, both primarily intended for graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but applicable to other domains, with Norman's seven principles developed in the 1980s.

C1993.name: Donald Norman's seven principles
C1993.definition: Some design guidelines are generic, small in number, and cover broad high-level aspects of interactive systems; examples are Shneiderman's eight golden rules and Donald Norman's seven principles, both primarily intended for graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but applicable to other domains, with Norman's seven principles developed in the 1980s.

C1994.name: Apple's human interface guidelines
C1994.definition: Other design guidelines are more detailed and specific, generally large in number, and cover the micro details of a particular system or product; for example, Apple's human interface guidelines were originally developed for Apple's user interfaces.

C1995.name: specific design guideline
C1995.definition: The virtual reality (VR)-specific guidelines for avoiding or minimizing cyber sickness are specific design guidelines that are typically applicable to virtual reality or immersive systems where immersion is very important, but may not be specifically applicable to augmented reality (AR) systems because augmented reality immersion differs from virtual reality immersion.

C1996.name: immersive system
C1996.definition: The virtual reality (VR)-specific guidelines for avoiding or minimizing cyber sickness are specific design guidelines that are typically applicable to virtual reality or immersive systems where immersion is very important, but may not be specifically applicable to augmented reality (AR) systems because augmented reality immersion differs from virtual reality immersion.

C1997.name: generic design guideline
C1997.definition: Generic design guidelines are guidelines applicable to any interactive system, including extended reality (XR) systems, although they are mostly, not fully, applicable to extended reality systems.

C1998.name: Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules
C1998.definition: Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are a set of eight generic design rules originally developed in 1986 primarily for graphical user interfaces (GUIs), and can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces, including extended reality (XR) systems.

C1999.name: generic design rule
C1999.definition: Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are a set of eight generic design rules originally developed in 1986 primarily for graphical user interfaces (GUIs), and can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces, including extended reality (XR) systems.

C2000.name: Shneiderman's first golden rule
C2000.definition: Shneiderman's first golden rule of system and interface design is to strive for consistency.

C2001.name: consistency
C2001.definition: Shneiderman's first golden rule of system and interface design is to strive for consistency.

C2002.name: internal consistency
C2002.definition: The consistency required by Shneiderman's first golden rule has two types: internal consistency and external or environmental consistency.

C2003.name: external consistency
C2003.definition: The consistency required by Shneiderman's first golden rule has two types: internal consistency and external or environmental consistency.

C2004.name: Shneiderman's second golden rule
C2004.definition: Shneiderman's second golden rule is to design for universal usability, meaning a system should provide facilities for all user categories and support different user categories rather than only specific user categories.

C2005.name: universal usability
C2005.definition: Shneiderman's second golden rule is to design for universal usability, meaning a system should provide facilities for all user categories and support different user categories rather than only specific user categories.

C2006.name: menu-based option
C2006.definition: Menu-based options can be preferable to hotkey options for users who may not remember hotkey combinations because menu options rely on recognition rather than recall, and recall is a skilled task, whereas hotkeys such as Control plus S (Ctrl+S) are faster for users who do not want to use slower menu-based options.

C2007.name: hotkey
C2007.definition: Menu-based options can be preferable to hotkey options for users who may not remember hotkey combinations because menu options rely on recognition rather than recall, and recall is a skilled task, whereas hotkeys such as Control plus S (Ctrl+S) are faster for users who do not want to use slower menu-based options.

C2008.name: Control plus S
C2008.definition: Menu-based options can be preferable to hotkey options for users who may not remember hotkey combinations because menu options rely on recognition rather than recall, and recall is a skilled task, whereas hotkeys such as Control plus S (Ctrl+S) are faster for users who do not want to use slower menu-based options.

C2009.name: recognition
C2009.definition: Menu-based options can be preferable to hotkey options for users who may not remember hotkey combinations because menu options rely on recognition rather than recall, and recall is a skilled task, whereas hotkeys such as Control plus S (Ctrl+S) are faster for users who do not want to use slower menu-based options.

C2010.name: recall
C2010.definition: Menu-based options can be preferable to hotkey options for users who may not remember hotkey combinations because menu options rely on recognition rather than recall, and recall is a skilled task, whereas hotkeys such as Control plus S (Ctrl+S) are faster for users who do not want to use slower menu-based options.

C2011.name: usable design
C2011.definition: The third rule of usable design is to provide informative feedback to users for whatever action the user performs.

C2012.name: informative feedback
C2012.definition: The third rule of usable design is to provide informative feedback to users for whatever action the user performs.

C2013.name: progress bar
C2013.definition: A progress bar is informative feedback that sometimes appears during a task, shows the percentage of the task completed, and gives the user a sense of how much longer to wait; without it, the user cannot tell what the system is doing or how much of the task is completed.

C2014.name: save icon
C2014.definition: A color change on a save icon after a save operation is informative feedback that indicates the save operation is done successfully; without it, the user cannot tell whether the save operation worked.

C2015.name: dialogue
C2015.definition: The fourth rule is to design dialogues to yield closure by organizing task execution into beginning, middle, and end parts and providing feedback at the end of each group, so the user feels the task is started, executed, and completed.

C2016.name: closure
C2016.definition: The fourth rule is to design dialogues to yield closure by organizing task execution into beginning, middle, and end parts and providing feedback at the end of each group, so the user feels the task is started, executed, and completed.

C2017.name: error prevention
C2017.definition: The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.

C2018.name: error handling
C2018.definition: The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.

C2019.name: user error
C2019.definition: In system design, user errors cannot be completely eliminated, so a design should aim to keep error rates low; for example, close and start options for the same interface should not be placed side by side because a user may accidentally choose the wrong action.

C2020.name: error rate
C2020.definition: In system design, user errors cannot be completely eliminated, so a design should aim to keep error rates low; for example, close and start options for the same interface should not be placed side by side because a user may accidentally choose the wrong action.

C2021.name: reversal of actions
C2021.definition: The sixth rule in system design is to permit easy reversal of actions, ideally by keeping a reversal option available so users can return from an erroneous situation.

C2022.name: reversal option
C2022.definition: The sixth rule in system design is to permit easy reversal of actions, ideally by keeping a reversal option available so users can return from an erroneous situation.

C2023.name: undo
C2023.definition: Undo and redo facilities are primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.

C2024.name: redo
C2024.definition: Undo and redo facilities are primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.

C2025.name: usability rule
C2025.definition: The seventh usability rule, keeping users in control, requires that lay users feel in control of the system, perceive that their interaction changes the system state, and receive feedback on their actions and results, because lack of this feeling makes them feel at a loss and reduces usability.

C2026.name: keeping users in control
C2026.definition: The seventh usability rule, keeping users in control, requires that lay users feel in control of the system, perceive that their interaction changes the system state, and receive feedback on their actions and results, because lack of this feeling makes them feel at a loss and reduces usability.

C2027.name: human memory
C2027.definition: In a broad sense, human memory comprises short-term and long-term memory, where short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.

C2028.name: short-term memory
C2028.definition: In a broad sense, human memory comprises short-term and long-term memory, where short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.

C2029.name: seven plus or minus two rule
C2029.definition: George Miller's 1956 psychological finding, the seven plus or minus two rule, gives the short-term memory limit as five to nine chunks of information at a time, so holding fewer underutilizes short-term memory and holding more overutilizes it and is harmful.

C2030.name: short-term memory limit
C2030.definition: George Miller's 1956 psychological finding, the seven plus or minus two rule, gives the short-term memory limit as five to nine chunks of information at a time, so holding fewer underutilizes short-term memory and holding more overutilizes it and is harmful.

C2031.name: chunk of information
C2031.definition: George Miller's 1956 psychological finding, the seven plus or minus two rule, gives the short-term memory limit as five to nine chunks of information at a time, so holding fewer underutilizes short-term memory and holding more overutilizes it and is harmful.

C2032.name: reducing short-term memory load
C2032.definition: The last usability rule, reducing short-term memory load, requires keeping the information needed to operate an interface or perform an interaction between five and nine chunks for the user's optimum outcome, and not forcing users to remember more than nine chunks.

C2033.name: short-term memory load
C2033.definition: The last usability rule, reducing short-term memory load, requires keeping the information needed to operate an interface or perform an interaction between five and nine chunks for the user's optimum outcome, and not forcing users to remember more than nine chunks.

C2034.name: object interaction
C2034.definition: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

C2035.name: navigation
C2035.definition: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

C2036.name: interaction for system control
C2036.definition: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

C2037.name: selection
C2037.definition: In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.

C2038.name: manipulation
C2038.definition: In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.

C2039.name: navigation technique
C2039.definition: Navigation techniques are interaction techniques for moving from one point to another in a virtual world.

C2040.name: system control
C2040.definition: In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

C2041.name: object selection technique
C2041.definition: For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.

C2042.name: selection performance
C2042.definition: For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.

C2043.name: selection task
C2043.definition: For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.

C2044.name: density
C2044.definition: For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.

C2045.name: target object
C2045.definition: For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.

C2046.name: number of targets
C2046.definition: For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.

C2047.name: target occlusion
C2047.definition: Target occlusion can also be an important factor in selection performance: if a target is partly occluded by other surrounding objects, locating and selecting it is challenging and specialized techniques may be required, while fully occluded objects may also be selected, but the user must first be made aware of their presence, and specialized selection of fully occluded objects is a special case, with the majority of cases involving partially occluded or partially visible objects.

C2048.name: selection with the hand
C2048.definition: Object selection techniques in a virtual world include selection with the hand, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection.

C2049.name: pointing-based selection
C2049.definition: Pointing-based selection is a selection technique in which the user operates a controller to extend a ray into the distance in the virtual world, sees the ray, and can select the first object intersected by the ray through a user-controlled trigger on the controller.

C2050.name: image plane selection
C2050.definition: The third category of object selection techniques is image plane or volumetric selection.

C2051.name: volume-based selection
C2051.definition: Object selection techniques in a virtual world include selection with the hand, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection.

C2052.name: bimanual selection
C2052.definition: Object selection techniques in a virtual world include selection with the hand, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection.

C2053.name: hand selection technique
C2053.definition: A hand selection technique selects virtual objects in a virtual world with the user's hand by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch the object and trigger a grab; conventionally, selection with hand involves one hand, using a single finger or multiple fingers of one hand.

C2054.name: grab
C2054.definition: A hand selection technique selects virtual objects in a virtual world with the user's hand by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch the object and trigger a grab; conventionally, selection with hand involves one hand, using a single finger or multiple fingers of one hand.

C2055.name: virtual hand technique
C2055.definition: Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.

C2056.name: go-go technique
C2056.definition: Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.

C2057.name: prism technique
C2057.definition: Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.

C2058.name: intent-driven selection
C2058.definition: Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.

C2059.name: one-to-one mapping
C2059.definition: The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements.

C2060.name: three-dimensional tracked controller
C2060.definition: The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements.

C2061.name: virtual arm length
C2061.definition: The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant objects that allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length, the length of the virtual hand, uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so that distant objects can be reached quickly.

C2062.name: hand velocity
C2062.definition: The prism technique is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and if the hand velocity is slower than a specified minimum velocity, the virtual hand remains still.

C2063.name: proximity sphere
C2063.definition: Intent-driven selection techniques typically use proximity spheres that encompass multiple objects at a larger distance and progressively reduce in size, depending on hand or finger postures, as the user moves closer to the intended object, refining the selection to a specific object.

C2064.name: travel technique
C2064.definition: In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

C2065.name: grabbing technique
C2065.definition: In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

C2066.name: virtual ray
C2066.definition: Pointing-based selection is a selection technique in which the user operates a controller to extend a ray into the distance in the virtual world, sees the ray, and can select the first object intersected by the ray through a user-controlled trigger on the controller.

C2067.name: hand pointing
C2067.definition: Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker.

C2068.name: head pointing
C2068.definition: Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker.

C2069.name: eye-gaze pointing
C2069.definition: Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker.

C2070.name: eye tracker
C2070.definition: Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker.

C2071.name: eye gaze
C2071.definition: A virtual ray in pointing-based selection is a short line segment or an infinite line that can be attached to the virtual hand, head, or eye, with head position or eye gaze used when hand tracking is unavailable.

C2072.name: ray casting
C2072.definition: Ray casting is the most basic way to extend a ray in pointing-based selection, in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

C2073.name: bend cast
C2073.definition: Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.

C2074.name: selectable object
C2074.definition: Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.

C2075.name: point-line distance
C2075.definition: Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.

C2076.name: depth ray
C2076.definition: Depth ray is an improvement over basic ray casting in which a user-controlled depth marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

C2077.name: depth marker
C2077.definition: Depth ray is an improvement over basic ray casting in which a user-controlled depth marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

C2078.name: two-dimensional
C2078.definition: Image plane selection, also known as occlusion and framing, is a two-dimensional (2D) selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance.

C2079.name: view plane
C2079.definition: Projection transformation maps objects described in a three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane.

C2080.name: head crusher technique
C2080.definition: The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common.

C2081.name: image plane
C2081.definition: In the head crusher technique, the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional (2D) image plane.

C2082.name: sticky finger technique
C2082.definition: The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common.

C2083.name: lifting palm technique
C2083.definition: The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common.

C2084.name: framing hands technique
C2084.definition: The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common.

C2085.name: volumetric selection
C2085.definition: The third category of object selection techniques is image plane or volumetric selection.

C2086.name: box
C2086.definition: Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone.

C2087.name: cube
C2087.definition: Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone.

C2088.name: sphere
C2088.definition: Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone.

C2089.name: cone casting flashlight technique
C2089.definition: The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique that extends ray casting by casting a cone instead of a ray to a distance and selecting the objects within the cone.

C2090.name: sphere casting flashlight technique
C2090.definition: The sphere casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique in which a sphere is cast onto the nearest intersected surface and the objects found within the sphere are selected.

C2091.name: two-handed box selection technique
C2091.definition: The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.

C2092.name: bimanual
C2092.definition: The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.

C2093.name: rectangular parallelepiped
C2093.definition: The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.

C2094.name: object manipulation
C2094.definition: Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.

C2095.name: scale
C2095.definition: Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.

C2096.name: texture
C2096.definition: A Unity model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data, and, if the object represents an animated character, it can also contain animation-related data.

C2097.name: behavior
C2097.definition: Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.

C2098.name: manipulation technique
C2098.definition: Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

C2099.name: hand manipulation
C2099.definition: Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

C2100.name: indirect manipulation
C2100.definition: Indirect manipulation is a method sometimes used to manipulate virtual objects in which the user does not directly manipulate the virtual object using the physical hand, but instead manipulates other objects mapped to the virtual object, and those other objects in turn manipulate the virtual object.

C2101.name: bimanual manipulation
C2101.definition: Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

C2102.name: integrated hybrid manipulation
C2102.definition: Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

C2103.name: hand selection
C2103.definition: Hand manipulation follows hand selection and is implemented using smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction, and it is the most intuitive way of manipulating objects.

C2104.name: gesture-based manipulation
C2104.definition: Hand manipulation follows hand selection and is implemented using smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction, and it is the most intuitive way of manipulating objects.

C2105.name: computational power
C2105.definition: Hand manipulation requires somewhat more computational power or specialized devices, which may be relatively costly.

C2106.name: three-dimensional widget
C2106.definition: Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object.

C2107.name: indirect proxy
C2107.definition: Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

C2108.name: local proxy
C2108.definition: Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

C2109.name: physical proxy prop
C2109.definition: Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

C2110.name: neurological data set
C2110.definition: Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

C2111.name: world in miniature
C2111.definition: World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world.

C2112.name: miniature model
C2112.definition: World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world.

C2113.name: bimanual manipulation technique
C2113.definition: A bimanual manipulation technique manipulates objects with both hands, and its hand movement can be synchronous, in which both hands move together, or asynchronous, in which the hands do not need to move simultaneously.

C2114.name: synchronous
C2114.definition: A bimanual manipulation technique manipulates objects with both hands, and its hand movement can be synchronous, in which both hands move together, or asynchronous, in which the hands do not need to move simultaneously.

C2115.name: asynchronous
C2115.definition: A bimanual manipulation technique manipulates objects with both hands, and its hand movement can be synchronous, in which both hands move together, or asynchronous, in which the hands do not need to move simultaneously.

C2116.name: spindle technique
C2116.definition: The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle.

C2117.name: imaginary axis
C2117.definition: The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle.

C2118.name: virtual spindle
C2118.definition: The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle.

C2119.name: virtual world object
C2119.definition: In the spindle technique, moving both hands in unison can move a virtual world object, and the technique can also be used to rotate the object simultaneously.

C2120.name: spindle plus wheel
C2120.definition: Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric but synchronous technique and an extension of the spindle technique, in which both hands need to be moved together but need not be symmetrically placed around the sides of an imaginary axis.

C2121.name: integrated hybrid manipulation technique
C2121.definition: Integrated hybrid manipulation techniques are techniques that switch automatically from selection to manipulation after selection, without any explicit signal from the user, and switch back to selection mode after manipulation.

C2122.name: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting
C2122.definition: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique that mixes ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation, so selection and manipulation are integrated and the user does not need to perform them separately.

C2123.name: system control interaction
C2123.definition: System control interaction is a third category of interaction that primarily relies on regular interaction techniques that are familiar when dealing with any computer system.

C2124.name: travel
C2124.definition: The movement involved in navigation in a virtual world has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.

C2125.name: wayfinding
C2125.definition: Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

C2126.name: exploration
C2126.definition: Travel in navigation can be done by exploration, search, or maneuvering: exploration has no explicit goal or target point and the user moves around to see, learn, or explore; search is moving to a specified target location; and maneuvering comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

C2127.name: search
C2127.definition: Travel in navigation can be done by exploration, search, or maneuvering: exploration has no explicit goal or target point and the user moves around to see, learn, or explore; search is moving to a specified target location; and maneuvering comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

C2128.name: maneuvering
C2128.definition: Travel in navigation can be done by exploration, search, or maneuvering: exploration has no explicit goal or target point and the user moves around to see, learn, or explore; search is moving to a specified target location; and maneuvering comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

C2129.name: walking-based locomotion
C2129.definition: Walking-based locomotion is a technique for traveling in a virtual environment in which physical walking or movement in the physical world is mapped to corresponding movement in the virtual environment.

C2130.name: selection-based locomotion
C2130.definition: Selection-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user selects where to go rather than continuously specifying how to move there by steering or looking.

C2131.name: manipulation-based locomotion
C2131.definition: Travel in navigation can be accomplished using four broad types of locomotion techniques: walking-based locomotion, steering-based locomotion, selection-based locomotion, and manipulation-based locomotion.

C2132.name: full gait technique
C2132.definition: Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

C2133.name: partial gait technique
C2133.definition: Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

C2134.name: gait negation technique
C2134.definition: Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

C2135.name: virtual navigation
C2135.definition: In full gait techniques, completely free walking is not practical or possible for virtual navigation, so walking is restricted within a specified limit in the physical space and translated to any amount of movement in a potentially infinite virtual space, creating a mismatch between physical and virtual movement.

C2136.name: immersive hardware
C2136.definition: Partial gait techniques require specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware to provide input, may involve active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors, or interfaces with pressure sensors, and map the user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

C2137.name: active walking interface
C2137.definition: Partial gait techniques require specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware to provide input, may involve active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors, or interfaces with pressure sensors, and map the user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

C2138.name: pressure mat
C2138.definition: Partial gait techniques require specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware to provide input, may involve active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors, or interfaces with pressure sensors, and map the user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

C2139.name: pressure sensor
C2139.definition: Partial gait techniques require specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware to provide input, may involve active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors, or interfaces with pressure sensors, and map the user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

C2140.name: linear treadmill
C2140.definition: Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.

C2141.name: motorized floor tile
C2141.definition: Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.

C2142.name: human-sized hamster ball
C2142.definition: Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.

C2143.name: friction-free platform
C2143.definition: Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.

C2144.name: steering-based navigation
C2144.definition: Steering-based navigation is a navigation category in which direction and speed are continuously controlled while the user moves from one point to another, and continuous control of direction and speed essentially indicates that a system has implemented steering-based navigation.

C2145.name: spatial steering-based navigation
C2145.definition: Steering-based navigation has two types: spatial steering-based navigation, which is controlled using the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, which is controlled using vehicular props or additional hardware.

C2146.name: physical steering-based navigation
C2146.definition: Steering-based navigation has two types: spatial steering-based navigation, which is controlled using the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, which is controlled using vehicular props or additional hardware.

C2147.name: gaze-directed
C2147.definition: Spatial steering-based navigation can be gaze-directed, where looking at a target location moves the user continuously in the direction of looking; hand-directed, where hand gestures determine the direction of travel; or body-leaning directed, where leaning the body toward a movement direction is mapped to corresponding travel.

C2148.name: hand-directed
C2148.definition: Spatial steering-based navigation can be gaze-directed, where looking at a target location moves the user continuously in the direction of looking; hand-directed, where hand gestures determine the direction of travel; or body-leaning directed, where leaning the body toward a movement direction is mapped to corresponding travel.

C2149.name: body-leaning directed
C2149.definition: Spatial steering-based navigation can be gaze-directed, where looking at a target location moves the user continuously in the direction of looking; hand-directed, where hand gestures determine the direction of travel; or body-leaning directed, where leaning the body toward a movement direction is mapped to corresponding travel.

C2150.name: bike locomotion platform
C2150.definition: Physical steering-based navigation involves physical setups or separate hardware, such as bike locomotion platforms and virtual reality (VR) simulators for aircraft, merchant ships, cars, boats and spaceships, in which physically moving the steering controls travel in the virtual world.

C2151.name: virtual reality simulator
C2151.definition: Physical steering-based navigation involves physical setups or separate hardware, such as bike locomotion platforms and virtual reality (VR) simulators for aircraft, merchant ships, cars, boats and spaceships, in which physically moving the steering controls travel in the virtual world.

C2152.name: target selection-based locomotion
C2152.definition: Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion.

C2153.name: route planning-based locomotion
C2153.definition: Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion.

C2154.name: map dragging
C2154.definition: Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

C2155.name: jumper technique
C2155.definition: Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

C2156.name: cave-type systems
C2156.definition: Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

C2157.name: virtual viewpoint
C2157.definition: In target selection-based locomotion, the user selects a destination or target, and the virtual viewpoint changes so that the user feels moved to the target.

C2158.name: homer technique
C2158.definition: Manipulation-based locomotion can be implemented using a combination of the go-go technique, homer technique, and world in miniature metaphor.

C2159.name: world in miniature metaphor
C2159.definition: Manipulation-based locomotion can be implemented using a combination of the go-go technique, homer technique, and world in miniature metaphor.

C2160.name: path
C2160.definition: Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

C2161.name: destination
C2161.definition: Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

C2162.name: spatial knowledge
C2162.definition: Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

C2163.name: environment design
C2163.definition: The objective of environment design is to make it easier for the user to build a mental map; if the design does not support creation of this mental map, many problems may occur and the overall user experience deteriorates.

C2164.name: wayfinding mental model
C2164.definition: The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.

C2165.name: landmark knowledge
C2165.definition: The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.

C2166.name: procedural knowledge
C2166.definition: The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.

C2167.name: topological knowledge
C2167.definition: The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.

C2168.name: knowledge base
C2168.definition: The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.

C2169.name: wayfinding support
C2169.definition: For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.

C2170.name: locomotion or travel support
C2170.definition: For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.

C2171.name: landmark support
C2171.definition: Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

C2172.name: landmark
C2172.definition: Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

C2173.name: map support
C2173.definition: Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.

C2174.name: world in miniature display
C2174.definition: Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.

C2175.name: path following support
C2175.definition: Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

C2176.name: breadcrumb support
C2176.definition: Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.

C2177.name: compass
C2177.definition: A compass or another direction indicator can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space, and a compass can be designed and placed in the environment.

C2178.name: direction indicator
C2178.definition: A compass or another direction indicator can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space, and a compass can be designed and placed in the environment.

C2179.name: two-dimensional space
C2179.definition: A compass or another direction indicator can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space, and a compass can be designed and placed in the environment.

C2180.name: command
