C2199.name: user experience design
C2199.definition: The design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was framed by its broader objectives of capturing tangible and intangible heritage, enhancing user presence, and minimizing cyber sickness, with corresponding design considerations of user experience design, exploration of the island, and handling cyber sickness.

C2200.name: minimap
C2200.definition: A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place on the island, such as a village or town; it differs in appearance from the global island map and is provided at each of the island's 24 information points to give the user a sense of belonging or local orientation to that place.

C2201.name: notification system
C2201.definition: User feedback and interaction with users for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour led to incorporated design elements such as a minimap, a notification system, and user controls.

C2202.name: user controls
C2202.definition: User feedback and interaction with users for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour led to incorporated design elements such as a minimap, a notification system, and user controls.

C2203.name: user categories
C2203.definition: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

C2204.name: information point
C2204.definition: The objective of the Majuli case study is an immersive, interactive virtual reality tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and each information point reveals related information for interactive exploration.

C2205.name: curved screen
C2205.definition: The starting point of the virtual tour uses a curved screen in an immersive setting to show an introductory video about Majuli island and a tutorial video that acquaints users with how to use the system.

C2206.name: introductory video
C2206.definition: The starting point of the virtual tour uses a curved screen in an immersive setting to show an introductory video about Majuli island and a tutorial video that acquaints users with how to use the system.

C2207.name: tutorial video
C2207.definition: The starting point of the virtual tour uses a curved screen in an immersive setting to show an introductory video about Majuli island and a tutorial video that acquaints users with how to use the system.

C2208.name: boat ride experience
C2208.definition: A boat ride experience at the very start of the virtual tour uses a 360-degree boat ride video to give the user the feeling of being transported by boat from one bank of a river to the other bank, that is, from the mainland to the island or from the island to the mainland.

C2209.name: 360-degree boat ride video
C2209.definition: A boat ride experience at the very start of the virtual tour uses a 360-degree boat ride video to give the user the feeling of being transported by boat from one bank of a river to the other bank, that is, from the mainland to the island or from the island to the mainland.

C2210.name: icon
C2210.definition: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

C2211.name: preprocessing
C2211.definition: Preprocessing of the collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and the user's quality of experience involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements, such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow.

C2212.name: quality of experience
C2212.definition: Preprocessing of the collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and the user's quality of experience involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements, such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow.

C2213.name: high-resolution content
C2213.definition: Preprocessing of the collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and the user's quality of experience involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements, such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow.

C2214.name: 360-degree camera
C2214.definition: Preprocessing of the collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and the user's quality of experience involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements, such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow.

C2215.name: image editing tool
C2215.definition: The images and videos, mostly the images, were edited with image editing tools for uniform illumination because the 360-degree images captured at different times have different illumination and changing illumination while the user moves from one image to another will make the user feel that something is odd.

C2216.name: ambient sound
C2216.definition: Ambient sounds such as temple bells, birds chirping, and bike horns were added and played depending on the place being visited to enhance realism and create an authentic ambience, with temple bells played for a satra or a religious site.

C2217.name: virtual tablet interface
C2217.definition: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

C2218.name: navigation tool
C2218.definition: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

C2219.name: video player
C2219.definition: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

C2220.name: information content
C2220.definition: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

C2221.name: island map
C2221.definition: The navigation tools of the virtual tablet interface include a left-side island map presented as a world in miniature and buttons for opening the mini map.

C2222.name: volume controller
C2222.definition: The video player in the virtual tablet interface has a volume controller and other controls and is used to view cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place.

C2223.name: control
C2223.definition: The video player in the virtual tablet interface has a volume controller and other controls and is used to view cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place.

C2224.name: information element
C2224.definition: The virtual tablet interface provides access to information content through info elements.

C2225.name: global map
C2225.definition: A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place on the island, such as a village or town; it differs in appearance from the global island map and is provided at each of the island's 24 information points to give the user a sense of belonging or local orientation to that place.

C2226.name: local orientation
C2226.definition: A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place on the island, such as a village or town; it differs in appearance from the global island map and is provided at each of the island's 24 information points to give the user a sense of belonging or local orientation to that place.

C2227.name: arrow
C2227.definition: An arrow shown to the user indicates a direction, and selecting the arrow moves the user in that direction along the arrangement of the 360-degree images.

C2228.name: notification
C2228.definition: At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.

C2229.name: cultural video
C2229.definition: At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.

C2230.name: information icon
C2230.definition: At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.

C2231.name: tablet interface
C2231.definition: In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos.

C2232.name: dual maps
C2232.definition: For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

C2233.name: local interface
C2233.definition: For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

C2234.name: orientation awareness
C2234.definition: The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

C2235.name: mental map
C2235.definition: The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

C2236.name: island tour
C2236.definition: In the island tour, each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.

C2237.name: view interpolation
C2237.definition: View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition between two 360-degree images by blurring their boundaries, preventing the sudden movement or jerks that an unhandled image transition would cause and that reduce the user experience.

C2238.name: navigation arrow
C2238.definition: Navigation arrows guide the user from one image to another, prevent random movement, and create a seamless exploration experience while supporting smooth travel.

C2239.name: virtual vehicle metaphor
C2239.definition: A virtual vehicle metaphor is a three-dimensional (3D) model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within the tour.

C2240.name: walking-based navigation
C2240.definition: Walking-based navigation is used for a single spot, but exploring the entire island by walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness, so a different travel technique was required.

C2241.name: virtual vehicle travel technique
C2241.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle when it is selected, changes the surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion, and lets the user operate the vehicle through ray casting interactions to provide a direction of movement and select a destination, to which the vehicle moves.

C2242.name: seated viewpoint
C2242.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle when it is selected, changes the surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion, and lets the user operate the vehicle through ray casting interactions to provide a direction of movement and select a destination, to which the vehicle moves.

C2243.name: selection-based locomotion technique
C2243.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

C2244.name: route
C2244.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

C2245.name: route selection
C2245.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

C2246.name: target selection
C2246.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

C2247.name: instantaneous movement
C2247.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

C2248.name: virtual tour system
C2248.definition: In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos.

C2249.name: location
C2249.definition: In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos.

C2250.name: user type
C2250.definition: The virtual tour system's tablet interface shows a list of videos available for a given spot, and when the user is at a spot the corresponding material for that spot is added to the interface so the user can choose it, giving access to the most relevant information for that spot, and that relevant information is also determined by the user type.

C2251.name: point of interest
C2251.definition: The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.

C2252.name: point-of-interest awareness
C2252.definition: In the virtual tour system, point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that indicate which way to move and guide users toward points of interest, and by information icons that, when selected, provide further details about the place, mostly as textual information, so users do not overlook important elements in the environment.

C2253.name: directional arrow
C2253.definition: In the virtual tour system, point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that indicate which way to move and guide users toward points of interest, and by information icons that, when selected, provide further details about the place, mostly as textual information, so users do not overlook important elements in the environment.

C2254.name: controlled navigation technique
C2254.definition: The system design implemented a controlled navigation technique to minimize cybersickness, in which users navigate or teleport using a joystick, so that controlled movement does not support abrupt movements that can cause discomfort and reduces the chances of discomfort.

C2255.name: vehicular movement
C2255.definition: In vehicular movement, the speed of change of viewpoint may cause cybersickness if it is not chosen carefully.

C2256.name: speed of change of viewpoint
C2256.definition: In vehicular movement, the speed of change of viewpoint may cause cybersickness if it is not chosen carefully.

C2257.name: visual cue
C2257.definition: Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in the system design help maintain spatial orientation, give the user a better feeling and awareness of the place, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.

C2258.name: smooth transition
C2258.definition: Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in the system design help maintain spatial orientation, give the user a better feeling and awareness of the place, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.

C2259.name: spatial orientation
C2259.definition: Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in the system design help maintain spatial orientation, give the user a better feeling and awareness of the place, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.

C2260.name: sensory conflict
C2260.definition: Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in the system design help maintain spatial orientation, give the user a better feeling and awareness of the place, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.

C2261.name: usability evaluation
C2261.definition: In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.

C2262.name: analysis and specification
C2262.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

C2263.name: quick evaluation
C2263.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

C2264.name: coding and implementation
C2264.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

C2265.name: code evaluation
C2265.definition: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and code or system evaluation in interactive system development are standard software development lifecycle (SDLC) stages with nothing special or distinct for virtual reality or augmented reality system design or implementation.

C2266.name: system evaluation
C2266.definition: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and code or system evaluation in interactive system development are standard software development lifecycle (SDLC) stages with nothing special or distinct for virtual reality or augmented reality system design or implementation.

C2267.name: cycle
C2267.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

C2268.name: experience design
C2268.definition: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

C2269.name: cost overrun
C2269.definition: A quick usability evaluation technique is required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle so that the many possible cycles can be accommodated within a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun and so that design ideas, once implemented, lead to a usable system; if usability evaluation is not done quickly, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun.

C2270.name: prototyping techniques
C2270.definition: Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

C2271.name: full implementation
C2271.definition: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.

C2272.name: final product
C2272.definition: A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

C2273.name: horizontal prototype
C2273.definition: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

C2274.name: vertical prototype
C2274.definition: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

C2275.name: functionality
C2275.definition: A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it.

C2276.name: system
C2276.definition: A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.

C2277.name: low-fidelity prototype
C2277.definition: A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example.

C2278.name: low-fidelity prototyping
C2278.definition: Low-fidelity prototyping provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes compared with approaches that require coding and computers, and it is used primarily to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability.

C2279.name: horizontal prototyping
C2279.definition: Low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with horizontal prototyping, but it is not limited to horizontal prototypes and can also be used to implement vertical prototypes.

C2280.name: interface sketch
C2280.definition: An interface sketch is a simple drawing that can be made on paper and depicts the major components of an interface, including the screen elements the user sees, buttons, selection options, their appearance, and their layout, so that an interface idea can be expressed to others or users for comments and feedback and its appearance can be envisioned.

C2281.name: storyboard
C2281.definition: To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

C2282.name: keyframe
C2282.definition: In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end.

C2283.name: medium-fidelity prototyping
C2283.definition: A medium-fidelity prototyping approach uses a computer to create simple prototypes without involving coding, whereas a low-fidelity prototyping approach does not rely on computers or digital media.

C2284.name: high-fidelity prototyping
C2284.definition: A high-fidelity prototyping approach uses computer programs or programming to create a prototype, so it is effectively actual software development, maybe on a reduced scale.

C2285.name: computer program
C2285.definition: A high-fidelity prototyping approach uses computer programs or programming to create a prototype, so it is effectively actual software development, maybe on a reduced scale.

C2286.name: programmer
C2286.definition: High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping, including skilled programmers with programming expertise.

C2287.name: programming expertise
C2287.definition: High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping, including skilled programmers with programming expertise.

C2288.name: static interface sketch
C2288.definition: In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

C2289.name: Adobe Flash animation video
C2289.definition: In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

C2290.name: Microsoft PowerPoint slideshow

C2293.name: wizard of oz approach
C2293.definition: The Wizard of Oz approach is a prototype-creation technique in which a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen human operator, called the wizard, operates the computer and returns the requested response or result to the subject.

C2294.name: wizard
C2294.definition: The Wizard of Oz approach is a prototype-creation technique in which a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen human operator, called the wizard, operates the computer and returns the requested response or result to the subject.

C2295.name: international business machines
C2295.definition: International Business Machines (IBM) used the Wizard of Oz approach in its 1984 listening typewriter experiment to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system idea before committing resources to build a speech recognizer, because speech recognizer technology was not yet available.

C2296.name: listening typewriter experiment
C2296.definition: International Business Machines (IBM) used the Wizard of Oz approach in its 1984 listening typewriter experiment to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system idea before committing resources to build a speech recognizer, because speech recognizer technology was not yet available.

C2298.name: throwaway prototype
C2298.definition: Prototypes can be used in different ways: as throwaway prototypes, incremental prototypes, and evolutionary prototypes.

C2299.name: incremental prototype
C2299.definition: Prototypes can be used in different ways: as throwaway prototypes, incremental prototypes, and evolutionary prototypes.

C2300.name: evolutionary prototype
C2300.definition: Prototypes can be used in different ways: as throwaway prototypes, incremental prototypes, and evolutionary prototypes.

C2301.name: low-fidelity cardboard mockup
C2301.definition: Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because they are less costly and discarding them does not incur significant cost, and throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, otherwise working with them becomes expensive.

C2302.name: paper sketch
C2302.definition: Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because they are less costly and discarding them does not incur significant cost, and throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, otherwise working with them becomes expensive.

C2303.name: module
C2303.definition: Incremental prototypes are created when the system design divides the system into units or modules, each module is separately prototyped and tested, and the modules are then integrated into the overall system.

C2304.name: expert evaluation
C2304.definition: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

C2305.name: robust evaluation technique
C2305.definition: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

C2306.name: evaluator
C2306.definition: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

C2307.name: evaluation setup
C2307.definition: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

C2308.name: evaluation team
C2308.definition: The prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation are at least a low-fidelity prototype, with higher-quality prototypes being better, and a team of evaluators.

C2309.name: usability test
C2309.definition: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.

C2310.name: user
C2310.definition: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.

C2311.name: design team
C2311.definition: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.

C2312.name: skilled designer
C2312.definition: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.

C2313.name: problem domain
C2313.definition: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.

C2314.name: domain expert
C2314.definition: Quick or expert evaluation can rely on design-team members or domain experts rather than end users because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.

C2315.name: usability issue
C2315.definition: In expert evaluation, each evaluator is presented with the prototype, evaluates it independently, and produces a report containing the usability issues perceived by that evaluator; the design team or team lead then combines these reports into a final list of usability issues.

C2316.name: cognitive walkthrough
C2316.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

C2317.name: usability inspection
C2317.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

C2318.name: usability problem
C2318.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

C2319.name: low-fidelity vertical prototype
C2319.definition: A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a prototype that supports several tasks and may be low- or medium-fidelity, and an evaluation team of three to five members; a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but involves more time and cost.

C2320.name: high-fidelity prototype
C2320.definition: A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a prototype that supports several tasks and may be low- or medium-fidelity, and an evaluation team of three to five members; a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but involves more time and cost.

C2321.name: paper prototype
C2321.definition: A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.

C2322.name: storyboarding approach
C2322.definition: A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.

C2323.name: scenario
C2323.definition: In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype.

C2324.name: interface-level task
C2324.definition: In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype.

C2325.name: usability question
C2325.definition: Usability questions are framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues, and evaluators use them as guidelines to identify problems users are likely to face while performing the tasks.

C2326.name: report
C2326.definition: For each usability question, evaluators must give a detailed report rather than a simple yes or no answer, explaining where they felt difficulty in the interface or interaction and why.

C2327.name: evaluation session
C2327.definition: The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end of the evaluation session to identify broader usability issues.

C2328.name: heuristic evaluation
C2328.definition: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

C2329.name: checklist
C2329.definition: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

C2330.name: heuristic
C2330.definition: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

C2331.name: task scenario
C2331.definition: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

C2333.name: system-specific checklist
C2333.definition: Available checklists for evaluating interfaces include detailed system-specific checklists and checklists focused on broader usability principles, and the broader checklists contain fewer heuristics because they are broader in nature and not specific to any particular interface.

C2334.name: usability principle
C2334.definition: Available checklists for evaluating interfaces include detailed system-specific checklists and checklists focused on broader usability principles, and the broader checklists contain fewer heuristics because they are broader in nature and not specific to any particular interface.

C2335.name: broader checklist

C2336.name: Nielsen's ten heuristics
C2336.definition: Nielsen's 10 heuristics is a general set of heuristics proposed in 1994 that is primarily related to graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but equally applicable to most interactive systems.

C2337.name: visibility of system status
C2337.definition: Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.
