C2346.name: user evaluation
C2346.definition: User evaluation is a quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly, and it requires user involvement, unlike expert evaluation techniques in which user involvement was optional.

C2347.name: subjective data
C2347.definition: User evaluation is often called evaluation with self-reports, and user feedback is collected with rating scales, with the data sometimes called subjective or preference data.

C2348.name: preference data
C2348.definition: User evaluation is often called evaluation with self-reports, and user feedback is collected with rating scales, with the data sometimes called subjective or preference data.

C2349.name: questionnaire
C2349.definition: In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.

C2350.name: post-task data collection
C2350.definition: In user evaluation, data can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, collecting data at both points is desirable if feasible, otherwise one of the two points must be chosen, and suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, so the questionnaires used after every task need not be the same as those used after the whole session.

C2351.name: after scenario questionnaire
C2351.definition: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements: 'I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario'; 'I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario'; and 'I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks'.

C2352.name: expectation measure
C2352.definition: Well-known questionnaires available for post-task data collection include the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), designed by Lewis in 1991, and the Expectation Measure (EM), designed by Albert and Dixon in 2003.

C2353.name: post-session data collection
C2353.definition: In user evaluation, data can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, collecting data at both points is desirable if feasible, otherwise one of the two points must be chosen, and suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, so the questionnaires used after every task need not be the same as those used after the whole session.

C2354.name: system usability scale
C2354.definition: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire, containing statements rather than questions, that is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all the tasks.

C2355.name: computer system usability questionnaire
C2355.definition: Well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection include the System Usability Scale (SUS), designed by Brooke in 1996; the Computer System Usability Questionnaire (CSUQ), designed by Lewis in 1995; the Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction (QUIS), designed by Chin et al. in 1988; and the Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire (USE), proposed by Lund in 2001.

C2356.name: questionnaire for user interface satisfaction
C2356.definition: Well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection include the System Usability Scale (SUS), designed by Brooke in 1996; the Computer System Usability Questionnaire (CSUQ), designed by Lewis in 1995; the Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction (QUIS), designed by Chin et al. in 1988; and the Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire (USE), proposed by Lund in 2001.

C2357.name: usefulness satisfaction and ease of use questionnaire
C2357.definition: Well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection include the System Usability Scale (SUS), designed by Brooke in 1996; the Computer System Usability Questionnaire (CSUQ), designed by Lewis in 1995; the Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction (QUIS), designed by Chin et al. in 1988; and the Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire (USE), proposed by Lund in 2001.

C2358.name: post-task questionnaire
C2358.definition: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements: 'I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario'; 'I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario'; and 'I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks'.

C2359.name: statement
C2359.definition: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements: 'I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario'; 'I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario'; and 'I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks'.

C2360.name: seven-point rating scale
C2360.definition: In the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), users rate each statement on a seven-point rating scale in which rating 1 means strongly disagree with the statement and rating 7 means strongly agree with the statement.

C2361.name: average rating
C2361.definition: Feedback from the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) can be summarised by taking either the average rating for each statement across all users who participated in the evaluation or the average rating for all statements taken together.

C2362.name: post-session questionnaire
C2362.definition: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire, containing statements rather than questions, that is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all the tasks.

C2363.name: five-point agreement scale
C2363.definition: Each System Usability Scale (SUS) statement is rated by the user on a 5-point agreement scale, where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.

C2364.name: System Usability Scale score
C2364.definition: The System Usability Scale (SUS) score S is calculated from all 10 statement ratings r_i, with i from 1 to 10, as S = 2.5 × (Σ_{i∈{1,3,5,7,9}}(r_i − 1) + Σ_{i∈{2,4,6,8,10}}(5 − r_i)), where r_i is the user's rating for statement i.

C2365.name: statement rating
C2365.definition: Each System Usability Scale (SUS) statement is rated by the user on a 5-point agreement scale, where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.

C2366.name: expert evaluation technique
C2366.definition: Unlike expert evaluation techniques, which give designers more detailed reports from each evaluator, the System Usability Scale (SUS) gives a quick general indication from user ratings of whether usability problems exist but does not explain the reasons, so designers must identify the specific problems through further brainstorming or by examining the scores of individual statements.

C2367.name: design review
C2367.definition: The System Usability Scale (SUS) score is interpreted directly as a percentage, and a score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, indicating that the interface is usable or has only minimal problems, while a score below 70% may indicate usability problems that may require a design review.

C2368.name: brainstorming
C2368.definition: Unlike expert evaluation techniques, which give designers more detailed reports from each evaluator, the System Usability Scale (SUS) gives a quick general indication from user ratings of whether usability problems exist but does not explain the reasons, so designers must identify the specific problems through further brainstorming or by examining the scores of individual statements.

C2369.name: aesthetic survey questionnaire
C2369.definition: The questionnaires identified as ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires applicable to any interactive system, not specifically meant for extended reality (XR) systems.

C2370.name: Majuli VR Tour
C2370.definition: The Majuli VR Tour was developed with Unity engine version 2021.3.22f1 for the Oculus Quest 2 platform and Android smartphones, with Android 6.0 as the operating-system requirement for both versions.

C2371.name: Unity engine
C2371.definition: The Majuli VR Tour was developed with Unity engine version 2021.3.22f1 for the Oculus Quest 2 platform and Android smartphones, with Android 6.0 as the operating-system requirement for both versions.

C2372.name: Oculus Quest 2
C2372.definition: The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone computing device comprising a headset and handheld controllers, with its own processor and memory, and does not need to be tethered to a fixed computer.

C2373.name: extended reality toolkit
C2373.definition: The Majuli VR Tour used the Extended Reality (XR) toolkit for its Oculus Quest version and the Google Virtual Reality (VR) software development kit (SDK) for its Google Cardboard version.

C2374.name: Autodesk Maya
C2374.definition: Autodesk Maya software was used to create the three-dimensional (3D) models for the Majuli VR Tour immersive experience, using real images as references and as textures on the modeled objects.

C2375.name: application size
C2375.definition: The initial Majuli VR Tour application size was 9.85 gigabytes (GB) because its content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread.

C2376.name: gigabyte
C2376.definition: The initial Majuli VR Tour application size was 9.85 gigabytes (GB) because its content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread.

C2377.name: cloud services
C2377.definition: To reduce the space requirements of the Majuli VR Tour, all videos were stored in cloud services and loaded from the cloud when a user clicked a video thumbnail in the Oculus Quest video player, so the videos were not always stored on the client device, reducing the application size to 5.1 gigabytes (GB).

C2378.name: video thumbnail
C2378.definition: To reduce the space requirements of the Majuli VR Tour, all videos were stored in cloud services and loaded from the cloud when a user clicked a video thumbnail in the Oculus Quest video player, so the videos were not always stored on the client device, reducing the application size to 5.1 gigabytes (GB).

C2379.name: client device
C2379.definition: To reduce the space requirements of the Majuli VR Tour, all videos were stored in cloud services and loaded from the cloud when a user clicked a video thumbnail in the Oculus Quest video player, so the videos were not always stored on the client device, reducing the application size to 5.1 gigabytes (GB).

C2380.name: video playback
C2380.definition: Because the Majuli VR Tour application was 5.1 gigabytes (GB) and not suitable for mobile deployment, a mobile version for Google Cardboard was made by compressing high-resolution 360-degree and two-dimensional (2D) images and removing most video playback support, reducing the application size to 0.7 gigabytes (GB).

C2381.name: Oculus Quest
C2381.definition: The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard.

C2382.name: 360-degree image tour
C2382.definition: The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard.

C2383.name: three-dimensional model tour
C2383.definition: The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard.

C2384.name: mobile-device tour
C2384.definition: The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard.

C2385.name: start screen
C2385.definition: In the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the start screen uses a ray-casting-based selection method and plays introductory videos about Majuli and a tutorial that explains how to control and use the system.

C2386.name: ray-casting-based selection method
C2386.definition: In the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the start screen uses a ray-casting-based selection method and plays introductory videos about Majuli and a tutorial that explains how to control and use the system.

C2387.name: tutorial
C2387.definition: In the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the start screen uses a ray-casting-based selection method and plays introductory videos about Majuli and a tutorial that explains how to control and use the system.

C2388.name: user group selection
C2388.definition: After user group selection in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the user experiences a boat ride from the mainland to Majuli island, using a 360-degree video captured during field trips.

C2389.name: arrow key
C2389.definition: Inside a location in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the user can move forward and backward using arrow keys and can see icons intended to provide information.

C2390.name: vehicle-metaphor route-planning method
C2390.definition: Travel from one point to another in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation uses teleportation together with a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method, in which the road route is fixed and the user experiences motion as if riding a vehicle along the road.

C2391.name: empirical evaluation
C2391.definition: Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, usability study, or empirical research, is a stage in interactive system development in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users.

C2392.name: quick prototype evaluation
C2392.definition: Quick prototype evaluations are limited-scale early evaluations that use a limited number of evaluators and evaluate prototypes, so they can quickly identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about the overall usability of the end system.

C2393.name: usability assessment
C2393.definition: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

C2394.name: fully implemented system
C2394.definition: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

C2395.name: controlled experiment
C2395.definition: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

C2396.name: user behavioral data
C2396.definition: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

C2397.name: research question
C2397.definition: An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

C2398.name: variable
C2398.definition: An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

C2399.name: experiment
C2399.definition: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

C2400.name: data
C2400.definition: An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

C2401.name: empirical data
C2401.definition: An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

C2402.name: data analysis
C2402.definition: In the system implementation process, stage 4, data analysis, is the stage in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about the efficacy of a design, such as its text-entry speed.

C2403.name: text entry
C2403.definition: The research question 'Is the new text entry graphical user interface (GUI) good?' is problematic because asking several users, for example five users, to judge its quality can produce divided judgments, such as two good, two poor or very bad, and one in between, neither good nor bad, so no answer to the question is likely and no conclusion can be drawn.

C2404.name: text input interface
C2404.definition: Research question 2 (RQ2), asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word (MS Word), elicits somewhat more concrete feedback than standalone evaluation, but it does not give a definitive quality conclusion because 'better' means more or fewer features to different users.

C2405.name: Microsoft Word
C2405.definition: Research question 2 (RQ2), asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word (MS Word), elicits somewhat more concrete feedback than standalone evaluation, but it does not give a definitive quality conclusion because 'better' means more or fewer features to different users.

C2406.name: standalone evaluation
C2406.definition: Research question 2 (RQ2), asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word (MS Word), elicits somewhat more concrete feedback than standalone evaluation, but it does not give a definitive quality conclusion because 'better' means more or fewer features to different users.

C2407.name: text input task
C2407.definition: Research question 3 (RQ3), asking whether the new interface lets a user enter text faster than Microsoft Word (MS Word), is less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.

C2408.name: subjective interpretation
C2408.definition: Research question 3 (RQ3), asking whether the new interface lets a user enter text faster than Microsoft Word (MS Word), is less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.

C2409.name: text entry speed
C2409.definition: Research question 3 (RQ3), asking whether the new interface lets a user enter text faster than Microsoft Word (MS Word), is less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.

C2410.name: subjective feedback
C2410.definition: Dependence on subjective feedback is problematic and may not support a definitive conclusion, even for a clear question about which text entry interface is faster, because responses can split.

C2411.name: objective data
C2411.definition: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

C2412.name: characters per minute
C2412.definition: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

C2413.name: testable research question
C2413.definition: A testable research question, also called a hypothesis, is a question for which a study can be conducted to collect objective data, such as text entry speed, and draw objective conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.

C2414.name: non-testable research question
C2414.definition: A non-testable research question, also called an untestable question, is a question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot be set up to collect objective data and, generally, a reliable scientific conclusion cannot be drawn.

C2415.name: scientific conclusion
C2415.definition: A non-testable research question, also called an untestable question, is a question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot be set up to collect objective data and, generally, a reliable scientific conclusion cannot be drawn.

C2416.name: generalized concept
C2416.definition: Research questions should not be framed from generalized concepts such as whether something is good, because such concepts are ambiguous and can lead to untestable questions.

C2417.name: testability
C2417.definition: To balance the trade-off between testability and generalization, stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system and combines their conclusions to reach a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question, such as the overall goodness of an interface.

C2418.name: generalization
C2418.definition: To balance the trade-off between testability and generalization, stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system and combines their conclusions to reach a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question, such as the overall goodness of an interface.

C2419.name: independent variable
C2419.definition: A variable whose values are assigned and controlled is called an independent variable, also called a factor.

C2420.name: level
C2420.definition: The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

C2421.name: test condition
C2421.definition: Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.

C2422.name: dependent variable
C2422.definition: A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; in research question 3 (RQ3), the text entry rate (TER) is the dependent variable because its value depends on the interface, specifically the interface levels.

C2423.name: text entry rate
C2423.definition: A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; in research question 3 (RQ3), the text entry rate (TER) is the dependent variable because its value depends on the interface, specifically the interface levels.

C2424.name: research question framing
C2424.definition: The empirical research process has four stages, the first stage being research question framing and the second stage being variables.

C2425.name: untestable question
C2425.definition: In empirical research, research question framing addresses broader generalizable questions that are untestable by framing multiple testable research questions, collecting objective data for each, reaching a definite conclusion for each, and combining those conclusions to draw a conclusion about the untestable questions.

C2426.name: experiment design
C2426.definition: In experiment design, the selected participants form a sample or subset of all potential users, and the subset must be chosen carefully to be representative of the whole user group; otherwise the conclusions drawn from the subset are not valid or reliable.

C2427.name: sample
C2427.definition: In experiment design, the selected participants form a sample or subset of all potential users, and the subset must be chosen carefully to be representative of the whole user group; otherwise the conclusions drawn from the subset are not valid or reliable.

C2428.name: homogeneous user group
C2428.definition: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

C2429.name: age group
C2429.definition: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

C2430.name: educational background
C2430.definition: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

C2431.name: socio-economic background
C2431.definition: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

C2432.name: cultural background
C2432.definition: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

C2433.name: homogeneous subset
C2433.definition: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

C2434.name: heterogeneous user group
C2434.definition: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

C2435.name: user profile
C2435.definition: In experiment design, a user profile is a set of well-defined user profile characteristics or entries; the user is first defined by such a user profile, and experiment participants are selected only on the basis of that profile.

C2436.name: user profile characteristic
C2436.definition: In experiment design, a user profile is a set of well-defined user profile characteristics or entries; the user is first defined by such a user profile, and experiment participants are selected only on the basis of that profile.

C2437.name: experiment participant
C2437.definition: In experiment design, the selected participants form a sample or subset of all potential users, and the subset must be chosen carefully to be representative of the whole user group; otherwise the conclusions drawn from the subset are not valid or reliable.

C2438.name: typing behavior
C2438.definition: Older people may have different typing behavior from teenagers, and regular computer users are likely to have different typing speeds from infrequent users of computers, so such user characteristics must be considered when choosing experiment participants based on user profiles.

C2439.name: typing speed
C2439.definition: Older people may have different typing behavior from teenagers, and regular computer users are likely to have different typing speeds from infrequent users of computers, so such user characteristics must be considered when choosing experiment participants based on user profiles.

C2440.name: number of participants
C2440.definition: For a controlled empirical experiment, the number of participants is generally assumed to be between 12 and 25 to draw reliable conclusions, more than 25 can be used, and below 12 the conclusions may not be reliable and may change if the number is increased.

C2441.name: task performance data
C2441.definition: In a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, users perform tasks, and the task performance data collected from them are mostly objective data that are analyzed to draw conclusions about the interface.

C2442.name: representative task set
C2442.definition: For an interface, a representative task set is a small, well-defined subset of tasks that are used by everybody most of the time, namely the tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use when the interface is deployed in practice, and in an empirical study one or more tasks from this set should ideally be chosen so that the collected data and drawn conclusions are reliable.

C2443.name: typing task
C2443.definition: For a typing task used to compare typing interfaces, a random piece of text is not a representative task, whereas representative tasks are text strings chosen based on certain metrics and measures that indirectly encompass activities spanning the entire interface and the users' typing skills.

C2444.name: typing interface
C2444.definition: For a typing task used to compare typing interfaces, a random piece of text is not a representative task, whereas representative tasks are text strings chosen based on certain metrics and measures that indirectly encompass activities spanning the entire interface and the users' typing skills.

C2445.name: random piece of text
C2445.definition: For a typing task used to compare typing interfaces, a random piece of text is not a representative task, whereas representative tasks are text strings chosen based on certain metrics and measures that indirectly encompass activities spanning the entire interface and the users' typing skills.

C2446.name: text string
C2446.definition: For a typing task used to compare typing interfaces, a random piece of text is not a representative task, whereas representative tasks are text strings chosen based on certain metrics and measures that indirectly encompass activities spanning the entire interface and the users' typing skills.

C2447.name: metric
C2447.definition: For a typing task used to compare typing interfaces, a random piece of text is not a representative task, whereas representative tasks are text strings chosen based on certain metrics and measures that indirectly encompass activities spanning the entire interface and the users' typing skills.

C2448.name: measure
C2448.definition: For a typing task used to compare typing interfaces, a random piece of text is not a representative task, whereas representative tasks are text strings chosen based on certain metrics and measures that indirectly encompass activities spanning the entire interface and the users' typing skills.

C2449.name: typing skill
C2449.definition: For a typing task used to compare typing interfaces, a random piece of text is not a representative task, whereas representative tasks are text strings chosen based on certain metrics and measures that indirectly encompass activities spanning the entire interface and the users' typing skills.

C2450.name: experimental study
C2450.definition: In an experimental study, tasks can be assigned using a within-subject (repeated measures) design, in which every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions, or a between-subjects design, in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

C2451.name: within-subject design
C2451.definition: In an experimental study, tasks can be assigned using a within-subject (repeated measures) design, in which every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions, or a between-subjects design, in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

C2452.name: between-subjects design
C2452.definition: In an experimental study, tasks can be assigned using a within-subject (repeated measures) design, in which every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions, or a between-subjects design, in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

C2453.name: practice effect
C2453.definition: In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice; it is also called a confounding variable and confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.

C2454.name: confounding variable
C2454.definition: In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice; it is also called a confounding variable and confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.

C2455.name: task sequence
C2455.definition: To reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design, the task sequence can be randomized or systematically varied; statistically, these random or systematic variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect.

C2456.name: Latin square design
C2456.definition: A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant, for example by shifting a numbered task sequence one position for each successive participant.

C2457.name: system implementation process
C2457.definition: In the system implementation process, stage 4, data analysis, is the stage in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about the efficacy of a design, such as its text-entry speed.

C2458.name: statistical significance
C2458.definition: In the system implementation process, stage 4, data analysis, is the stage in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about the efficacy of a design, such as its text-entry speed.

C2459.name: empirical interface study
C2459.definition: In empirical interface studies, the data are obtained from a sample of users rather than the actual population, while the conclusions of interest are about the larger population, such as any user and any text-entry interface.

C2460.name: population
C2460.definition: In empirical interface studies, the data are obtained from a sample of users rather than the actual population, while the conclusions of interest are about the larger population, such as any user and any text-entry interface.

C2461.name: text-entry interface
C2461.definition: In empirical interface studies, the data are obtained from a sample of users rather than the actual population, while the conclusions of interest are about the larger population, such as any user and any text-entry interface.

C2462.name: statistical significance test
C2462.definition: A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

C2463.name: observed data difference
C2463.definition: A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

C2464.name: statistically significant difference
C2464.definition: A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

C2465.name: non-significant difference
C2465.definition: A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

C2466.name: mean text-entry speed
C2466.definition: In comparing two text-entry interfaces, the analysis uses the mean text-entry speed of each group and concerns the relative difference between the means rather than the absolute values.

C2467.name: relative difference
C2467.definition: In comparing two text-entry interfaces, the analysis uses the mean text-entry speed of each group and concerns the relative difference between the means rather than the absolute values.

C2468.name: absolute value
C2468.definition: In comparing two text-entry interfaces, the analysis uses the mean text-entry speed of each group and concerns the relative difference between the means rather than the absolute values.

C2469.name: experimental design
C2469.definition: The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data.

C2470.name: absolute difference
C2470.definition: The result of a statistical significance test can include the absolute difference in group means, the two-tailed p-value, the T value, the degrees of freedom, and whether the difference is statistically significant, and such results are typically reported, for example, as t = 1.70, p < 0.05, statistically significant, which is the standard way of representing any statistical significance test.

C2471.name: group mean
C2471.definition: The result of a statistical significance test can include the absolute difference in group means, the two-tailed p-value, the T value, the degrees of freedom, and whether the difference is statistically significant, and such results are typically reported, for example, as t = 1.70, p < 0.05, statistically significant, which is the standard way of representing any statistical significance test.

C2472.name: p-value
C2472.definition: The result of a statistical significance test can include the absolute difference in group means, the two-tailed p-value, the T value, the degrees of freedom, and whether the difference is statistically significant, and such results are typically reported, for example, as t = 1.70, p < 0.05, statistically significant, which is the standard way of representing any statistical significance test.

C2473.name: t value
C2473.definition: The result of a statistical significance test can include the absolute difference in group means, the two-tailed p-value, the T value, the degrees of freedom, and whether the difference is statistically significant, and such results are typically reported, for example, as t = 1.70, p < 0.05, statistically significant, which is the standard way of representing any statistical significance test.

C2474.name: paired sample t-test
C2474.definition: In a statistical significance test, such as a paired sample t-test, the p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, and a lower p-value means the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.

C2475.name: parametric test
C2475.definition: There are many statistical significance tests, which fall into two groups, parametric tests and non-parametric tests.

C2476.name: non-parametric test
C2476.definition: There are many statistical significance tests, which fall into two groups, parametric tests and non-parametric tests.

C2477.name: scale of measurement
C2477.definition: For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design.

C2478.name: nominal scale
C2478.definition: For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design.

C2479.name: categorical scale
C2479.definition: For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design.

C2480.name: factor
C2480.definition: For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design.

C2481.name: chi-square test
C2481.definition: For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design.

C2482.name: McNemar's test
C2482.definition: For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design.

C2483.name: independent samples t-test
C2483.definition: For an experimental design with one factor having two levels and no other condition mentioned, a between-subject design can use the parametric independent samples t-test or the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test, and a within-subject design can use the parametric paired sample t-test or the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

C2484.name: Mann-Whitney U test
C2484.definition: For an experimental design with one factor having two levels and no other condition mentioned, a between-subject design can use the parametric independent samples t-test or the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test, and a within-subject design can use the parametric paired sample t-test or the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

C2485.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
C2485.definition: For an experimental design with one factor having two levels and no other condition mentioned, a between-subject design can use the parametric independent samples t-test or the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test, and a within-subject design can use the parametric paired sample t-test or the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

C2486.name: analysis of variance
C2486.definition: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

C2487.name: one-way analysis of variance
C2487.definition: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

C2488.name: factorial analysis of variance
C2488.definition: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

C2489.name: Kruskal-Wallis test
C2489.definition: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

C2490.name: repeated measures analysis of variance
C2490.definition: For a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the parametric repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.

C2491.name: Friedman test
C2491.definition: For a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the parametric repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.

C2492.name: case study
C2492.definition: The objective of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour case study is to capture tangible and intangible ecological and cultural heritage aspects of the Majuli river island and to digitally preserve that heritage information by providing users an immersive experience, because the island is disappearing.

C2493.name: user engagement
C2493.definition: The evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour aims to measure usability aspects of the system, specifically user engagement, presence, and comfort in the virtual environment, and to identify potential areas for improvement by analyzing participants' responses and symptoms of cyber sickness.

C2494.name: comfort
C2494.definition: The evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour aims to measure usability aspects of the system, specifically user engagement, presence, and comfort in the virtual environment, and to identify potential areas for improvement by analyzing participants' responses and symptoms of cyber sickness.

C2495.name: structured questionnaire
C2495.definition: The evaluation of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour collected data from end users through a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire, and participant responses were collected subjectively, objectively, or both.

C2496.name: behavioral data
C2496.definition: The structured questionnaire used in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour evaluation was related to the evaluation research question and could be used to measure objective data or behavioral data, or sometimes to collect data through a rating scale.

C2497.name: mean age
C2497.definition: The participants in the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour had ages between 23 and 40 years, with a mean age of 25.1 years and a standard deviation of 3.03 years.

C2498.name: standard deviation
C2498.definition: The participants in the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour had ages between 23 and 40 years, with a mean age of 25.1 years and a standard deviation of 3.03 years.

C2499.name: joystick-based controller

C2512.name: total sickness

C2513.name: pre-experiment training session
C2513.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) experiment, unfamiliar users may produce results much different from familiar users, so a brief pre-experiment training session that demonstrates the system's features and how to use them can bring participants to the same level and reduce or nullify familiarity or prior-experience bias, which otherwise may lead to incorrect conclusions.

C2514.name: prior-experience bias

C2515.name: pre-exposure assessment

C2516.name: exploration time

C2517.name: pilot study

C2518.name: involvement

C2534.name: stable interface design

C2550.name: agile development
C2550.definition: Agile development is a development framework or approach that encourages fast development in practice, starts small by not trying to do everything from the beginning, does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning, eliminates unnecessary elements and documentation, and ensures quick turnaround of projects that are more acceptable to clients.

C2551.name: conceptualization

C2570.name: optimization

C2574.name: susceptibility to motion sickness
C2574.definition: The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

C2578.name: cybersickness mitigation strategies

C2579.name: virtual locomotion technique

C2587.name: system-controlled virtual reality tour

C2588.name: system-controlled tour
C2588.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) tour, a system-controlled tour is a navigation mode in which the system forces the user to move from one place to another.

C2589.name: navigation mode
C2589.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) tour, a system-controlled tour is a navigation mode in which the system forces the user to move from one place to another.

C2590.name: realistic walking experience
C2590.definition: A realistic walking experience in a system-controlled tour is important because it helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system and reduces awareness of the difference between realistic and unrealistic elements.

C2591.name: user input
C2591.definition: System-controlled tours, also described as system-automated tours, typically do not allow continuous user input, making it difficult to align user input with walking speed or to judge whether the speed provided by the system is natural.

C2592.name: walking speed
C2592.definition: System-controlled tours, also described as system-automated tours, typically do not allow continuous user input, making it difficult to align user input with walking speed or to judge whether the speed provided by the system is natural.

C2593.name: optic flow
C2593.definition: Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and movement is perceived through this change in the view of the surroundings; in a virtual reality (VR) tour, user movement appears as a constantly changing scene.

C2594.name: user movement
C2594.definition: Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and movement is perceived through this change in the view of the surroundings; in a virtual reality (VR) tour, user movement appears as a constantly changing scene.

C2595.name: real-world walking speed
C2595.definition: When the navigation in a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is assumed to be walking, the scene-change speed (optic flow) should match the user's actual, or typical, real-world walking speed rather than VR walking speed; otherwise the movement looks unrealistic because it may be too fast or too slow.

C2596.name: virtual reality walking speed
C2596.definition: When the navigation in a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is assumed to be walking, the scene-change speed (optic flow) should match the user's actual, or typical, real-world walking speed rather than VR walking speed; otherwise the movement looks unrealistic because it may be too fast or too slow.

C2597.name: instantaneous walking speed
C2597.definition: A more realistic system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour requires matching its optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed using a model of the user's typical walking behavior, because a constant optic flow is not very realistic as people rarely walk at constant speed.

C2598.name: walking speed model
C2598.definition: A more realistic system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour requires matching its optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed using a model of the user's typical walking behavior, because a constant optic flow is not very realistic as people rarely walk at constant speed.

C2600.name: realistic walking behavior model
C2600.definition: A model of natural walking behavior can be used as a realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation to address the need for a realistic walking experience.

C2601.name: natural walking behavior
