C2603.name: empirical research
C2603.definition: The development of the realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation is carried out in four steps: empirical research to collect empirical data used to build the model, analysis of the data, creation of the model, and validation of the model.

C2604.name: creation
C2604.definition: The development of the realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation is carried out in four steps: empirical research to collect empirical data used to build the model, analysis of the data, creation of the model, and validation of the model.

C2605.name: validation
C2605.definition: The development of the realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation is carried out in four steps: empirical research to collect empirical data used to build the model, analysis of the data, creation of the model, and validation of the model.

C2606.name: speed estimation model
C2606.definition: The empirical study was conducted to collect real-life data of a user moving from one point to another and to propose a speed estimation model.

C2607.name: walking behavior
C2607.definition: In the empirical study, participant heights were recorded because earlier studies indicate that height affects walking behavior, and the participants' heights ranged from 150 to 184 centimeters.

C2608.name: corridor experiment
C2608.definition: The corridor experiment used a corridor in a physical building in which seven paintings representing images of the seven wonders of the world were placed at distances of 20, 20, 13, 16, 6.4, 19, and 4 meters from the start.

C2609.name: video recording
C2609.definition: Video recordings of the user's footsteps were made with a Samsung M30 smartphone camera fixed on the user's back and focused on the user's legs; the recording started just before the user started walking and was captured at 30 frames per second.

C2610.name: data-analysis stage
C2610.definition: In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps.

C2611.name: step frequency
C2611.definition: In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps.

C2612.name: step
C2612.definition: In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps.

C2613.name: foot strike
C2613.definition: In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps.

C2614.name: timestamp
C2614.definition: In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps.

C2615.name: slow-in-slow-out pattern
C2615.definition: When step frequency was plotted against distance, a pattern more or less followed by all participants was seen: step frequency started low, increased to a maximum, plateaued, and then decreased to zero at the target painting where the user stopped to click a photo; this pattern is called the slow-in-slow-out pattern.

C2616.name: slow-in-slow-out walking pattern
C2616.definition: The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern observed in the study is similar to the Fourier-series approximation of a square pulse wave, which starts, remains approximately constant, and then returns to zero.

C2617.name: fourier series
C2617.definition: The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern observed in the study is similar to the Fourier-series approximation of a square pulse wave, which starts, remains approximately constant, and then returns to zero.

C2618.name: square pulse wave
C2618.definition: The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern observed in the study is similar to the Fourier-series approximation of a square pulse wave, which starts, remains approximately constant, and then returns to zero.

C2619.name: continuous periodic function
C2619.definition: A Fourier series with appropriate weights can approximate any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision, and a practical approximation can be obtained by taking the first few terms of the corresponding Fourier expansion.

C2620.name: sinusoid
C2620.definition: The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids, and the weights of those sinusoids are calculated from empirical data.

C2621.name: virtual walking
C2621.definition: In virtual walking, the user's actual movement speed and perceived movement speed need not be the same, and generally an individual perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than the actual movement.

C2622.name: actual movement speed
C2622.definition: In virtual walking, the user's actual movement speed and perceived movement speed need not be the same, and generally an individual perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than the actual movement.

C2623.name: perceived movement speed
C2623.definition: In virtual walking, the user's actual movement speed and perceived movement speed need not be the same, and generally an individual perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than the actual movement.

C2624.name: visual gain
C2624.definition: The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency.

C2625.name: instantaneous step frequency
C2625.definition: The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency.

C2626.name: initial frequency
C2626.definition: The instantaneous step frequency f(x) is computed from the Fourier-series expression f(x) = (4/π) × 1.8 × Σ_{k=0}^{d/2−1} [1/(2k+1) × sin((2k+1)ωx)], where ω = 2πf0, f0 is the initial frequency and equals 1/(2d), and d is the distance between the source and destination.

C2627.name: natural walking speed model
C2627.definition: The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.

C2628.name: computed natural walking behavior
C2628.definition: The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.

C2629.name: visual gain factor
C2629.definition: The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.

C2630.name: constant speed
C2630.definition: The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model, described as instantaneous speed, enhances perceived realism compared with a constant average speed.

C2631.name: perceived realism
C2631.definition: The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model, described as instantaneous speed, enhances perceived realism compared with a constant average speed.

C2632.name: virtual art exhibition environment
C2632.definition: The empirical study used a virtual art exhibition environment experienced with an Oculus Rift, in which system-controlled navigation moved the user at constant speed or instantaneous natural walking speed through pictures, with a forced 10-second stop at each picture.

C2633.name: system-controlled navigation
C2633.definition: The empirical study used a virtual art exhibition environment experienced with an Oculus Rift, in which system-controlled navigation moved the user at constant speed or instantaneous natural walking speed through pictures, with a forced 10-second stop at each picture.

C2634.name: randomized order
C2634.definition: Each participant experienced both constant speed and instantaneous speed conditions in a randomized order, with breaks between the conditions, to avoid practice effect and bias in the subsequent data collection.

C2635.name: bias
C2635.definition: Each participant experienced both constant speed and instantaneous speed conditions in a randomized order, with breaks between the conditions, to avoid practice effect and bias in the subsequent data collection.

C2636.name: user preference
C2636.definition: The study used two 1-to-10 rating scales, with 1 representing worst and 10 representing the best value, to rate level of realism and user preference, and speed with levels constant and instantaneous was the independent variable, with realism and preference as the dependent variables.

C2637.name: natural walking model
C2637.definition: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement.

C2638.name: perceived instantaneous walking speed
C2638.definition: In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act).

C2639.name: perception of movement
C2639.definition: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement.

C2640.name: experience optimization
C2640.definition: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour does not provide anything related to experience optimization; it can only be used to enhance presence in the virtual world.

C2641.name: virtual reality navigation experience
C2641.definition: The approach to optimizing virtual reality (VR) navigation experience that uses the natural walking model addresses cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.

C2642.name: virtual reality environment
C2642.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) environment, cyber sickness is correlated with exposure duration, with the degree of the symptoms rising proportionally as the VR session duration increases, so if possible, shorter exposure duration can help eliminate or at least minimize the onset of cyber sickness.

C2643.name: virtual reality exposure duration
C2643.definition: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

C2644.name: virtual world size
C2644.definition: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

C2645.name: virtual travel speed
C2645.definition: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

C2646.name: travel time
C2646.definition: The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

C2647.name: interaction time
C2647.definition: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

C2648.name: virtual terrain
C2648.definition: Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

C2649.name: distance between points of interest
C2649.definition: Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

C2650.name: system-controlled virtual reality tool
C2650.definition: In a purely system-automated or system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tool, users do not interact with virtual objects, so the interaction time required to interact with virtual objects can be ignored.

C2651.name: semi-interactive tour
C2651.definition: A semi-interactive tour in virtual reality (VR) is a system-controlled navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact with objects after a navigation task is complete, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at points of interest (POIs), while users cannot interact with other objects in the virtual environment.

C2652.name: system-controlled navigation scenario
C2652.definition: A semi-interactive tour in virtual reality (VR) is a system-controlled navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact with objects after a navigation task is complete, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at points of interest (POIs), while users cannot interact with other objects in the virtual environment.

C2653.name: semi-interactive virtual tour
C2653.definition: In a semi-interactive virtual tour, interaction time at each point of interest (POI) can be limited to an estimate in advance of the maximum time an average user needs to interact with that POI, after which the system automatically forces the user to move to another POI.

C2654.name: optimum path
C2654.definition: In a semi-interactive virtual reality (VR) tour, the duration of exposure can be optimized, under a limit on interaction time, by finding an optimum path that either minimizes the total navigation and interaction time required to experience all points of interest (POIs) or maximizes the number of POIs experienced within a fixed time limit for navigation and interaction.

C2655.name: weighted graph
C2655.definition: The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

C2656.name: vertex set
C2656.definition: The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

C2657.name: weighted edge
C2657.definition: The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

C2658.name: vertex
C2658.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

C2659.name: edge weight
C2659.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

C2660.name: euclidean distance
C2660.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

C2661.name: infinity symbol
C2661.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

C2662.name: optimum travel path problem
C2662.definition: The optimum travel path problem covering all points of interest (POIs) is to find a path P in the given graph G that covers all vertices in V, which are the POIs, and finishes in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed throughout, so that the user gets a realistic feeling.

C2663.name: travel-time algorithm
C2663.definition: The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

C2664.name: directly connected node pair
C2664.definition: The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

C2665.name: actual instantaneous realistic walking speed
C2665.definition: In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act).

C2666.name: distance element
C2666.definition: Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

C2667.name: instantaneous time
C2667.definition: Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

C2668.name: integral
C2668.definition: Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

C2669.name: fourier-series expansion
C2669.definition: After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).

C2670.name: travel-time estimate
C2670.definition: After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).

C2671.name: V naught
C2671.definition: After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).

C2672.name: graph
C2672.definition: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

C2673.name: total travel time
C2673.definition: For a path P in a graph that contains n vertices, the total travel time for P is the sum over i = 1 to n - 1 of the edge weight epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) between consecutive vertices, and epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) is the Euclidean distance between that pair of vertices.

C2674.name: travel-time minimisation problem
C2674.definition: In the travel-time minimisation problem for a graph, the objective is to find a path P that contains all vertices of the graph with the minimum total travel time, and this problem is a variation of the travelling salesman problem (TSP).

C2675.name: travelling salesman problem
C2675.definition: In the travel-time minimisation problem for a graph, the objective is to find a path P that contains all vertices of the graph with the minimum total travel time, and this problem is a variation of the travelling salesman problem (TSP).

C2676.name: complete graph
C2676.definition: The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G.

C2677.name: shortest path
C2677.definition: The travelling salesman problem (TSP) asks, given a complete graph, for the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node, where the shortest path is defined by the total weight of the edges in the path.

C2678.name: hamiltonian path
C2678.definition: The graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is not assumed to be a complete graph, so there may be no Hamiltonian path in that graph, where a Hamiltonian path is a path that covers all nodes and visits each node exactly once.

C2679.name: hypothetical edge
C2679.definition: For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

C2680.name: modified edge weight
C2680.definition: For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

C2681.name: shortest path length
C2681.definition: For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

C2682.name: connected
C2682.definition: The shortest path lengths used for the hypothetical edges are well-defined because the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is connected.

C2683.name: edge set
C2683.definition: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

C2684.name: optimal time
C2684.definition: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

C2685.name: optimal path
C2685.definition: Existing vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) solvers can be used to find the optimal path that maximizes total importance of the nodes within the given time threshold.

C2686.name: complete time-weighted graph
C2686.definition: After the graph is complete, the algorithm replaces the Euclidean-distance edge weights with the travel time between each pair of vertices, producing a complete time-weighted graph G'' whose edge weights are travel times rather than Euclidean distances.

C2687.name: travelling salesman problem solver
C2687.definition: In the minimum-time approach, the computed travel times become the weights of a complete graph formed by adding hypothetical edges, and this complete graph is given as input to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, which outputs the optimum time and optimal path.

C2688.name: cybersickness time threshold
C2688.definition: The minimum travel time to cover all vertices, as computed by the algorithm that maps the original graph to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) instance, may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold when the terrain or virtual environment is large, so its purpose may be defeated in such cases.

C2689.name: time limit
C2689.definition: There are two approaches to minimizing the possibility of cybersickness in a virtual world: finding a path that covers all points of interest in minimum time, and finding a path that covers the maximum possible points of interest within a given time limit.

C2690.name: minimum-time approach
C2690.definition: There are two approaches to minimizing the possibility of cybersickness in a virtual world: finding a path that covers all points of interest in minimum time, and finding a path that covers the maximum possible points of interest within a given time limit.

C2691.name: optimum time
C2691.definition: In the minimum-time approach, the computed travel times become the weights of a complete graph formed by adding hypothetical edges, and this complete graph is given as input to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, which outputs the optimum time and optimal path.

C2692.name: final solution path
C2692.definition: The optimal path produced by the travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver may contain hypothetical edges, which must be removed before the final solution path is produced.

C2693.name: threshold
C2693.definition: The minimum-time approach that covers all points of interest may still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, motivating the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach.

C2694.name: alternative path optimization approach
C2694.definition: The minimum-time approach that covers all points of interest may still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, motivating the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach.

C2695.name: time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach
C2695.definition: A time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach seeks an optimal path that covers the maximum number of points of interest (POIs) while completing within the time threshold (TTH).

C2696.name: time threshold
C2696.definition: A time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach seeks an optimal path that covers the maximum number of points of interest (POIs) while completing within the time threshold (TTH).

C2697.name: movement time
C2697.definition: The time threshold (TTH) for cybersickness (CS) is the maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) tour, meaning the user's movement time, experience time, or VR exposure time should be kept within it, because crossing it may cause cybersickness.

C2698.name: experience time
C2698.definition: The time threshold (TTH) for cybersickness (CS) is the maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) tour, meaning the user's movement time, experience time, or VR exposure time should be kept within it, because crossing it may cause cybersickness.

C2699.name: virtual reality exposure time
C2699.definition: The time threshold (TTH) for cybersickness (CS) is the maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) tour, meaning the user's movement time, experience time, or VR exposure time should be kept within it, because crossing it may cause cybersickness.

C2700.name: virtual world graph
C2700.definition: A virtual tour optimized to cover all vertices of a virtual world graph in minimum time may still induce cybersickness (CS) if its traversal time exceeds the threshold above which cybersickness occurs.

C2701.name: traversal time
C2701.definition: A virtual tour optimized to cover all vertices of a virtual world graph in minimum time may still induce cybersickness (CS) if its traversal time exceeds the threshold above which cybersickness occurs.

C2702.name: movement speed
C2702.definition: There is no easy way to determine the time threshold (TTH); recommended thresholds may depend on content and movement speed, and a threshold can be obtained from an empirical study with a limited number of users or from pre-existing study results.

C2703.name: tour
C2703.definition: When planning a tour to be completed within a given time threshold, visiting every node or vertex representing a point of interest is neither mandatory nor always possible.

C2704.name: importance
C2704.definition: The importance of a node is assigned by an importance function that maps every node, vertex, or point of interest to a positive real number, with a larger number indicating higher importance.

C2705.name: importance function
C2705.definition: The importance of a node is assigned by an importance function that maps every node, vertex, or point of interest to a positive real number, with a larger number indicating higher importance.

C2706.name: total importance
C2706.definition: The total importance of a path P containing nodes V1 through Vn is the sum of the individual importance f(Vi) for i = 1 to n, where n is the number of nodes in the path.

C2707.name: virtual reality path optimization model
C2707.definition: In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.

C2708.name: waiting time
C2708.definition: In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.

C2709.name: waiting time function
C2709.definition: In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number.

C2710.name: total waiting time
C2710.definition: For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

C2711.name: total completion time
C2711.definition: The revised virtual reality path optimization problem maximizes the total importance F(P) of a path P subject to the constraint that the path's total completion time, T(P) + W(P), is less than or equal to the time threshold T_H.

C2712.name: vehicle routing problem with profit
C2712.definition: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

C2713.name: vehicle routing problem
C2713.definition: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

C2714.name: operations research problem
C2714.definition: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

C2715.name: profit
C2715.definition: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

C2716.name: vehicle routing problem with profit solver
C2716.definition: Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

C2717.name: optimal-path algorithm
C2717.definition: The input to the optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment is the original graph G, which is a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.

C2718.name: original graph
C2718.definition: The input to the optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment is the original graph G, which is a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.

C2719.name: fully connected graph
C2719.definition: The input to the optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment is the original graph G, which is a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.

C2720.name: importance value
C2720.definition: The desired output of the algorithm is the optimal path P that maximizes the importance value F, covers the maximum number of most important points of interest (POIs), and keeps the total exposure time, i.e. the traveling time plus the waiting time, less than the time threshold.

C2721.name: total exposure time
C2721.definition: The desired output of the algorithm is the optimal path P that maximizes the importance value F, covers the maximum number of most important points of interest (POIs), and keeps the total exposure time, i.e. the traveling time plus the waiting time, less than the time threshold.

C2722.name: final graph
C2722.definition: The algorithm then replaces the edge weights in the complete graph, which are originally the Euclidean distances between node pairs, with travel times t computed using the natural walking model, producing the final graph G double dash, whose edges are weighted by travel duration to give a realistic experience.

C2723.name: virtual reality path planning solver
C2723.definition: The final graph G double dash, together with the importance f and waiting time w of each node, is given as input to a virtual reality path planning (VRPP) solver, and the solver returns the optimal path P_opt.

C2724.name: modified optimal path
C2724.definition: The optimal path returned by the solver is modified by replacing each hypothetical edge between vertices V_i and V_j with the shortest path between those vertices in the original graph, and the algorithm returns this modified optimal path.

C2725.name: optimal path approach
C2725.definition: The optimal path approach in virtual reality (VR) navigation optimization identifies a path that lets a user explore all points of interest in minimum time, but in a very large virtual world such as the Majuli River Island virtual tour, that minimum time may still be very large compared with the expected user exposure duration, so the approach may still lead to cybersickness.

C2726.name: navigation optimization
C2726.definition: The optimal path approach in virtual reality (VR) navigation optimization identifies a path that lets a user explore all points of interest in minimum time, but in a very large virtual world such as the Majuli River Island virtual tour, that minimum time may still be very large compared with the expected user exposure duration, so the approach may still lead to cybersickness.

C2727.name: Majuli River Island virtual tour
C2727.definition: The optimal path approach in virtual reality (VR) navigation optimization identifies a path that lets a user explore all points of interest in minimum time, but in a very large virtual world such as the Majuli River Island virtual tour, that minimum time may still be very large compared with the expected user exposure duration, so the approach may still lead to cybersickness.

C2728.name: walking-based exploration
C2728.definition: In a walking-based virtual reality (VR) exploration, the optimal path under a time constraint approach sets an upper time limit, called the time threshold, for the user's exposure to the virtual tour, and within that duration it identifies a path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, where covering includes interacting with or inspecting those points and navigating from one to another.

C2729.name: optimal path under a time constraint approach
C2729.definition: In a walking-based virtual reality (VR) exploration, the optimal path under a time constraint approach sets an upper time limit, called the time threshold, for the user's exposure to the virtual tour, and within that duration it identifies a path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, where covering includes interacting with or inspecting those points and navigating from one to another.

C2730.name: covering
C2730.definition: In a walking-based virtual reality (VR) exploration, the optimal path under a time constraint approach sets an upper time limit, called the time threshold, for the user's exposure to the virtual tour, and within that duration it identifies a path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, where covering includes interacting with or inspecting those points and navigating from one to another.

C2731.name: Majuli
C2731.definition: Majuli is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the state of Assam, surrounded on all sides by the Brahmaputra River and its tributaries.

C2732.name: Auniati Satra
C2732.definition: Auniati Satra is one of the largest, most prominent, and most visited Satras on Majuli, with a campus covering approximately 1200 square meters and at least 25 points of interest.

C2733.name: optimized navigation path
C2733.definition: For the exploration of Auniati Satra in virtual reality (VR), an optimized navigation path can be proposed using either the optimal path approach or the optimal path under a time constraint approach to maximize the user experience.

C2734.name: navigation optimization approach
C2734.definition: When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior.

C2735.name: minimum time
C2735.definition: When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior.

C2736.name: relative importance
C2736.definition: When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior.

C2737.name: maximum wait time
C2737.definition: When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior.

C2738.name: traveling salesman problem
C2738.definition: Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

C2739.name: traveling salesman problem solver
C2739.definition: Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

C2740.name: resource
C2740.definition: Extended reality (XR), in particular virtual reality (VR), is resource hungry, meaning that XR and VR require a lot of resources.

C2741.name: virtual reality resource optimization
C2741.definition: The objectives of virtual reality (VR) resource optimization are to minimize resource requirements without compromising the VR experience, that is, to maximize the VR experience.

C2742.name: manpower
C2742.definition: In extended reality (XR) and particularly in virtual reality (VR), resources can include any or all of hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure; in VR these include hardware such as input devices, processing devices, and output devices; software such as development tools, software development kits, software packages, or application packages; manpower such as staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing; and supporting infrastructure such as rooms to store the hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

C2743.definition: In extended reality (XR) and particularly in virtual reality (VR), resources can include any or all of hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure; in VR these include hardware such as input devices, processing devices, and output devices; software such as development tools, software development kits, software packages, or application packages; manpower such as staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing; and supporting infrastructure such as rooms to store the hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers.
