C2751.definition: In extended reality (XR) and particularly in virtual reality (VR), resources can include any or all of hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure; in VR these include hardware such as input devices, processing devices, and output devices; software such as development tools, software development kits, software packages, or application packages; manpower such as staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing; and supporting infrastructure such as rooms to store the hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

C2752.name: server
C2752.definition: In extended reality (XR) and particularly in virtual reality (VR), resources can include any or all of hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure; in VR these include hardware such as input devices, processing devices, and output devices; software such as development tools, software development kits, software packages, or application packages; manpower such as staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing; and supporting infrastructure such as rooms to store the hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

C2753.name: resource type
C2753.definition: Each resource type in extended reality (XR) can be optimized separately, but such optimization is not easy because the considerations vary widely and include money such as availability of funds and how resources are managed, availability of the resources before use, policy issues, and geopolitical issues.

C2754.name: client end
C2754.definition: Virtual reality (VR) resource optimization generally does not try to optimize every resource, assumes some resources are given, and instead focuses on hardware requirements at the client end (the user end), because focusing on client-end hardware is the most straightforward way to optimize resources without being entangled in many issues; the objective is for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.

C2755.name: hardware requirement
C2755.definition: Virtual reality (VR) resource optimization generally does not try to optimize every resource, assumes some resources are given, and instead focuses on hardware requirements at the client end (the user end), because focusing on client-end hardware is the most straightforward way to optimize resources without being entangled in many issues; the objective is for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.

C2756.name: client-end hardware
C2756.definition: For a good virtual reality (VR) immersive experience, client-end hardware is needed to support requirements arising from rendering or computer graphics and to manage rendering or computer graphics related issues, and the complexity required to render a scene corresponds to the need for high-end hardware support.

C2757.name: interface object
C2757.definition: The image displayed on a computer screen is the whole interface, that is the content seen on the screen, not only the main object, and it comprises geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.

C2758.name: menu
C2758.definition: The image displayed on a computer screen is the whole interface, that is the content seen on the screen, not only the main object, and it comprises geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.

C2759.name: binary representation
C2759.definition: Computers understand only binary representation, that is zeros and ones, whereas humans perceive realistic representation, not strings of zeros and ones.

C2760.name: representation
C2760.definition: Computers understand only binary representation, that is zeros and ones, whereas humans perceive realistic representation, not strings of zeros and ones.

C2761.name: synthesis
C2761.definition: The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to create or represent objects, synthesize objects into a scene, and render the scene on a computer display so that humans can perceive it.

C2762.name: generic graphics system
C2762.definition: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

C2763.name: host computer
C2763.definition: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

C2764.name: display controller
C2764.definition: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

C2765.name: video memory
C2765.definition: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

C2766.name: video controller
C2766.definition: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

C2767.name: display command
C2767.definition: In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.

C2768.name: interaction data
C2768.definition: In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.

C2769.name: image generation
C2769.definition: The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

C2770.name: analog voltage
C2770.definition: The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

C2771.name: graphic device
C2771.definition: Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices.

C2772.name: vector scan device
C2772.definition: Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices.

C2773.name: geometric primitive
C2773.definition: Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived.

C2774.name: line
C2774.definition: Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived.

C2775.name: curve
C2775.definition: Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived.

C2776.name: precision
C2776.definition: Vector scan devices require high precision to target and excite specific pixels, which makes vector scan devices costly and typically unaffordable for mass production or mass consumption; vector scan devices are therefore typically used in specialized settings where limited quantities are required.

C2777.name: raster scan device
C2777.definition: Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices.

C2778.name: pixel grid
C2778.definition: A display device uses a pixel grid to render an image, and points on that pixel grid can only have integer coordinates.

C2779.name: scanning
C2779.definition: A raster scan device views an image as represented by the whole pixel grid, activates all pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, with appropriate inputs that make the pixels emit light at appropriate intensities, and the sequential activation of all pixels is called scanning or raster scanning.

C2780.name: raster scan rendering
C2780.definition: In raster scan rendering, pixels are excited in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order, so the top-left pixel is excited much earlier than the bottom-right pixel; because the emitted light decays, pixels may fade out of sync and the displayed image may appear non-uniform or distorted.

C2781.name: vector scan rendering
C2781.definition: Raster scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than vector scan rendering.

C2782.name: television
C2782.definition: Commercial products such as smartphones, televisions, and any device with a computer and display typically comprise raster scan displays.

C2783.name: raster scan system
C2783.definition: In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

C2784.name: frame buffer
C2784.definition: In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

C2785.name: memory location
C2785.definition: In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

C2786.name: bit string
C2786.definition: In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

C2787.name: screen resolution
C2787.definition: The size of a frame buffer is the size of the screen and is equal to the screen resolution of a raster scan device.

C2788.name: light-emitting element
C2788.definition: In a raster scan device, the light emitted from excited pixel elements decays over time, causing the rendered scene to fade even when the image is not changing.

C2789.name: screen refreshing
C2789.definition: Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels on a raster scan device, done to avoid fading and distortion and to keep the rendered image uniform even when the image is not changing.

C2790.name: refresh rate
C2790.definition: The refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second on a screen, is represented in hertz, and a good refresh rate for most devices is 60 hertz.

C2791.name: virtual reality screen
C2791.definition: A higher refresh rate is always preferable for a virtual reality (VR) experience because the VR screen is much closer to the eyes than in typical computer usage, where the screen and the eyes are at a reasonable distance.

C2792.name: color display
C2792.definition: In a color display, each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three although sometimes four can be used for different purposes; the typical three elements emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities.

C2793.name: red
C2793.definition: In a color display, each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three although sometimes four can be used for different purposes; the typical three elements emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities.

C2794.name: green
C2794.definition: In a color display, each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three although sometimes four can be used for different purposes; the typical three elements emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities.

C2795.name: blue
C2795.definition: In a color display, each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three although sometimes four can be used for different purposes; the typical three elements emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities.

C2796.name: primary color
C2796.definition: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

C2797.name: three-dimensional computer graphics pipeline
C2797.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) computer graphics pipeline (3D graphics pipeline) is a stage-wise process of computation starting from object representation to rendering on the pixel grid.

C2798.name: object representation
C2798.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

C2799.name: color value
C2799.definition: The color values stored in the frame buffer are computed by the display processor, which is part of the display controller, in distinct stages.

C2800.name: display processor
C2800.definition: The color values stored in the frame buffer are computed by the display processor, which is part of the display controller, in distinct stages.

C2801.name: graphics pipeline
C2801.definition: The graphics pipeline is the set of the distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

C2802.name: display mechanism
C2802.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.

C2803.name: local coordinate system
C2803.definition: The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system.

C2804.name: modeling transformation
C2804.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

C2805.name: world coordinate system
C2805.definition: The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

C2806.name: device coordinate system
C2806.definition: The device coordinate system is equivalent to the screen, but it is not the same as the screen.

C2807.name: viewing pipeline
C2807.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

C2808.name: viewing transformation
C2808.definition: The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

C2809.name: hidden surface removal
C2809.definition: Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

C2810.name: projection transformation
C2810.definition: The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

C2811.name: window-to-viewport transformation
C2811.definition: The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

C2812.name: three-dimensional view coordinate system
C2812.definition: Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

C2813.name: two-dimensional view coordinate system
C2813.definition: Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

C2814.name: scan conversion
C2814.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

C2815.name: screen coordinate system
C2815.definition: The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, scan conversion, transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can take real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer.

C2816.name: three-dimensional object representation
C2816.definition: The fundamental objective of three-dimensional (3D) object representation is to balance the requirement to represent objects of different shapes and sizes with their intricate details so that they render realistically in a synthesized environment, rather than as simplistic geometric approximations that lose realism, and the requirement to make the operations of the subsequent stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline efficient in space and time.

C2817.name: pixel intensity
C2817.definition: In intensity mapping, a lighting model computes a pixel intensity that can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, whereas a display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel on an 8-bit display.

C2818.name: three-dimensional object representation technique
C2818.definition: A single three-dimensional (3D) object representation technique is not sufficient because different object representation techniques are available, and the appropriate technique must be chosen for a particular problem.

C2819.name: point sample rendering
C2819.definition: The broad representation categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation.

C2820.name: boundary representation
C2820.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

C2821.name: space partitioning based representation
C2821.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

C2822.name: mesh representation
C2822.definition: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

C2823.name: parametric representation
C2823.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

C2824.name: implicit representation
C2824.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

C2825.name: octree method
C2825.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

C2826.name: binary space partitioning method
C2826.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

C2827.name: constructive solid geometry method
C2827.definition: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

C2828.name: data point
C2828.definition: Point sample rendering is the simplest broad representation category, in which the captured scene information is represented as a set of raw data points on the scene, with each point carrying that information as attributes.

C2829.name: attribute
C2829.definition: Point sample rendering is the simplest broad representation category, in which the captured scene information is represented as a set of raw data points on the scene, with each point carrying that information as attributes.

C2830.name: three-dimensional range scanner
C2830.definition: In point sample rendering, the scene information is captured from the real world in the form of points using input sensors such as three-dimensional (3D) range scanners, range finders, or computer vision techniques.

C2831.name: range finder
C2831.definition: In point sample rendering, the scene information is captured from the real world in the form of points using input sensors such as three-dimensional (3D) range scanners, range finders, or computer vision techniques.

C2832.name: synthetic image
C2832.definition: In point sample rendering, the captured points are processed or mapped to pixels to generate a synthetic image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.

C2833.name: polygon
C2833.definition: Boundary representation is a broad representation category in which objects are represented by the surfaces that define the object's boundary, and those surfaces can be polygonal or curved.

C2834.name: mesh
C2834.definition: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

C2835.name: vertex list
C2835.definition: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

C2836.name: edge list
C2836.definition: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

C2837.name: polygonal mesh
C2837.definition: In Unity, three-dimensional (3D) meshes are the main graphics primitives, and Unity supports triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal meshes, meaning meshes whose polygons are triangles or quadrangles.

C2838.name: triangle
C2838.definition: Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used.

C2839.name: simple convex polygon
C2839.definition: Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used.

C2840.name: pipeline
C2840.definition: Mesh representation is the most basic form of representation for any object in a rendered scene used in computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to a mesh representation at the end of the pipeline before the objects are rendered.

C2841.name: spline representation
C2841.definition: Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curved surfaces or curves that falls under parametric representation.

C2842.name: curved surface
C2842.definition: Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curved surfaces or curves that falls under parametric representation.

C2843.name: simple polygon
C2843.definition: Spline representation is typically preferred by developers or designers of scenes who want to create an artificial environment, and it is used to construct quality scenes for rendering and to represent complex surfaces with complex properties that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.

C2844.name: polynomial equation
C2844.definition: Spline representation is typically preferred by developers or designers of scenes who want to create an artificial environment, and it is used to construct quality scenes for rendering and to represent complex surfaces with complex properties that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.

C2845.name: polynomial representation
C2845.definition: In polynomial representation of a curve, a more complex curve is represented by a polynomial of higher degree, and computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming.

C2846.name: polynomial
C2846.definition: In polynomial representation of a curve, a more complex curve is represented by a polynomial of higher degree, and computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming.

C2847.name: polynomial piece
C2847.definition: In spline representation, a complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree complex polynomial, and each piece is called a blending function or basis function so that simpler polynomials can compute points on the curve segment represented by that piece.

C2848.name: basis function
C2848.definition: In spline representation, a complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree complex polynomial, and each piece is called a blending function or basis function so that simpler polynomials can compute points on the curve segment represented by that piece.

C2849.name: curve segment
C2849.definition: In spline representation, a complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree complex polynomial, and each piece is called a blending function or basis function so that simpler polynomials can compute points on the curve segment represented by that piece.

C2850.name: third-order polynomial
C2850.definition: Third-order polynomials are the most common form of polynomial used to construct spline curves.

C2851.name: spline curve
C2851.definition: Third-order polynomials are the most common form of polynomial used to construct spline curves.

C2852.name: space partitioning representation
C2852.definition: Space partitioning representation is a broad category of object representation in which the three-dimensional (3D) space occupied by an object is divided into several disjoint, non-overlapping regions, so that any point inside the object lies in exactly one region and the object can be represented by representing the occupied regions.

C2853.name: space partitioning tree
C2853.definition: A space partitioning tree is a hierarchical, tree-like structure that represents the space occupied by an object and is used to create a space partitioning representation.

C2854.name: binary space partitioning
C2854.definition: Space partitioning representations include the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods.

C2855.name: constructive solid geometry
C2855.definition: Space partitioning representations include the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods.

C2856.name: fractal representation
C2856.definition: Fractal representation is a specialized representation method for self-repeating structures, such as a leaf whose individual parts repeat in the larger part.

C2857.name: particle system representation
C2857.definition: Particle system representation is a specialized representation method for objects such as a waterfall that relies on the simulation of physical properties.

C2858.name: skeletal model
C2858.definition: A skeletal model is a specialized representation method for complex characters such as a cat that captures the character's overall appearance and motion behavior, and such models are typically used in animation or computer animation to represent objects or complex characters.

C2859.name: computer animation
C2859.definition: A skeletal model is a specialized representation method for complex characters such as a cat that captures the character's overall appearance and motion behavior, and such models are typically used in animation or computer animation to represent objects or complex characters.

C2860.name: pipeline stage
C2860.definition: In an implementation of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, all pipeline stages are present, the stages are more important than their sequence, and the order of the stages and sub-stages may differ from the stage-wise sequence used to show how the computations occur.

C2861.name: sub-stage
C2861.definition: In an implementation of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, all pipeline stages are present, the stages are more important than their sequence, and the order of the stages and sub-stages may differ from the stage-wise sequence used to show how the computations occur.

C2862.name: intensity calculation
C2862.definition: Object representation in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is called the first stage for simplicity, although there is no computation as such related to intensity calculation or determination of the pixel intensities.

C2863.name: screen coordinate
C2863.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description.

C2864.name: object coordinate system
C2864.definition: Modeling transformation, also called geometric transformation and referred to as stage 2, applies operations to an object's local or object coordinate system description to place the object in a common scene or world coordinate system so that multiple objects can be assembled into a scene.

C2865.name: dimension
C2865.definition: An object's local or object coordinate system description is an individual definition of the object in which its position and dimension are defined in its own coordinate reference frame.

C2866.name: translation
C2866.definition: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

C2867.name: angle
C2867.definition: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

C2868.name: axis
C2868.definition: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

C2869.name: scaling
C2869.definition: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

C2870.name: shearing
C2870.definition: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

C2871.name: matrix
C2871.definition: Each transformation is typically represented by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added, so a two-dimensional (2D) transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional (3D) transformation can be represented by a 4 by 4 matrix.

C2872.name: homogeneous coordinate system
C2872.definition: Each transformation is typically represented by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added, so a two-dimensional (2D) transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional (3D) transformation can be represented by a 4 by 4 matrix.

C2873.name: two-dimensional transformation
C2873.definition: Each transformation is typically represented by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added, so a two-dimensional (2D) transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional (3D) transformation can be represented by a 4 by 4 matrix.

C2874.name: three-dimensional transformation
C2874.definition: Each transformation is typically represented by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added, so a two-dimensional (2D) transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional (3D) transformation can be represented by a 4 by 4 matrix.

C2875.name: translation amount
C2875.definition: Two-dimensional (2D) translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing in the homogeneous coordinate system can be represented by 3 by 3 matrices, using translation amounts Tx and Ty along the x and y directions, the rotation angle phi, scaling factors Sx and Sy along the x and y directions, and shearing factors Sx, Shx, and Shy along the x and y directions.

C2876.name: rotation angle
C2876.definition: Two-dimensional (2D) translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing in the homogeneous coordinate system can be represented by 3 by 3 matrices, using translation amounts Tx and Ty along the x and y directions, the rotation angle phi, scaling factors Sx and Sy along the x and y directions, and shearing factors Sx, Shx, and Shy along the x and y directions.

C2877.name: scaling factor
C2877.definition: Two-dimensional (2D) translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing in the homogeneous coordinate system can be represented by 3 by 3 matrices, using translation amounts Tx and Ty along the x and y directions, the rotation angle phi, scaling factors Sx and Sy along the x and y directions, and shearing factors Sx, Shx, and Shy along the x and y directions.

C2878.name: shearing factor
C2878.definition: Two-dimensional (2D) translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing in the homogeneous coordinate system can be represented by 3 by 3 matrices, using translation amounts Tx and Ty along the x and y directions, the rotation angle phi, scaling factors Sx and Sy along the x and y directions, and shearing factors Sx, Shx, and Shy along the x and y directions.

C2879.name: column vector
C2879.definition: A point (x, y) in an object's local coordinate system can be transformed to the world coordinate system by representing the point as the column vector P, multiplying it by the transformation matrix S to obtain the new point P dash, and thereby performing a matrix multiplication of points on the object's surface into new points that ideally should be in the world coordinate system.

C2880.name: transformation matrix
C2880.definition: A point (x, y) in an object's local coordinate system can be transformed to the world coordinate system by representing the point as the column vector P, multiplying it by the transformation matrix S to obtain the new point P dash, and thereby performing a matrix multiplication of points on the object's surface into new points that ideally should be in the world coordinate system.

C2881.name: matrix multiplication
C2881.definition: A point (x, y) in an object's local coordinate system can be transformed to the world coordinate system by representing the point as the column vector P, multiplying it by the transformation matrix S to obtain the new point P dash, and thereby performing a matrix multiplication of points on the object's surface into new points that ideally should be in the world coordinate system.

C2882.name: composite transformation matrix
C2882.definition: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

C2883.name: world coordinate scene
C2883.definition: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

C2884.name: basic transformation
C2884.definition: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

C2885.name: scaling matrix
C2885.definition: In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).

C2886.name: x-direction scaling factor
C2886.definition: In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).

C2887.name: y-direction scaling factor
C2887.definition: In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).
