C2888.definition: In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).

C2889.name: translation along the x-axis
C2889.definition: In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).

C2890.name: translation along the y-axis
C2890.definition: In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).

C2891.name: order of application
C2891.definition: A composite transformation matrix is formed by arranging the individual transformation matrices from right to left according to the order of application: the first transformation applied is placed rightmost, each subsequent transformation is placed to its left, and the matrices are multiplied.

C2892.name: transformed vertex
C2892.definition: To obtain transformed vertices in the world coordinate scene, each current vertex is multiplied by the transformation matrix; in the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, A′ = M A, B′ = M B, C′ = M C, and D′ = M D, where M is the composite transformation matrix.

C2893.name: computer graphics pipeline
C2893.definition: The Unity platform is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, including object definition, scene construction, lighting effects, view transformation, and scan conversion or rendering, so that a developer can focus on building the immersive experience rather than mastering and implementing the pipeline.

C2894.name: color computation
C2894.definition: In the computer graphics pipeline, the third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene; if a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced, whereas properly assigning colors can give a more realistic perception.

C2895.name: shading model
C2895.definition: In the computer graphics pipeline, the third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene; if a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced, whereas properly assigning colors can give a more realistic perception.

C2896.name: depth
C2896.definition: In the pixel processing stage, hidden surface removal uses a depth buffer algorithm in which a dedicated depth buffer stores the depth information for points in a three-dimensional (3D) scene before projection onto a two-dimensional (2D) plane, where depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel.

C2897.name: continuous intensity value
C2897.definition: Lighting models compute colors in terms of continuous intensity values, which are essentially real numbers, typically within the range 0 to 1 and typically normalized, and these values are mapped to computer-supported discrete values.

C2898.name: discrete value
C2898.definition: Lighting models compute colors in terms of continuous intensity values, which are essentially real numbers, typically within the range 0 to 1 and typically normalized, and these values are mapped to computer-supported discrete values.

C2899.name: surface point
C2899.definition: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.

C2900.name: reflected light
C2900.definition: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.

C2901.name: simple lighting model
C2901.definition: In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec).

C2902.name: ambient light intensity
C2902.definition: In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec).

C2903.name: diffuse reflection intensity
C2903.definition: In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec).

C2904.name: specular reflection intensity
C2904.definition: In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec).

C2905.name: direct light
C2905.definition: In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec).

C2906.name: ambient light component
C2906.definition: In the simple lighting model, the ambient light component is light that falls on a surface after being reflected from surrounding surfaces.

C2907.name: diffuse light component
C2907.definition: In the simple lighting model, the diffuse light component is light that comes directly from a light source and is reflected in a diffuse manner from the surface.

C2908.name: specular reflection component
C2908.definition: In the simple lighting model, the specular reflection component is light that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot.

C2909.name: reflected light intensity
C2909.definition: The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity.

C2910.name: incident light intensity
C2910.definition: The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity.

C2911.name: reflection coefficient
C2911.definition: The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity.

C2912.name: diffuse reflection
C2912.definition: The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.

C2913.name: specular reflection
C2913.definition: The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.

C2914.name: ambient reflection coefficient
C2914.definition: The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.

C2915.name: diffuse reflection coefficient
C2915.definition: The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.

C2916.name: specular reflection coefficient
C2916.definition: The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.

C2917.name: ambient component
C2917.definition: The ambient component of the reflected light intensity is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by the reflection coefficient for ambient light Ka.

C2918.name: diffuse reflection component
C2918.definition: The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection.

C2919.name: source light intensity
C2919.definition: The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection.

C2920.name: dot product
C2920.definition: The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection.

C2921.name: surface normal vector
C2921.definition: The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection.

C2922.name: light source direction vector
C2922.definition: The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection.

C2923.name: specular component
C2923.definition: The specular component is computed using an approximate model named after its inventor, Phong.

C2924.name: Phong model
C2924.definition: The specular component is computed using an approximate model named after its inventor, Phong.

C2925.name: specular angle
C2925.definition: The angle phi in the specular calculation is the angle between the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, which is the direction a mirror would reflect the light, and cos phi is the dot product V dot r.

C2926.name: viewer direction vector
C2926.definition: The angle phi in the specular calculation is the angle between the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, which is the direction a mirror would reflect the light, and cos phi is the dot product V dot r.

C2927.name: ideal specular reflection direction vector
C2927.definition: The angle phi in the specular calculation is the angle between the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, which is the direction a mirror would reflect the light, and cos phi is the dot product V dot r.

C2928.name: light intensity
C2928.definition: In lighting, the intensity of light from a source typically diminishes with the distance from the source to a surface point, so an intensity attenuation factor over distance is needed.

C2929.name: radial intensity attenuation factor
C2929.definition: In lighting, the intensity of light from a source typically diminishes with the distance from the source to a surface point, so an intensity attenuation factor over distance is needed.

C2930.name: inverse quadratic function
C2930.definition: The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of the distance d between the light source and the surface point, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2 that can be varied for a more realistic effect.

C2931.name: coefficient
C2931.definition: The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of the distance d between the light source and the surface point, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2 that can be varied for a more realistic effect.

C2932.name: angular intensity attenuation
C2932.definition: Angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for generating spotlight effects, in which elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.

C2933.name: spotlight effect
C2933.definition: Angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for generating spotlight effects, in which elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.

C2934.name: spotlight region
C2934.definition: Angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for generating spotlight effects, in which elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.

C2935.name: angular intensity attenuation factor
C2935.definition: A commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor is 0 when the surface point is outside the angular limit theta, the range of the spotlight cone, and when the surface point is within that angular limit it varies as the cosine of phi raised to the power A1, where A1 is a positive angular attenuation exponent that can be varied to achieve different effects.

C2936.name: angular limit
C2936.definition: A commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor is 0 when the surface point is outside the angular limit theta, the range of the spotlight cone, and when the surface point is within that angular limit it varies as the cosine of phi raised to the power A1, where A1 is a positive angular attenuation exponent that can be varied to achieve different effects.

C2937.name: angular attenuation exponent
C2937.definition: A commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor is 0 when the surface point is outside the angular limit theta, the range of the spotlight cone, and when the surface point is within that angular limit it varies as the cosine of phi raised to the power A1, where A1 is a positive angular attenuation exponent that can be varied to achieve different effects.

C2938.name: intensity component
C2938.definition: In the simple lighting model modified for radial and angular intensity attenuation, the I_M intensity component is left unchanged, while the sum of the diffuse reflection component I_D and the specular reflection component I_SPEC is multiplied by the radial and angular attenuation factors; if those factors are 1, the model reduces to I_M + I_D + I_SPEC.

C2939.name: colored light source model
C2939.definition: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

C2940.name: source intensity
C2940.definition: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

C2941.name: vector
C2941.definition: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

C2942.name: red component
C2942.definition: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

C2943.name: green component
C2943.definition: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

C2944.name: blue component
C2944.definition: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

C2945.name: single-light-source lighting model
C2945.definition: For n light sources, the single-light-source lighting model is revised to I_P = I_ambient plus the summation from i = 1 to n of the contribution from each light source, with each contribution calculated separately and added together, and for colored light sources each contribution is computed separately for the red, green, and blue components.

C2946.name: colored light source
C2946.definition: For n light sources, the single-light-source lighting model is revised to I_P = I_ambient plus the summation from i = 1 to n of the contribution from each light source, with each contribution calculated separately and added together, and for colored light sources each contribution is computed separately for the red, green, and blue components.

C2947.name: intensity mapping
C2947.definition: In intensity mapping, a lighting model computes a pixel intensity that can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, whereas a display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel on an 8-bit display.

C2948.name: 8-bit display
C2948.definition: In intensity mapping, a lighting model computes a pixel intensity that can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, whereas a display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel on an 8-bit display.

C2949.name: intensity value
C2949.definition: In intensity mapping, a lighting model computes a pixel intensity that can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, whereas a display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel on an 8-bit display.

C2950.name: device-supported intensity value
C2950.definition: The determination of device-supported intensity values uses the number n of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value I0 measured with a photometer, and the known maximum intensity value 1.

C2951.name: intensity level
C2951.definition: The determination of device-supported intensity values uses the number n of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value I0 measured with a photometer, and the known maximum intensity value 1.

C2952.name: minimum device-supported intensity value
C2952.definition: The determination of device-supported intensity values uses the number n of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value I0 measured with a photometer, and the known maximum intensity value 1.

C2953.name: photometer
C2953.definition: The determination of device-supported intensity values uses the number n of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value I0 measured with a photometer, and the known maximum intensity value 1.

C2954.name: maximum intensity value
C2954.definition: The determination of device-supported intensity values uses the number n of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value I0 measured with a photometer, and the known maximum intensity value 1.

C2955.name: multiplicative factor
C2955.definition: The successive device-supported intensity values are represented by I1 = r I0, I2 = r^2 I0, I3 = r^3 I0, and so on up to In = r^n I0, where the factor r is computed using the relation In = r^n I0.

C2956.name: psychophysiological property
C2956.definition: The use of a multiplicative factor r in the successive device-supported intensity levels is based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative changes between two intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity values.

C2957.name: relative change
C2957.definition: The use of a multiplicative factor r in the successive device-supported intensity levels is based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative changes between two intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity values.

C2958.name: absolute change
C2958.definition: The use of a multiplicative factor r in the successive device-supported intensity levels is based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative changes between two intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity values.

C2959.name: table
C2959.definition: A table stores the calculated device-supported intensity values and their assigned bit patterns, and a lighting-model pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity so that the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.

C2960.name: bit pattern
C2960.definition: A table stores the calculated device-supported intensity values and their assigned bit patterns, and a lighting-model pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity so that the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.

C2961.name: two-dimensional display
C2961.definition: The basic idea of view transformation, which is the viewing pipeline, is that an image on a screen or head-mounted display (HMD) is produced by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional (3D) scene and projecting the portion onto a two-dimensional (2D) display or view plane.

C2962.name: view coordinate system
C2962.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

C2963.name: three-dimensional world coordinate system
C2963.definition: The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

C2964.name: two-dimensional view plane
C2964.definition: The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

C2965.name: two-dimensional device coordinate space
C2965.definition: The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

C2966.name: three-dimensional viewing transformation
C2966.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

C2967.name: world coordinates
C2967.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

C2968.name: view coordinates
C2968.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

C2969.name: camera viewing mechanism
C2969.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

C2970.name: camera parameters
C2970.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

C2971.name: origin vector
C2971.definition: The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

C2972.name: view-up point
C2972.definition: The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

C2973.name: center of interest
C2973.definition: The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

C2974.name: unit basis vector
C2974.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

C2975.name: looking direction
C2975.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

C2976.name: view-up direction
C2976.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

C2977.name: origin point
C2977.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

C2978.name: cross product
C2978.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

C2979.name: view-coordinate axis vector
C2979.definition: Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components.

C2980.name: scalar component
C2980.definition: Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components.

C2981.name: view volume
C2981.definition: A view volume is a three-dimensional (3D) region in the scene that defines the portion of the scene that is projected onto the view plane, so objects inside the view volume are projected and objects outside it are discarded.

C2982.name: perspective projection
C2982.definition: Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated.

C2983.name: center of projection
C2983.definition: Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated.

C2984.name: parallel projection
C2984.definition: Parallel projection is a projection type in which the projectors from the object to the view plane are parallel to each other, so their center of projection or point of projection is at infinity and they never meet.

C2985.name: frustum
C2985.definition: For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region, and for perspective projection, the view volume is a frustum, with one face or side of the view volume serving as the clipping window on which objects inside the view volume are projected.

C2986.name: naive clipping method
C2986.definition: The naive clipping method computes the intersection of view volume boundaries with object boundaries, and this calculation is computationally intensive for arbitrarily shaped view volumes such as frustums.

C2987.name: canonical view volume
C2987.definition: A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted in order to simplify pipeline computations.

C2988.name: unit cube
C2988.definition: A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted in order to simplify pipeline computations.

C2989.name: point vector
C2989.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

C2990.name: parallel projection matrix
C2990.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

C2991.name: origin
C2991.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

C2992.name: homogeneous coordinate value
C2992.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

C2993.name: homogeneous factor
C2993.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

C2994.name: cartesian coordinate
C2994.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

C2995.name: perspective projection matrix
C2995.definition: A perspective projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a perspective projection matrix that is more complex than the parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance from the clipping window to the center of projection, which is typically assumed to be at the origin but not always; the obtained homogeneous coordinate values are then divided by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates.

C2996.name: viewport
C2996.definition: A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions.

C2997.name: device space
C2997.definition: A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions.

C2998.name: window point
C2998.definition: The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).

C2999.name: viewport point
C2999.definition: The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).

C3000.name: window-to-viewport transformation matrix
C3000.definition: In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.

C3001.name: homogeneous coordinate representation
C3001.definition: To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

C3002.name: cartesian point
C3002.definition: To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

C3003.name: computational complexity
C3003.definition: Clipping defines a view volume, discards objects or portions of objects outside that view volume, and is performed before projection so that projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced.

C3004.name: viewer position
C3004.definition: Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

C3005.name: occlusion
C3005.definition: Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

C3006.name: geometric transformation
C3006.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline has five stages, and the first four stages are object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling or geometric transformation from the local coordinate system to the world coordinate system; lighting in the world coordinate system; and viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

C3007.name: view pipeline
C3007.definition: In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, after the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

C3008.name: continuous coordinate system
C3008.definition: The device coordinate system used to define the two-dimensional (2D) viewport is a continuous coordinate system, so its coordinate values can be any real number.

C3009.name: mapping algorithm
C3009.definition: Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is, after the earlier four stages, the fifth stage in which mapping algorithms transform continuous two-dimensional (2D) viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

C3010.name: viewport coordinates
C3010.definition: The device coordinate system used to define the two-dimensional (2D) viewport is a continuous coordinate system, so its coordinate values can be any real number.

C3011.name: pixel-grid coordinate system
C3011.definition: Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is, after the earlier four stages, the fifth stage in which mapping algorithms transform continuous two-dimensional (2D) viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

C3012.name: point rendering
C3012.definition: In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles.

C3013.name: real-number coordinate
C3013.definition: In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles.

C3014.name: integer coordinate value
C3014.definition: In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles.

C3015.name: discrete space
C3015.definition: In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles.

C3016.name: rounding
C3016.definition: In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles.

C3017.name: circle
C3017.definition: In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles.

C3018.name: line rendering
C3018.definition: A naive line-rendering method requires many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, the objective of efficient line-rendering algorithms is to avoid floating-point operations.

C3019.name: floating-point operation
C3019.definition: A naive line-rendering method requires many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, the objective of efficient line-rendering algorithms is to avoid floating-point operations.

C3020.name: line-rendering algorithm
C3020.definition: A naive line-rendering method requires many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, the objective of efficient line-rendering algorithms is to avoid floating-point operations.

C3021.name: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm
C3021.definition: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a popular line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line without using floating-point operations.

C3022.name: line slope
C3022.definition: The Bresenham line-drawing algorithm is described for line slopes between -1 and +1, with minor modification needed for other slopes; its input is the two line endpoints and its output is the set of pixels that approximate the line segment.

C3023.name: line endpoint
C3023.definition: The Bresenham line-drawing algorithm is described for line slopes between -1 and +1, with minor modification needed for other slopes; its input is the two line endpoints and its output is the set of pixels that approximate the line segment.

C3024.name: line segment
C3024.definition: The Bresenham line-drawing algorithm is described for line slopes between -1 and +1, with minor modification needed for other slopes; its input is the two line endpoints and its output is the set of pixels that approximate the line segment.

C3025.name: x coordinate
C3025.definition: In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.

C3026.name: y coordinate
C3026.definition: In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.

C3027.name: delta x
C3027.definition: In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.

C3028.name: delta y
C3028.definition: In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.

C3029.name: decision parameter
C3029.definition: In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.

C3030.name: integer arithmetic
C3030.definition: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication.

C3031.name: division
C3031.definition: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication.

C3032.name: floating-point multiplication
C3032.definition: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication.

C3033.name: interactive graphics
C3033.definition: Speeding up line rendering makes the system more efficient because at any instant a system may need to render a large number of line segments, and in interactive graphics such as virtual reality each user input can change the scene and require redrawing hundreds of thousands of lines.

C3034.name: ellipse
C3034.definition: Similar efficient rendering algorithms exist for other geometric shapes, such as circles, ellipses, filled areas, and polygons, and they are more complex than line rendering.

C3035.name: filled area
C3035.definition: Similar efficient rendering algorithms exist for other geometric shapes, such as circles, ellipses, filled areas, and polygons, and they are more complex than line rendering.

C3036.name: distortion
C3036.definition: Aliasing is distortion that may occur in an original shape after scan conversion because scan conversion renders pixels that are close to points on the original shape rather than exactly rendering the points, so an approximated line may not exactly match the original line.

C3037.name: anti-aliasing
C3037.definition: Anti-aliasing operations are additional operations, using complex algorithms, that remove or reduce the distortion caused by aliasing so that the end effect is better.

C3038.name: rendering stage
C3038.definition: Anti-aliasing is essential and adds further computation to the overall computation of pixel intensities along with the other rendering stages.

C3039.name: dynamic scene
C3039.definition: In virtual reality (VR), a realistic experience with rich realistic content, a dynamic scene that changes with user input, a high degree of interaction, motion achieved through animation or video, and the fact that a simple lighting model may not be a good option increase the computational complexity of rendering manifold.

C3040.name: lag
C3040.definition: The challenge in virtual reality (VR) rendering is to handle a computationally complex rendering process without the user perceiving lag or distortion.

C3041.name: graphics library
C3041.definition: A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements.

C3042.name: argument
C3042.definition: The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries are predefined sets of functions that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks.

C3043.name: graphics application

C3373.name: unity player settings
C3373.definition: For this sample project, the Unity player settings are configured under Edit > Project Settings > Player > Other by removing Vulkan and adding the Open Graphics Library (OpenGL) application programming interface (API), unchecking AutoGraphics API, unchecking Advanced RISC Machines (ARM) version 7, checking ARM 64, using the IL2CPP scripting backend, and ensuring the minimum API level is greater than 7; these settings are application-specific and may not work for other projects or platforms.

C3377.name: universal serial bus
C3377.definition: For the Android platform, the build is created by following File > Build Settings > Android > Switch Platform, connecting the Android device through a universal serial bus (USB) cable with USB debugging enabled, and selecting Build and Run, which creates an Android package (APK) file and deploys it directly to the device; alternatively, the Android package (APK) file can be developed first and then transferred and installed separately.
